Mother Rosa Gattorno.

THE SPIRITUAL PROFILE OF ROSA GATTORNO.

Foundress of the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Rome: Generalate

Daughters of Saint Anne 1989.

Ecclesiastical approval of the Vicariate of Rome, 1-12-1989

In response to the wish of Mother A. Virginia Sinagra, superior general of the Daughters of Saint Anne, I accepted the welcome task of studying the personality of Mother Rosa Gattorno, one of the most successful foundresses among the many the Church had in the second half of the nineteenth century. I must confess, however, that when I found myself faced with the mass of the Servant of God's writings, the problems raised around her Cause of Canonization and the complexity of the manifestations of her spirituality, in certain respects truly disconcerting, I was somewhat perplexed.

As I went further into an analytical reading of the rich testimony about herself that she left in her Memoirs and in her book Trials and Consolations, however, I saw her spiritual and apostolic stature grow.

This image then presented itself to me in its full evangelical dimension when I compared the results of my study with the hundreds of index cards drawn from the Foundress's letters, thanks to the diligence of the sisters who assisted, under the direction of Sister A. Roberta Frati, head of the Institute's Historical Archive.

If our only source of information were the external testimony of the witnesses heard in the various ordinary processes, everything would have been straightforward; for the fortunate foundress, as her contemporaries saw her, especially her spiritual daughters and the various figures who had close dealings with her, appears as a soul of high union with God, of intrepid faith, full of charity and sacrifice, goodness and humility, extremely penitential, adorned with charismatic gifts of every kind. But it was precisely the image of herself that she drew in her writings, specifically in the book Trials and Consolations, that gave rise to the Holy Office's Dilata when, in 1932, the Congregation of Rites asked for the nihil obstat to introduce the Cause.

In 1979 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (formerly the Holy Office) granted the nihil obstat, but asked that "the state of normality or otherwise" of the Servant of God be studied. The Congregation for the Causes of Saints then judged a medical and psychiatric assessment to be necessary.

Fr. Paolino Zavarella, a doctor of medicine, with his most carefully weighed and exhaustive "opinion," dispelled once and for all every shadow of uncertainty: Rosa Gattorno was a woman who was not only fully normal from a psychological point of view, but endowed with remarkable intellectual and volitional balance, as well as an extraordinary practical sense, enterprising initiative and ease in human relationships; qualities which, raised and enriched by supernatural gifts, won her the esteem and veneration of prominent civil and ecclesiastical figures (1). Normality, however, does not mean mediocrity; Rosa Gattorno was no ordinary woman, and her spiritual stature could not be contained within the usual banks.

Even in her lifetime she had to undergo examinations of the authenticity of her spirit. Among the priests with whom she tried in vain to find suitable guidance, there were indeed some skeptics who wanted to see clearly into a case that fell outside the ordinary ascetical frameworks.

She herself writes on July 21, 1887:

"By order of my direction, I had to submit to an examination of my spirit by a priest of holy life. After examining it well - which he did in a moment - he said and wrote this: that in me one must not look at the creature, but only at the work of the Creator. I remained as though he had well understood that it was and always is the most skilled Craftsman who works in me and through me, and that, looking at the creature, there is nothing but misery and nothingness" (M 5.5, p. 57).

Leaving aside the Servant of God's own interpretation, inspired by humility, we can say that the good religious's verdict still holds for an objective judgment on the case of Rosa Gattorno. We might, for example, question the supernatural character of many of her visions, of her prophetic predictions, of her insight into the inner life of others; we might not accept her inhuman torturing of her body...; but one thing is beyond doubt: the work of the Creator. This action of the "supreme Good," as she likes to call him, is evident both in the Servant of God's mystical experience and in her direction, as foundress, of what she invariably calls the "Work of the Lord."

Four centuries ago Saint John of the Cross established the relationship between God's action, even infused action, and the conditioning it meets in the subject who receives it: God moves things, and people, "according to the mode of being of each" (2). The invasion of the divine takes the most varied and surprising forms, not only according to the plan God has for the subject he has chosen for a particular mission, but also because of the different ways in which the same free gifts are received and bear fruit in different human lives; it is almost a mystery of incarnation, in which God, even at the summit of transforming union, respects the person, without dehumanizing or de-individualizing her.

The conditions that determine, to a greater or lesser degree, the manifestations of divine action are related to sex, age, psychosomatic constitution, culture and education, environment and external influences, and pathological components (3).

In mystical experience it is not easy to draw a dividing line between what proceeds freely from God and what is the product of the human subject's activity, not least because one cannot speak of two parallel or superimposed zones. The subject who opens to the gift is always one and indivisible with the subject who passively receives it, assimilates it and translates it into attitudes of quiet contemplation, of loving transports or swoons, of self-giving in the exercise of charity.

The individual's peculiarities play an even more decisive part in the secondary elements of infused experience, such as raptures, visions and revelations, and in accessory phenomena of a psychosomatic nature, when the intensity of inner absorption upsets the normal patterns of psychological and even physiological activity. As a rule there is no direct supernatural intervention in this bodily projection of what God works in the spirit. Regarding, for example, the bodily repercussions of ecstatic union, Saint John of the Cross himself specifies that it is an "imperfection"; rapture is in fact due to the insufficient adaptability of the faculties and senses to the invasion of the divine (4).

Let us now try to outline, as far as the data allow, the human components of Rosa Gattorno's personality.

1. Family and social background.

Rosa was born on October 14, 1831, into a Genoese family of good social standing and deep Christian sentiments. She was the second of six children, three boys and three girls, to whom must be added the half-sister her mother had from her first marriage.

Her father, Francesco Gattorno, was engaged in commerce. He seems to have had a very positive influence on his daughter's human formation, above all in that her filial relationship with him predisposed her to a special relationship with God the Father; in one of her writings Mother Rosa mentions the security one draws from a father's affection, "which can never deceive." We may also attribute to her father's influence the administrative ability she would later show.

Her father's correspondence reveals a relationship of great trust and affection.

For her religious and moral orientation Rosa was indebted from childhood to the attentive care of her mother, Adelaide Campanella, a woman of notable piety and sensitive character. Mother and daughter were completely in tune.

Rosa lived through, at close quarters, the political and ideological turmoil that shook Italian society, and Genoese society in particular, in the years of her childhood and youth. A maternal uncle, Federico Campanella, was a member of the Ligurian committee of Young Italy. In 1833 he had to take refuge in the Gattorno home to escape arrest; exiled to France, he returned in 1848 and succeeded in winning Rosa's brother, Federico Gattorno, to his Masonic and republican ideas and his anticlericalism.

It was a hard blow for our young woman, and it helped strengthen her attachment to the Church and the Pope. Federico's clearly antireligious stance would be a thorn in her heart all her life, as appears in a letter of May 13, 1897, to Princess Emilia di Fitalia. Yet despite his ideological positions he had a true veneration for his sister, whom he considered a "saint"; he would proclaim her so publicly in parliament in 1907 (FIOCCHI, I, p. 2). Both he and his brother Francesco, who testified in the informative process of Genoa, remembered Rosa as an angel of peace and goodness in the family (cf. Summ., p. 1002).

At the age of 21 Rosa married, more by her parents' will than by her own inclination according to many of the testimonies, Gerolamo Custo, likewise a merchant trading internationally. Life as wife and mother would become for her a source of great sacrifices and a school of heroic virtue. The first trial was her husband's financial failure in his business in Marseilles; reduced to poverty, they were taken in at the home of Rosa's father.

The second trial: their firstborn, Carlotta, became deaf and mute as a result of an illness in early childhood. Three years later Alessandro was born. In 1857 her husband left for Russia on a commercial venture that went well, but he had to return ill with tuberculosis. In December of that year their third child, Francesco, was born.

A faithful and loving wife, Rosa stayed in those months at the bedside of her husband, who was slowly fading, until he died on March 9, 1858. Besides conjugal affection, there was also a harmony of spirit between them: during his illness they held spiritual conversations, as they had been accustomed to do earlier, when Gerolamo was in good health.

To the grief of losing her husband and the orphanhood of her three children was added, already at the funeral, a dispute between the two families. Rosa saw all their goods seized, even the furniture of her home, and once again she was taken in with her children at her father's house.

Three months later the youngest, Francesco, died, leaving her inconsolable.

Her own grief and privations helped her open her heart to the sufferings and needs of others, and to discover the meaning of suffering in the embrace of her Crucified.

2. Education and intellectual gifts.

At that time families of the Gattornos' social standing sent their sons to public schools, while for their daughters' education they brought teachers of Italian letters, French, drawing and music into the home. Rosa acquired particular skill in embroidery, as well as in singing and the piano; she was invited to sing and play at family celebrations (FIOCCHI, I, p. 7, 17). She must have improved her rudimentary French during her brief stay with her husband in Marseilles; later, her command of that language would be useful on her journeys to France as foundress (M 9.5, p. 1-30).

Judging from her writings, Rosa Gattorno's literary culture cannot be said to have exceeded the average level: she writes with many spelling mistakes, neglects punctuation, and frequently uses dialect expressions and endings. But she has a surprising fluency in writing, which allows her to write for many hours a day without a break. She also has the gift of varying her style according to the content and purpose of what she writes. In her Letters she adopts a lively, incisive, vigorous language, full of sincerity and immediacy, not without a certain causticity, yet always cordial and affectionate, and varying with the addressee. In the Memoirs, written out of an inner need to express what she experiences and lives in secret, with no addressee in mind but her supreme Good, feelings count more than ideas; she quickly writes down what she feels or remembers at the moment, inserts exclamations, and pays no attention to sentence structure. In her book Trials and Consolations, on the other hand, which she knew would be printed and circulated, her exceptional intelligence suggested to her, for understandable reasons, an entirely different style: a succession of allegorical scenes, ingenious and wholly original, with a surprising variety of images and richness of vocabulary; it is hard to identify the author of the book with the author of the Memoirs.

Yet it is precisely this unique facility for allegory that gives us the key to interpreting what, as we shall see, is a constant of her inner experience: the uninterrupted sequence of her visions and representations of the demonic. Rosa Gattorno's culture is typically a culture of the symbol, to which the language of mystics in general refers, because of their need to go beyond the limits of human expression by symbolizing concepts that are experienced rather than mentally worked out (5).

As for the Servant of God's religious culture, one certainly cannot speak of a theological formation beyond what she received in catechesis and through preaching and reading. In her writings we find frequent quotations from Sacred Scripture, made from memory and often imprecisely; at times she introduces texts from the Psalms or Saint Paul with the phrase "the holy Gospel says." She likes to cite examples from the lives of the Saints; in a conference to the sisters she explained this hagiographical learning of hers: "I know these things from having read them in books, and not by any other way" (6).

The two censors of her writings pointed out certain terminological inaccuracies, as when she repeatedly uses the expression apostatic union - instead of hypostatic - to indicate the experience of a very lofty union with God, a meaning very different from the one it has in theology (cf. M 1.2, p. 122f; 12.1, p. 26).

Among the difficulties she had to face in her mission as foundress, her lack of education was not the least frequent. In the book Trials and Consolations we find an echo of this opinion, common inside and outside the Institute, in a very lively page worth reproducing:

"One of them - one of the commanders of the great ships - approaches and wants to know how the matter had gone, and that I should take good care not to do this or that any more. I turned and said to him:

- I beg you to leave me alone! Your argument is not very logical: in the Work of the Lord philosophy and calculation have no place; they are all empty chairs.

- What kind of reasoning is this? - he said to me.

- Poor slave that I am, I never studied and understand nothing. One thing alone have I tried to study and to perfect myself in that subject: the will of God, trying to do it blindly in perfect abandonment to him, like a faithful slave to her beloved Master.

He looks at me, and then, with a gesture of contempt:

- She's a fanatic! She has little judgment. Let it go!

And he addressed words to my workers to win them over; but they answered him imperiously that he had nothing to do with them.

In what he said about me he had hit the mark exactly, namely that I am a foolish woman who knows nothing, truly uneducated in the sciences.

  • "And that is why Jesus took you to work on you in his own way, so that no one can say this work is man's, but only cooperated by divine wisdom" - so the voice said to me" (TC, p. 219f).

    • It would not be hard to identify the historical moment and the person alluded to. But what matters is the Servant of God's humble assurance: her knowledge, her true specialization, is the will of God. We must add that this clarity of vision, where God's interests were concerned, was the fruit of that super scientia of which Saint Paul speaks (1 Cor 2:2; Eph 3:19; Col 2:3; Phil 3:8), which comes from divine Wisdom and is communicated through the infused light of contemplation.

    3. Character and temperament.

    The data from which we must outline Mother Rosa's traits of character, both autobiographical and drawn from testimonies, belong for the most part to the period of her consecrated life; so it is not easy to distinguish what reveals her natural way of being from what is instead the fruit of a journey of purification, of overcoming her faults and of progress in virtue. In any case these are always components of her personality, placed at the service of that great love which is the driving force of her whole existence.

    A strong and courageous spirit.

    A woman of character: so she is described by those who knew her. The Benedictine Dom Domenico Serafini, who for two years during Mother Rosa's lifetime had been apostolic visitor of the Daughters of Saint Anne, describes her as "a woman of piety, of no ordinary mind and of great energy" (7).

    At the critical moments of her life she showed herself self-possessed, decisive and courageous: for example, in family troubles, as wife and as widow; in the choice of leaving her children and parents to consecrate herself to the interests of God; and in the attitude she took towards the people and situations, some of them harsh and humiliating, that she had to face as foundress.

    Ill from the beginning of her widowhood, weakened by fasts, vigils and other penances, subject moreover to the pain of hidden stigmata and to the burning of her heart, which caused her frequent fainting spells, she worked tirelessly in her office, undertook long and tiring journeys, visited the houses of the Institute listening to all the sisters, dealt with prelates and benefactors...; and she managed to master her own weakness and fatigue, so as to seem, as they say, always in good form.

    And she knew how to instill courage in her collaborators, the superiors, the individual sisters and the others who confided in her. There is hardly a letter of hers in which the word Courage! does not appear. Here are some of the words of encouragement we find in her letters to the sisters, amid vibrant expressions of affection:

    "My dear child, come now, courage!" - "Be of good heart, for heaven is on your side!" - "Courage, my dear! Let us work, for afterwards we shall rest in bliss. Stand firm, do not be afraid!" - "Patience, my dear, courage!... courage!" - "My beloved ones, courage, for one day you will see your God and enjoy the fruit of your labors" - "Courage, and complete trust in the good God!" - "Courage, for in the time of trial one needs courage and patience, peace and resignation. With these everything is obtained and every obstacle overcome" - "Courage! If the road is closed on every side, we must go forward by dint of sweating blood, as long as we have a drop of it in our veins!" - "First commend yourself to God, and then forward with courage!" - "Courage, my daughter! for one day we shall taste the fruit of the blood we have shed and of the sweat of our labors!" - "Courage, forward! for one day we shall be at rest for an eternity!"

    What we might call this pedagogy of courage appears especially in her correspondence with Princess di Fitalia, her spiritual daughter, who was sorely tried by aridity and other sufferings. She tells her again and again:

    "Courage, for in time of trial much is gained!" - "Oh! I may well call you gracious and strong, resolute of spirit, a noble warrior, always victorious in your undertakings" - "Courage in your undertaking! The work you are doing is pleasing to God..., courage!" - "Courage, never be dismayed; Jesus is with you, who can be against you?" - "Courage; let us press upon the Heart of Jesus, he will console us" (L 26-6-1885, 15-1-1886, 20-7-1893, 2-9-1893, 2-11-1893, 27-2-1895).

    In the catalogue of virtues there is one linked to fortitude, a virtue and a gift of the Holy Spirit, which goes by the name of magnanimity and also of daring: it helps overcome faintheartedness before obstacles to be surmounted. In a note to Mons. Granito di Belmonte Mother Rosa wrote:

    "A hurried line to give you good news: I have signed the contract for the schools (in Naples), and they are already at work. Long live daring! What do you say? It is not daring, but only trust in my God" (L 22-9-1896).

    Here is the secret of that strength of character which aroused admiration: Mother Rosa was a woman of faith; she was sure that in her weaknesses she could always count on God's strength: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13). And she was convinced she had God on her side, since the Institute she had founded was the Work of the Lord; hence Saint Paul's well-known text crops up now and then in her writings: If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

    Serenity and balance.

    Measured in her words, affable and gentle with everyone, with the unshakable peace of her spirit showing in her eyes: so her contemporaries saw her, according to the testimonies of the informative processes.

    When Princess di Fitalia was introduced to Gattorno for the first time, she had "a great impression of majesty, like a queen of extraordinary austerity and great gentleness at the same time" (Summ, p. 602).

    But what no one guessed was the price of such an achievement in a temperament as strong and passionate as hers. This is how she saw herself in February 1879, weighed down by a heavy sorrow caused by a sister:

    "Having to do violence to myself, so that no one would notice my agonizing pain, I feel, as I see it appears, that I have changed character. I do not notice it, but they tell me so. And yet my God gave me an indescribable strength because, while I was reading or receiving reports of what was told me, which was agonizing to the point that I felt my whole inner self as if writhing from the violence, because at that moment I had to appear indifferent so that all who came near me would not notice my state..." (M 4.5, p. 84).

    Such equanimity was, moreover, the effect of a peaceful conscience before God; one who acts uprightly fears nothing. She wrote to Mons. Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte in 1898, after receiving news of the apostolic visitation that was to sadden the last two years of her life: "I am perfectly calm and content: this way they will see everything better. When there are no subterfuges, there is nothing to fear" (L 2-9-1898).

    The same prelate, who knew her intimately, testified in the Process when he was a cardinal:

    "In temperament, the Servant of God, as I knew her, was neither lively nor phlegmatic, but calm, with that calm which goes with resolution and firmness. This firmness was constantly put to the test through the many difficulties of her life, but these made that virtue of hers shine all the more..." (Summ. p. 38).

    She tried to form the sisters in self-control and serenity of spirit; she suffered deeply when she was told that some superior scolded the sisters intemperately. She urged Sister A. Adelaide Pezzoni:

    "Try always to appear in the same mood...; always to keep that bearing and composure, joined with meekness and charity, which are the true portrait of the Daughters of Saint Anne" (L 1871, 8-1-1872).

    And to Sister A. Francesca Camisa:

    "Do everything calmly... I recommend meekness to you, for this is the true character of a daughter of Saint Anne" (L 13-3-1870, 13-5-1872).

    Moral balance shows itself in two important virtues called "cardinal": justice and prudence.

    The sisters speak in the informative processes of the Foundress's sense of justice, emphasizing that she showed no favoritism of any kind; on this point she was very demanding with the superiors of the communities and would not tolerate discriminatory treatment among the sisters.

    As for the human habit of prudence, it certainly does not shine in the way she treated herself: her manner of life was almost a permanent assault on her health, as we shall see later. Confessors, doctors and ecclesiastical superiors had to admit defeat before that mystery which overturned every rule of discretion. Mons. Granito di Belmonte tried to make her moderate her penances, appealing to her duty to preserve her health for the service of the Institute; but she replied that "her penances did not prevent her from attending to her duties." He himself attests:

    "And the facts showed that she was quite right, since she always attended to and carried out her office perfectly and ended her days at an advanced age" (Summ., p. 44).

    In 1898, when Mother Rosa's two secretaries appealed to the Cardinal Protector to dissuade her from traveling to Sicily, he replied: "The sufferings the Mother bears are not ordinary, and so I do not feel I can resist her" (FIOCCHI, II, p. 275).

    Rigid and merciless with herself, she was all care and solicitude when it came to the possible indiscretions of others.

    Sincerity and frankness.

    Out of nobility of heart and evangelical uprightness, Rosa Gattorno loved the truth. Sincerity and frankness stand out in all her writings, without ambiguous or flattering formulas. Here is a passage from her letter to Mons. Granito di Belmonte in which she seeks to clear up a misunderstanding caused by a letter he had received:

    "Take this letter of mine as you see fit; you know that I am as ignorant as a donkey, but experience and what I feel out of the gratitude and appreciation I owe you drive me to speak frankly" (L 22-8-1890).

    We have confirmation in the testimony of the same prelate:

    "In my dealings with the Servant of God I became convinced that she was completely free of any artifice or of hiding ulterior motives; I always knew her to be frank, upright and loyal" (Summ., p. 47).

    And she asked the same frankness of others. To Princess di Fitalia she wrote in the years when she already addressed her familiarly: "Tell me frankly what you think, because Jesus wants it so, for you must be frank: Yes! No!" (L 29-5-1893).

    Mother Rosa made Saint Paul's rule her own: Living the truth, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ (Eph 4:15).

    She practiced and insistently taught the cult of truth. This is how she expresses herself in her letters:

    "Let the truth be kept before our eyes. One cannot go astray on the way of the Lord; whoever acts with charity loves God greatly and his neighbor as himself"

    - "Answer frankly the questions (the bishop) may ask you, because truth must be on the lips of the Daughters of Saint Anne"

    - "Open your heart with complete frankness, as I do with you, your very poor mother"

    - "Let truth always remain on your lips, and simplicity in your heart"

    - "Always remember these words: let truth always be your treasure"

    - "For charity's sake, always keep in mind what this poor Mother told you and tells you: never tell lies, but let truth always be on your lips, and you will live safe in the heart of Saint Anne our Mother"

    - "Daughter, sincerity, charity, the love of God, is all we need: everything else is a fine nothing and less than nothing"

    - "This poor Mother of yours holds her head high and fears nothing, because truth is the queen of the whole world, and sooner or later Jesus brings it to light"

    - "Dear daughters, act with an upright intention, always in the presence of God, with truth in your heart and on your lips" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1871, 1-2-1872; to Sr. A. Franc. Camisa: 19-9-1867, 12-4-1869, 2-7-1869, 11-6-1871, 29-4-1872; to Sr. A. Felicita Maggioli: 28-10-1880; LCirc.: 20-1-1892).

    We know from the testimonies of the Processes that "her bearing had nothing artificial or affected about it, but was simple and natural; and she also wanted her religious to be without affectation" (Summ., p. 66).

    This quality appears above all in her letters to the sisters, especially to superiors. Suddenly blunt, strong expressions crop up about certain sisters, explicable only by the assurance that the addressee would keep them secret: "brainless heads," "crackpots," "odd ones," "flighty," "little heads"; "that ugly devil of a woman," "that ignorant superior," "wretches," "little beasts," "wicked ones," "vipers."

    Similar expressions are also found in her quick notes during visits to the communities.

    The second of the censors of her writings, after listing a long series of such outbursts, saw nothing in them that could cloud the heroicity of the Servant of God's virtues, given her lively way of writing and above all the context in which each expression was written. Mother Rosa, moreover, did not care about leaving behind her a reputation for conventional holiness, but about being honest with herself and with God. Her letters are the best answer to any suspicion of pseudo-mystical attitudes in her conduct.

    There is also another quality joined to sincerity and objectivity of judgment: a certain instinct of hers for seeing beyond people's words and behavior - not to speak of the charismatic gift of perceiving their inner life and foreseeing events -; a certain clear-sightedness that made her detect others' insincerity, a dangerous instinct that can lead to distrust and pessimism, viewing things too negatively. And she herself was aware of this risk, as appears in her very frank letters to Mons. Granito di Belmonte. She wrote to him in 1885 about the problems that had arisen with the Sacred Congregation:

    "As for Rome, it is a mystery; but by the mercy of God I have understood it, because I am very shrewd and have a lot of experience. That way things are easily understood, aren't they?" (30-9-1885).

    Two years later, replying to one of his letters:

    "Everything is fine. Just one thing I would like you to explain to me: you did not speak to just anyone, but to a confessor? Do you mean no or yes to this? Forgive me! It's true, this insolence of mine!... You see more and more of my bad character! Bear with me" (1-6-1887).

    He tried to help her examine herself on this tendency, as appears from another reply:

    "You put it very well that I see everything black. That may be so, but the blows that come my way are plain and truly black; yet I always take them like a donkey. Certainly it is my way of always seeing the bad side, because it is my wicked instinct always to see the bad side; but facts are like pain... For all that I am completely resigned, nothing troubles me: as a Christian, I know by faith that I have Jesus with me" (19-8-1888).

    I could not say whether this instinct came partly from Ligurian mercantile shrewdness or rather from the evangelical art of harmonizing the simplicity of the dove with the wisdom of the serpent (cf. Mt 10:16). But it is quite true that she recommended it to the superiors of the Institute.

    "I urge you to be very shrewd: do not trust appearances," she wrote to Sister A. Adelaide Pezzoni (2-1-1872).

    Objectivity and practical sense.

    As a young woman living in her father's house she had shown a special aptitude and rare perspicacity in administrative matters, so that the running of the household was almost entirely entrusted to her (8). This ability, later developed through successive responsibilities, can be seen in many of her actions as foundress, especially in new foundations and in her instructions to superiors and others. See, for example, two of the letters written to Mons. Granito di Belmonte on how to meet the expenses of two new houses (16-9-1891, 15-1-1892). Francesco Gattorno, who directed the construction of the Generalate in Rome, testifies:

    "In all this administration my sister showed extraordinary energy and uncommon insight. When I went to her about these matters, she had usually already worked out in her mind the plans to follow, which I, as a businessman, found well made" (Summ., p. 1000f).

    And she wanted the sisters to acquire a realistic sense of life, without fanciful notions or overly angelic attitudes. This is how she writes to two superiors:

    "My daughter, for charity's sake, do not let yourself be taken by whims and vague ideas, things that only muddle the mind and serve no purpose but to disturb us and make us irritable: let us keep to what is concrete!" (To Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, 16-1-1870).

    - "You know? I am a practical woman: that is how I like the daughters of Saint Anne to be" (To Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, 20-12-1880).

    Certainly the style of sister the foundress wanted was not easy: on the one hand separated from the world, immersed in supernatural realities, always recollected and attentive to the presence of God, and on the other with eyes open to temporal realities, objective and practical: the mind in heaven and the feet on the ground.

    We read in a circular of 1877: "The bearing of the Daughters of Saint Anne in the street must be both natural and modest" (LC, 1877).

    A cheerful spirit and a sense of humor.

    We have spoken of a pedagogy of courage; I think that in Mother Rosa's methods of formation there is also a remarkable pedagogy of joy, an essential component of genuine Christian holiness, one of the fruits of the Holy Spirit's dwelling in us.

    By nature Rosa Gattorno was jovial and outgoing. As a young woman she took part in the legitimate amusements of her family circle, contributing her skill in singing and at the piano, and she did not refuse an occasional dance, for which she would later feel remorse as for an infidelity to God; passing one day along Via di S. Rocchino in Genoa, she stopped in front of a house that the Daughters of Saint Anne had lived in for some time and, looking at it sadly, said to a priest: "How many dances I had in this house!" All who knew her, however, remembered her as a girl who was cheerful, yes, but most modest and angelic (FIOCCHI, I, p. 17).

    She had learned the secret of "perfect joy" in the school of Francis of Assisi, finding it precisely in contempt and adversity.

    She wrote in confidence to Sister A. Francesca Camisa:

    "Daughter, courage! for to die on the cross one needs strength and resignation. I have no rest day or night: always at my desk writing from morning till evening, worries upon worries, labors upon labors; on every side I find cruel thorns...; but always cheerful and always resigned: this is what my Jesus teaches me" (13-3-1872).

    This was her teaching to the sisters, as appears repeatedly in her letters:

    "Tell all my daughters to be cheerful, as their Mother is"

    - "Be cheerful, my daughter, if you want to become a saint!"

    - "My dear, be cheerful! Do you understand?"

    - "Why are you crying? That is for children. Come now! Cheer up!"

    - "Be cheerful, and live!"

    - "Be cheerful! Everything else we will place in the heart of God the Father"

    - "In prosperity as in adversity, always joyful; for in adversity we must be all the more content, because we know that by rejoicing we please our Lord. What greater consolation can we seek, when it pleases our Jesus?"

    - "Always cheerful, for that is what God wants!"

    - "Trust in God and you will have everything; be cheerful with Jesus: yes, my daughter, when we have the eternal God with us, what more do we lack? Nothing, nothing!" (9).

    And here are some fine expressions chosen from her letters to Princess di Fitalia, who was prone to discouragement:

    "I see you are a little worried: no! I want you cheerful, content! God is with you: whoever has God with them has nothing to fear"

    - "Do not let melancholy get the better of you. Do you know? This is the net the devil spreads for good souls... So away with melancholy! It is treacherous through and through"

    - "You see, I am as cheerful as I can be, calm and happy to be able to do some small thing for my Jesus"

    - "You are in the country: enjoy yourself, keep the prince cheerful, do not be upset if you cannot recollect yourself: Jesus is pleased with the desire... Make your morning offering, that everything be done for the glory of God: eating, drinking, laughing, walking..."

    - "I am wretched and good for nothing... Patience! Joy! May Jesus accept my miserable sufferings" (10).

    To Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte she wrote:

    "Pray that God may always give me strength and courage. He has always given me, and I do not know how to thank him for it, that I never lack cheerfulness. Oh! how I mean to make you laugh, if it pleases God that I speak with you!" (Nov. 1883).

    True joy is not merely a way of being, the product of functional or stimulating factors, but the effect of inner liberation from the causes of sadness, of peace of heart and of trusting abandonment to God.

    "Melancholy is the devil's net," Mother Rosa repeats. In a circular of 1898 she explains the relationship between inner peace and a cheerful spirit:

    "I cannot understand how a sister, making her examination of conscience in the evening, does not see all her faults written before her eyes and does not make firm resolutions to give them up and, with zeal and love, to make amends for all the harm done... Oh! then your heart will be full of joy and will lose that uncertain beat which belongs to a conscience that needs to be brought into full accord with the will of God" (LC, 10-2-1898).

    Psychologists regard a sense of humor as one of the signs of personal integrity and maturity. Psychopathic, neurotic, fanatical or pseudo-mystical individuals do not grasp the optimistic dimension of life, which is expressed in the art of looking at events and at people's attitudes with humor, without dramatizing the anxieties of one's own ego.

    "Lord," Saint Thomas More prayed, "do not let me worry too much about that awkward thing called 'I': Lord, give me a sense of humor."

    Mother Rosa offers us this test of her human and spiritual normality as well. A spontaneous and delicate humor gives her letters a certain human warmth, which can also be found in her brief notes during visits to the houses. There is humor too when she speaks of herself in self-abasement and when she jokes about her own faults or the ailments of old age. And the same wit is present even in the most anguished moments of her tribulations and of her struggles with the infernal enemy, on whom she bestows many joking epithets.

    It is humor of the finest quality that seasons her correspondence with Princess di Fitalia. The two friends began by addressing each other formally, but ended up on familiar terms. Out of the respect due to the office of superior general, the princess kept the formal address in her telegrams, so that Mother Rosa wrote to her:

    "It is funny that when you telegraph me you address me formally: this donkey is illustrious indeed! Don't do it any more, call me 'tu': aren't you convinced that I am the Savior's donkey?" (2-2-1890).

    The same can be seen in her letters to Mons. Granito di Belmonte. One example is the letter of July 29, 1888, in which she tells of her sufferings because of Fr. Tornatore's demands, and that of March 4, 1889, in which she recounts a small adventure while visiting, together with another sister, some noble families to collect alms. On January 27, 1890, she spoke of herself in these terms:

    "Here I am, enthroned like a patriarch, all bandaged up on a chair; I lack only the crozier to be an Abbess. That is how one runs; without the wheels of tribulation one does not go well."

    And in two other letters:

    "Are you pleased? Is the teacher still doing well? Who will give me a present for doing well? I'm a funny one: the donkey loses its coat but never its vices" - "It seems to me a certain something... Enough! Let us put everything in God's hands. The what? It's a mystery! How will it be, joyful or sorrowful? Well, that is how one lives on this earth, a thrush today, a stone tomorrow. Isn't it so? I'm always the same: I'll be laughing even under the ground. Pray that I may be converted" (10-1-1891, 18-7-1892).

    An exquisitely feminine sensitivity.

    Rosa Gattorno possessed to an eminent degree the treasure that, humanly speaking, best characterizes the normal woman: the capacity to attune herself to what is good, beautiful and pleasant in life and to avoid what is morally ugly or unworthy; the gift of sensing people's inner situations and of feeling close to those who suffer; an eye for detail... When such a treasure is translated into self-giving, we have the ideal image of the wife and mother who lives entirely for her family, or that of the consecrated woman who sacrifices herself for God and for others under the impulse of love.

    Mother Rosa was a woman with a delicately sensitive heart. Here too her letters offer us the most eloquent testimony. She always keeps in mind the person she is writing to, with their particular traits, beginning with their name, which she knows how to insert at just the right moment so as to reach the heart, with the state of their health and with their problems.

    Like the most solicitous of mothers, she worries whether the sisters and the girls entrusted to them have enough food, whether they are protected from the cold... A few of her recommendations to superiors will serve as examples:

    "How sorry I am to hear that you are cold! My Jesus, give them your fire, and so they will be warm. Dear Francesca, I thought all the blankets were quilted; if you are short of any, tell the bursar... Tell the bursar also to provide you with winter habits and little jackets, as we agreed, and the blankets. For charity's sake, cover yourselves up!"

    - "Comfort poor little Carlottina, take care of her and have compassion on her... I commend the little girls to you; see that they are well covered at night so that they do not catch a cough; likewise the little ones, heads clean..." (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 10-10-1867, 2-7-1869; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 25-9-1870).

    Sensitive to the needs and situations of others, she was equally grateful for the kindnesses she received from the sisters and from others. Her letters are full of expressions of gratitude in very warm terms.

    The gift of sensitivity, however, runs the risk of degenerating either into touchiness, when it closes in on itself, or into anxiety, when the spirit loses freedom and breathing space under fears that disturb inner peace. Mother Rosa was free of any self-centreed withdrawal, but she had to struggle against the second risk, anxiety. She writes in her Memoirs in 1873:

    "How my wretched character makes me suffer! For more and more I feel torment at the mere thought of having to say a single word of what happens to me. I try everything to correct it, but it is useless, worse! I renew the thought, and lo, a strong pain awakens in me... It is true that when this apprehension grows to the point of making me despair, my God comes to my aid, and I remain in peace" (M 4.2, p. 6f) (11).

    She acknowledges it similarly in the book Trials and Consolations, in an imagined dialogue with a "worker" (a sister): "I must confess to you that it is my wretched character" (TC, p. 277).

    Worse still was when this tendency crept into the secret of her spiritual experiences themselves, as one of the most painful factors of the passive purifications. In 1889 she confided to Mons. Granito di Belmonte in these terms:

    "Hell, that is, meditating on how many souls it swallows up - no, my God! I shall only tell you that my first confessor forbade me this meditation. I am too apprehensive, and it arouses fears of every kind in me. And if to this were added those times when the Being of my life hides himself, oh! what one feels!... I seem to have committed every horrendous evil. O my Love, no! I am a poor unhappy creature who feels in need of nothing but love!" (L Feb. 1889) (12).

    As a rule, when she was alone in her little room, she gave way to tears, clasping her Crucifix; but very often aridity dried up her eyes as well, and then, with no tears, she experienced in agonizing form the suffering of an emotional life that found no outlet (M. 1.2, p. 99 (1874); 2, p. 86, 98 (1864); 3, p. 72 (1872)).

    With age she became aware of how hard it was to control her sensitivity. On September 14, 1889, she made this introspective observation:

    "I find that the older I get the more sensitive I am to (external contradictions), and many times I weep over them. Whereas before, oh! I was never cast down, now I am: something of a deep sensitivity, so that I no longer have the strength to master myself. They notice it and I become shaken, my strength fails me; I feel that my nerves have suffered greatly and have become very weak. At least that is how I judge it myself from what I feel...; at the slightest thing that happens, I am frightened in spite of myself" (M 11.1, p. 26f).

    Tender affection, but free of sentimental dependence.

    In her youth, before and after her marriage, Rosa won the affection of many people in Genoese society by her delicate and courteous manner and her noble uprightness. It was not hard for her to find friends and collaborators when, as a widow, she devoted herself to works of piety and charity; indeed, a good number of those friends entrusted themselves fully to her guidance in the ways of the spirit (13). Later others would experience the strong attraction of her heart, always sociable and affectionate, even within the restraint of her social relations, for which she had no time.

    Of all her friendships, none was as deep and intimate as the one she maintained with Emilia Labecka, Polish by birth, married to Prince Gerolamo Settimo di Fitalia (Palermo). A woman of genuine spiritual experience, she became not only an admirer and generous benefactor of Mother Rosa's work but her confidante and true spiritual daughter (14).

    The long correspondence she kept up with the princess until her last illness is a model of warmth between two souls who have no secrets from each other: an affectionate and noble friendship, without affectation. Everything is natural, yet everything takes place on the plane of the interests of the spirit.

    Her other great friendship was with another figure of the southern Italian nobility, Gennaro, son of the princes Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, whom she met in Naples in 1877 when he was still a layman; he became a priest in 1879, then served at the nunciature in Paris (1897), and was nuncio in Brussels (1899) and Vienna (1904); finally, in 1911, he was created cardinal by Pius X. He died in 1948. He had great veneration for Mother Rosa; as was to be expected, the friendship became in time a relationship of genuine spiritual direction; the correspondence she assiduously kept up with him always had a tone of trust and deep understanding, together with warm spontaneity. Further on we shall mention her family affections and her charity towards the sisters. Here it is enough to say that through the thousands of letters, carefully preserved by her spiritual daughters, Mother Rosa's affectionate heart is revealed, all tenderness and heartfelt care.

    Each of the sisters is for her a gift of God, with a name, an individuality, a personal context. Her expressions of affection, always original and beautiful, never conventional, are especially beautiful in her closing words:

    "God bless you: I am your poor Mother"

    - "May the blessing of the eternal Father be with you, wholly mine forever, my daughter. I am your poor Mother Rosa"

    - "I always keep you in mind: wherever I go, I always carry all my blessed daughters with me"

    - "Greet all the religious for me: tell them that every morning I enclose them in the Heart of Jesus, and the dear little girls too"

    - "Goodbye, I hold you close in the Heart of Jesus, and am always yours"

    - "Believe me your Mother, who blesses you and holds you to her heart, never to leave you again and to call herself always your Mother Rosa."

    She trained the sisters in the right measure of affective behavior, as brides of Jesus, who is a jealous Bridegroom and must absorb all their affection. But when the heart is full of this preferential love, there is no need to be wary of affection for creatures.

    "God put into your heart the great affection for this poor Mother of yours," she wrote to Sister A. Celsa Speranza: "it is solely God's work, not yours, and there is nothing human in it at all" (12-11-1886).

    In her relations with the sisters Mother Rosa was no slave to formalities. She had grown used to addressing them all familiarly; they felt her closer that way; but the Rule required the formal form of address. Having learned that in one community this rule was not being observed, she wrote to the superior:

    "Be careful: I confess that this bad habit may have crept in because I gave a bad example; but from now on it will not happen to me again, and I ask pardon of God, and of them for the bad example" (L to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi: undated, no. 256).

    But she did not manage to keep up the formal address, judging from her letters (15).

Spiritual writers customarily present the ascetical-mystical process as a fascinating but arduous ascent towards the summit of perfection, that is, towards transformation into God through love; or as a journey ever further into the interior castle, from whose center God calls and draws the soul, as a magnet draws iron, until he unites it to himself in an embrace of love; or again as a plunging, sailing among waves and reefs, into the immense sea of God's reality, until the soul finds itself immersed, like a fish in water, in that ocean of love.

In reality these are three allegories expressing one and the same journey, which always has as its starting point and unavoidable premise the conversion or penitential choice of what is called the purgative way; this is traveled through the active and passive purifications, up to the night of the spirit, which constitutes the soul's greatest liberation, fitting it at last for union in pure love.

And as the spirit becomes purified and nimble, freed of the impediments that bound it, it advances along the illuminative way, always in pure faith, until life itself becomes almost a transparency of God. And the fruit is freedom to love, to reach Love, climbing the ascent of the unitive way up to transforming union.

We should keep this general overview of the paths of holiness in mind in order to understand how and to what extent we can speak of God's success, so to speak, in the wholly singular life of Rosa Gattorno; bearing in mind, however, that God's ways are infinite and that his action in each one he calls does not submit to preset patterns. We rely, though not exclusively, on her own testimony, set down in her writings.

It must be said at the outset, however, that Rosa Gattorno is not a theorist of the ways of the spirit. Her writings show no trace of reading books on spirituality. She had no time, and perhaps did not even feel the need. She mentions several times the readings done in community, specifically the lives of the saints. So she has no conventional terminology; she expresses in simple words, often in exclamations, her own experiences and their effects on her spirit.

  • Discovering God's plan.

    • The family atmosphere, especially her mother's example of piety, fostered in little Rosa a spontaneous attraction to religious practices. When she reached adolescence she began to feel strongly drawn to prayer, seeking solitude. One of her sisters attests: "At times she could be heard pouring herself out in such ardent aspirations of love for God that, however much she thought she was alone, she could not hide them" (FIOCCHI, I, pp. 11-15; II, p. 256).

    But not all was the sweetness of fervor in those years. The amusements she took part in, as we have seen, however wholesome and justified, became at times a source of troublesome unease of conscience, a foretaste of the future sufferings caused by the absence of her Good.

    As late as 1873 the enemy was still tormenting her with the memory of those anxieties (M 4.1, p. 41f).

    We have no information on the method of interior life she followed in her six years of married life, but judging by the one she undertook as soon as she was widowed, we may suppose that, under the direction of the priest Don Giuseppe Firpo, she not only knew how to sanctify the events of family life but lived the sacramental life and the practice of prayer even more assiduously, as well as the exercise of charity, visiting hospitals and helping with other works.

    The "conversion."

    Rosa Gattorno was convinced that she was a convert, that is, that there had been a moment in her life when God's mercy drew as it were a dividing line between a past to be erased, because still oriented towards the earth, and a new existence to be offered to God, discovered as the one Good for whom and in whom life is worth living.

    Looking back, when she begins writing her Memoirs, she sees the change worked in her in 1858 in this way:

    "Free of every tie, I devoted myself more fervently to works of piety and to visiting hospitals and the poor sick in their homes, helping them, giving them what aid I could and serving them in everything.

    By the Lord's grace I noticed that all earthly affections were fading away; nothing gave me pleasure any more; my God alone was the pasture of all my delights.

    The family troubles were beyond compare. I poured everything into the heart of my dear Crucified: for him alone - I kept repeating to myself - all my suffering is little! Because I had committed many sins, I could not entirely give up certain small things, because, living with my family, I was not allowed to. Oh! how much I had to fight!!!" (M 1.1).

    We already know what those many sins could have been; that is how they appeared to her when her spirit was already flooded with the splendor of God's holiness. Deep within she felt something like a debt of love to be paid at any cost. Thus was born her insatiable thirst for penances; she says so herself immediately afterwards, in a heroic outpouring of love:

    "Always clinging to my Good, I kept repeating: Oh! my sins deserve worse, even hell itself; and I would gladly go there to feel those pains, provided I am led by you, close and held tight: you alone are my paradise! And I wept much for having offended him. With the permission of obedience I increased my penances as much as I could..." (M 1.1, p. 2f).

    But the Lord came to relieve her of that burden. Repeatedly, while she was in contemplation, he showed her two books held by two angels. In the first, "very beautiful and not so thick," a list of names was written, with the addition: And then saints; at the end of the list her own name was clearly visible, with the words: And then a saint. In the other book, "which was thick," she saw her own sins written, "but I saw them all blotted out," she says, "with the blood of my dear Redeemer." At the end her name was there too, with the same addition: And then a saint.

    But the fear of not having been completely forgiven came back to torment her. One day she saw those sins covered with a black veil, and she wept inconsolably until the veil was removed. Later, as confirmation of the pardon sealed by God, she saw over the blotted-out sins now a palm, now a most beautiful crown; this was then replaced by the crown of thorns, to her great joy. At the end of the account she exclaims:

    "Oh! poor sinner! Oh! goodness of a God who is Father! Who would not spend herself entirely for this dear Father? To give him all of ourselves is truly nothing compared with such immensity of greatness. Oh! boundless goodness!" (M 1.1, pp. 5-7).

    The more she discovered the greatness of divine mercy, the more she saw herself, in the presence of the supreme Good and loving Father, as "a miserable sinner, a loathsome worm of the earth"; but she responded full of gratitude and assurance: "It is no longer I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me!" (cf. Gal 2:20).

    As late as 1862 she felt pursued by the tempter with the fear of not having merited God's pardon, because her sins had not been properly confessed. She would have liked to make her general confession again; fortunately her director, Don Firpo, did not allow her to go back over her past life. At last, with her peace restored, she heard the Lord's reproach: "Was it not enough for you to have seen everything blotted out?" (M 1.1, pp. 27-29).

    Yet the assurance of pardon would not prevent her from finding in the memory of her offenses against God a reason to humble herself with expressions like this: "My wickedness allows nothing, because I am a wretch" (M 1.1, p. 39, year 1866).

    Her own sufferings and her compassion for others who suffered had prepared her for the encounter with the Crucified, in whom every mystery of human pain finds explanation and comfort. Moreover, feeling redeemed and forgiven led her to an ever more passionate love for the wounded Savior. Thus she began to open herself to the gift of infused contemplation.

    It was during the novena of Our Lady of the Vines that she felt herself favored with great consolations, with visions, interior words and a deep joy never felt before. Afterwards she also experienced aridity and abandonment, to the point of losing her peace: "because I did not yet know," she reasons, "how to fight under the banner of the holy Cross, so delightful and dear; but how many mistakes one makes as a beginner!"

    Her director helped her regain inner calm by making her understand the meaning of those alternations of fervor and aridity, of light and darkness on the way of perfection. And she goes on, recounting and commenting:

    "O dear Jesus! Yes, let us grow fond of Calvary, and in suffering we shall see its delights; drawing near to the object one loves, all suffering becomes a balm one longs for.

    In the caresses he often gave me, he made me a present of some of his gifts, such as that of meditation, and this after holy Communion, clinging to my Good, which was more contemplation than meditation, because I would place myself in one of his wounds and stay there for hours without being aware that I was alive, and it grew ever more in me. At other times I was absorbed and, as if in conversation, I stayed with my Jesus. He taught me many things" (M 1.1, pp. 3-5).

    She decides on total consecration to God.

    With the past now erased and the future entrusted to God's plan, Rosa waited for what he might wish to show her. The moment had come to seal the choice she had made with fundamental commitments. In 1858, just after her husband's death, she had bound herself by a vow of chastity for one year; on the feast of the Immaculate Conception that same year, with her director's approval, she made perpetual vows of chastity and obedience; four years later she was allowed to add the vow of poverty. It was like the beginning of a new life, she would later comment in her Memoirs:

    "I laid everything at Mary's feet, that she might make a gift of it to my Good Jesus and ask him to accept me as his bride. Oh! what I felt! as though I had entered another state of life, and I did not know whether I was living or who was living for me" (M 1.1, p. 2).

    It is not specified whether the vow of obedience was in relation to her spiritual Father or what its scope was. The fact is that Rosa was not satisfied; she felt she had kept back for herself what above all required a gift of love: her will. And one day she wished to sacrifice it by vow:

    "One thing remained that I had not made over to him in sacrifice and vow, and it was, O my Beloved! my will. And indeed I renounced it to him, telling him that this vow was certainly not worthy to stand with the other vows, because with my will I had offended him so many times, so I laid it beneath his feet and begged him to use it as his footstool. I want only to live by your love, O my sweet Love!" (M 1.1, p. 20).

    These experiences belong to the months she spent at S. Francesco d'Albaro, a country place where she had moved to recover her health. It was for her almost a providential retreat at that decisive moment in the direction of her life. In that peace she experienced intimacy with God and the lights of contemplation more intensely, while she discovered unmistakably her special vocation to a life of suffering. This was the answer she received from her director Don Firpo after he had observed that every spiritual consolation given her was always preceded and followed by agonizing days of aridity, abandonment, fears and temptations, and ugly diabolical suggestions (16).

    From then on love and suffering would be inseparable in her life; indeed, suffering would be her way of loving. And in her logic of loving expiation she would choose to redouble her bodily penances.

    On September 24, 1861, in the church of S. Francesco d'Albaro, she made her profession of the Rule of the Franciscan Third Order; three years earlier she had put on the tunic of the sons of Saint Francis, which she wore under her lay clothes, girded with a thick cord.

    "I chose this good Father," she writes, "as my advocate and the protector of my soul" (M 1.1, p. 13).

    Indeed, she could not fail to find in the stigmatized saint of La Verna, a living copy of the Crucified, her model of a crucified life.

  • In the secrets of the experience of God.

    • When Rosa resumed her work in the service of the poor sick at the end of 1863, she suddenly found herself at the center of the various pious and charitable organizations of the city of Genoa: such was the opinion people had of her as a woman of mature faith, of creative zeal and above all of a spirit guided by a higher light. Her life of prayer was known to all: she could be seen spending long hours in church, absorbed in contemplation.

    The year 1864 was for her a true apprenticeship that introduced her to the secrets of ineffable communications and mystical union. Looking back, she seems still to savor the discovery of those unsuspected landscapes of the spirit under the divine light which, on the one hand, dazzled her, paralysing her faculties, and on the other filled her mind with infused knowledge and teaching, while kindling her will with the sweetness of a love never felt before. Let us hear her words:

    "Oh! what beautiful and great things he showed me in these contemplations of 1864! I would like to write so many things, but I will always say: if my Jesus wished, he would surely make my pen move as he pleases; thus he would give me an angelic prompter, so that I could describe them as I see and feel them. Firm in this principle, I set to work, sure that I will write nothing but what my beloved prompts me."

    There follows a kind of profession of faith in the mystery of the Trinity, as she understood it with the help of infused light. Then an ardent outpouring of the soul, overwhelmed by such great condescension shown to her by such a God:

    "Great mystery! Oh! if only I could make you known to the whole world! You are, if one may say so, mad about man; and he, alas!... A voice that says to me:

    - Yes, I love him, but my love is not returned!

    As he said this, he came so close that I felt myself enraptured. Oh! sanctifying Spirit, divine Essence, ever ready to pour yourself into the ungrateful hearts of men! what precious nectar a single drop breathes forth, if man came to taste it! O sweetness beyond compare! Oh! whoever comes to taste and possess this divine Essence, surely everything earthly only sickens him.

    The intellect, opened by divine power, communicates with his immortal Being and, in that infinite ocean of infinite greatness, understands everything, is blissful and delights in Love. Oh! how infinite you are in your despotic, absolute power! and then, Father and beloved Bridegroom of hearts. Oh! strength of loving souls and of those who live in you and for you!" (M 1.2, p. 1f).

    In those hours of quiet contemplation there was no lack of ecstasies and raptures, when absorption in God was so strong that it disconnected her deep consciousness from the mechanism of the senses; her concern then was not to be noticed by others:

    "My Good, by his union and closeness, filled me with bliss, gave me strength, and I could think of nothing, because Love absorbed everything and I needed strength not to fall into ecstasy. I tried everything to distract myself... O my Love! the effort I had to make not to remain absorbed in you, my Beloved, was the greater pain... I did not understand myself in that intoxication in which I found myself..." (M 1.1, p. 85, year 1864).

    Her meditation, always affective, had become a true loving participation in which she lived, as it were from within, the life of Jesus, especially the scenes of the Passion, completely identified with the sufferings of her Good and with Our Lady's sorrow, as well as the mysteries celebrated in the various liturgical solemnities, the sentiments of Jesus in the Eucharist, etc. (cf. M 1.1, p. 36f).

    From 1862 this participation became a bodily mystical phenomenon, to which we shall return later: the experience of the pain of the wounds in her hands, feet and side; her heart, moreover, at moments of great fervor and inner consolation, became inflamed and swelled so as to force even her ribs.

    An example of this way of living the mysteries she contemplated is the interesting diary of meditations she kept during Lent of that same year 1864, accompanying Jesus in his forty-day retreat in the desert. In it we find valuable observations on her progress in unitive experience. On the 14th day she noted:

    "With my mind always fixed on my God on the mountain, today such pain seized me that I could neither speak nor consider anything, but all at once I found myself united to my Good, and I saw everything: his sufferings and beautiful, sublime lessons. O sweet union! My soul gained much knowledge, and was so strengthened that, back at my work, I felt neither pain nor the smell of my sick: it was sweet to serve them, and I felt I was doing everything in my God."

    On the 22nd day she made another discovery: she remained "silent, in sweet contemplation," experiencing an intense union, but without rapture, "because," she explains, "I was perfectly in full possession of my power to feel physically and to reason" (17).

    Each day her meditations looked ahead to the Lord's coming Passion, in a crescendo of compassionate and unitive love. At times she felt herself as if consumed by a devouring fire; she writes on the 33rd day:

    "I rejoiced immensely, and yet it was a terrible agony, and most delightful; I felt a great and consoling pleasure in feeling myself destroyed, and I would never have wanted it to stop. Oh! how sweet it is to die of love!"

    The experience of the 35th day helped her distinguish between simple recollection and true infused union:

    "Always with my Good, and today I remained absorbed in him, receiving graces and great knowledge of the soul with God, its center... I hardly felt any pain, nor could I have a distinct thought of it, since in union nothing is within our power: all the faculties are concentrated in God and in his absolute divinity; the soul remains wholly absorbed in his Being."

    With such preparation, continued through Holy Week, everything culminated in the splendid experience of Easter day:

    "Oh! what shall I say of the day of the Resurrection? What I felt! I stayed by the tomb the whole time and never tried to eat or pray. I called him and wanted to be shut up with him in that tomb. When he had risen, I sought him, as Magdalene did, and having found him, oh! my Love! who can describe what I went through and what I received from you? I will say it was a continual rapture, always conversing with my God, and so many beautiful lessons and so much knowledge I received. Oh! love only my God, you creatures who seek the Good! in him alone is everything, and outside him everything is mud" (M 2, p. 106f, 122f, 144f, 147f, 186f).

    Overwhelmed by such condescension on God's part, annihilated in her own littleness and misery, on May 28, 1864, she poured out her heart in these terms:

    "What are you doing, my Beloved? Have you forgotten my wickedness? You fill me with your treasures, and what more can I give you? Everything I had I have already given you and, because I am a poor creature, having given what I had - life, will, everything! - nothing is left me. Oh! how small a thing the creature is beside your infinite greatness! a nothing and less than nothing. So that... the soul, which is a portion of you, my Good (18), longs to return to its center, which is my Being...

    Reasoning thus, I became absorbed and found myself in him in the greatest ecstasy. I saw very great and infinite things. My Beloved seemed to pour into me something I cannot express. He taught me great things..." (M 1.2, p. 2f).

    As the invasion of the divine made itself felt in her spirit, Rosa felt ever more purified, lightened of the impediments that hindered her soaring towards the supreme Good. Here is how she describes in the book Trials and Consolations the effect of those passive purifications, in a fine page worthy of the great masters of mysticism:

    "My Crucified subdues human nature, gives it vigor and energy, strengthens the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the faculties, which then remain so well subject.

    Self-love dissipates, goes astray, is lost, so much so that one's very name is forgotten. Pride is defeated and regarded as an instrument of disdain, as an enemy. One feels great pleasure and great consolation in seeing them crushed.

    The will, which is overbearing, grows quiet. My Crucified has exchanged my will for his, and it is infinitely sweet and pleasant no longer to possess it. Oh! how it would have rebelled had he not nailed it fast, though it remains ever free!" (TC, p. 3f).

    With the same capacity for self-analysis, though in her own way, she describes the various ways in which she experiences God's intimate presence and his communications: infused recollection, a simple gaze of love, interior invitations, languors of love... She knows that none of this is the fruit of her own effort, but that everything is pure gift of God, the experience of a life that is not hers. To express this newness she very often makes Saint Paul's well-known text her own: It is not I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me (cf. Gal 2:20). She writes in 1867:

    "Such was my union with my God that, as soon as I began to pray, I was at once absorbed in him; and I always saw new things... He taught me, corrected me, showed me how I was to do his work..., as though I were not living, but there were in me a person who acted and lived for me continually. And I saw before me a light so beautiful that, even when I was listening to someone speak, unless I kept control of myself I would remain spellbound, and many times they thought me simple-minded..." (M 1.1, p. 64).

    Towards transformation, through love, into the supreme Good.

    While her spirit was thus growing accustomed to God's inner workings, Rosa Gattorno multiplied her apostolic works. Indeed, among the gifts she recalls receiving from the Lord at that time is the ease with which she was able to harmonize the two dimensions of charity:

    "O Love, you make me languish with love! Oh! blessed days when, having a little freedom, I spend the whole day going from the church to the hospital, beside my dear sick, offering them my poor service!" (M 1.1, p. 57).

    At times the union of fruition made her feel as if "exiled, shut up in the prison of the body," and she would have liked to break free to clasp her Good in an eternal embrace (M 1.1, p. 57f).

    In 1865 her mission as foundress began to take shape. Reassured of God's will from the lips of Pope Pius IX, and having received from him a categorical answer regarding her responsibilities as a mother - "God will take care of your children" - she did not hesitate to free herself of her other family, social and financial ties in her native Genoa as well, in order to give herself entirely to what would henceforth be for her the Work of the Lord, of which she would consider herself the mere, poor instrument.

    In Piacenza, where she settled in March 1866, her spiritual life unfolded in two settings: the community chapel and her beloved little room, which for many years would be the silent witness of her penances and raptures.

    On December 8, 1866, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne was born with the clothing of the first novices; the foundress, for well-considered reasons, had to postpone her own clothing until the feast of Saint Anne, July 26, 1867.

    Not content with the long periods set aside for community prayer, both vocal and mental, Rosa devoted most of the night to contemplation. The brief rest she took on the cross that served as her bed, or sometimes stretched out on the altar step, was almost always disturbed by troublesome diabolical suggestions. By day she worked at household tasks or at the many matters the direction of the Institute required, writing without pause. Now and then, however, she would interrupt her work, saying: "Oh! I'm going up there to recollect myself and lift my spirits a little"; and she would take refuge in her little room; when she came down, her radiant face showed the effects of her communion with God (19).

    Her spiritual ascent is known to us through the experiences recorded in her Memoirs, all the more reliable because they were written with no addressee in mind; they are so many moments of her dialogue with the supreme Good, almost snapshots of what she is living at the time.

    The raptures and burnings of love, which visibly affect her heart, become more and more frequent. Very often she is forced to hide to avoid attracting attention, though she always trusts in the Lord's promise that every bodily manifestation of what he works within her will remain hidden. Even so, the sisters and others around her often have to shake her hard to bring her back from the immobility of her recollection. Especially after communion she remains absorbed in God for a long time.

    In the early years she spent her nightly vigils of prayer on her knees; but later she prayed "prostrate on the ground with her arms stretched out on the floor in the form of a cross" (M 3, p. 29, May 1872).

    A few passages from the Memoirs will be enough to give an idea of what she secretly experienced at moments when union was most intense.

    1872, September 10:

    "It was a night of contemplation more than of sleep... And such was the union that bound me to my God that I began to taste a sweetness of paradise. My right side was already beginning to rise. Alas! you are making me die! But I could say no more, because all my faculties were taken up into him alone and, held close, close, without knowing that I lived, I lived in that Being, for at that moment he alone was in me, and I knew nothing, saw nothing: I only felt myself filled with bliss" (M 3, p. 64f).

    1873, June:

    "Beyond all creation, my mind conceives nothing else, my intellect sees nothing but God alone. And so I spend the nights... Ah! it has been so many months! I feel nothing else, see nothing else that can comfort me but staying with my God. O Love! O Love! you alone are my All. And I have to force myself to push him away..." (M 4.1, p. 102f).

    1874, January:

    "At night, when my Good unites me to himself so gently that my mind has nothing but him alone, all thoughts of his Work leave me: only my God remains; in him alone my faculties are placed, on him alone they feed. There is no more human lowliness, only divine (greatness). I spend whole nights absorbed in him: Ah! vigil of love!" (M 4.2, p. 27).

    1875, January 17:

    "I spent the night clinging to my Good. Oh! joy! I was dying, so great was the love I felt; not a single instant was I outside him. My eternal All, who can describe what you do and communicate to the soul and what it experiences in you? Today in you, and you live for me; I feel that I have no life but yours. A calm, an inner peace I cannot describe to you. I speak, or rather feel, or better still, my spirit feels that there is something which is felt and not seen with bodily eyes, but the intellect sees and understands everything" (M 4.3, p. 15f).

    The habit of unitive contemplation becomes ever more natural; without effort she manages to keep her mind constantly fixed on God, feels herself enfolded by God's presence, accompanied by him even in the business she has to deal with, in her work and on her journeys; but it is in the solitude of night that she abandons herself to union:

    "I do not have a single earthly thought. I work, I act, because my Good is always with me. For four days and nights now he has been constantly visible at my side; every so often, while I work, I cannot help (saying to him): Alas! you are making me die! Ah! have pity on me, my Beloved, move away, for I am dying! But at night I do not say so: I abandon myself entirely to him and my sleep is a continuous ecstasy. Oh! if God is with me, who can be against me? (cf. Rom 8:31). The whole world is nothing, less than nothing; to me everything I see on earth is rottenness" (M 1.1, p. 112).

    It is an active presence, to the point that at the most delicate moments she sees herself almost replaced by the Lord, who answers for her:

    "I always find myself in the presence of God... There are times when I feel certain words actually coming out of my mouth to answer in the affairs of his Work, and so I never think about what I am to say, because my Love speaks for me, and at times I listen to those very words with pleasure, one might say, as if someone else were saying them..." (M 1.1, p. 149f).

    Lights and ineffable communications.

    The most secret and most fruitful phase of the unitive process in mystics is that of infused illumination, of ineffable communications, for which there is no adequate language, since they are not the product of the mind's elaboration of sense perceptions or of the association of images and notions stored in the brain - the species impressa and species expressa of the scholastics - but are infused directly by God into the soul. As the mystics repeat, one can speak only of the effects they leave in the faculties and the influence they have on life. Moreover, such penetration of God's light is not subject to duration in time, since in an instant the soul grasps immeasurable truths.

    Rosa Gattorno often speaks of this experience, which she is unable to put into words with her pen. Here are some of her recollections:

    "I remained absorbed in God, and received a thousand beautiful enlightenments and insights into everything" (Christmas 1867) (M 1.1, p. 48f).

    "At meditation, as soon as I had begun, I was absorbed in my Good, and I had nothing but love. My soul was in bliss, my intellect was furnished with the most beautiful insights and lights" (1874) (M 1.1, p. 180).

    "The night of August 20, 1874, and likewise the whole of the following day: my God!... He taught me about his love, its degree and how it is communicated to the soul. But I am not able to repeat it all: I feel I have clear ideas, as he told them to me, but I cannot describe them. I saw everything immense, great beyond compare..." (M 1.2, p. 45).
