    She writes in similar terms of the infused light she received in April 1877 regarding the mystery of the Incarnation; she cannot explain it, though she had it so clearly in her mind (M 4.4, p. 136).

    Not only the intimate communications but union with God itself is ineffable. On April 18, 1892, at a Mass celebrated by the Cardinal Protector, she felt herself set on fire with love and then entered into intimate union:

    "How clearly one sees this union with God! How can it be explained, when there is no comparison? Everything is experienced, and in the experience itself everything is understood, but one cannot manage to explain it. They are so intertwined that it is not possible, not even for the one experiencing it, and in the very act one cannot explain it. Only God could explain this" (M 12.1, p. 60f).

    The intimate illuminations must not be confused, however, with the charism of insights and penetrating knowledge that, as we shall see, Mother Rosa very often received from God regarding people and the decisions she had to make.

  • Between the longing for solitude and the demands of God's work.

    • Like all great apostles, Mother Rosa experienced the tension between the need to seek divine intimacy in silence and the peace of retreat and, on the other hand, the impulse to bring to others the good she had received, spreading truth and love, that is, bringing people closer to God.

    In her Genoa years she already knew how to combine this twofold dimension - contemplation and action - dividing her day between the church and the hospital. Once she became foundress, she would make up for the time given during the day to her ever more pressing occupations by taking it from her night's rest to abandon herself to contemplation. Prayer was by now an integral part of her existence; God's infused presence kept her spirit turned unceasingly towards her Good.

    Nevertheless her writings often reveal an almost nostalgic longing for hermit-like solitude. In October 1869, during her spiritual exercises, she was able to enjoy to her heart's content peaceful retreat in her little room in Piacenza; the Lord "gave her very great consolations"; and she envied the happiness of cloistered life:

    "Oh! my God, how happy those souls must be who have given themselves to the contemplative life, blessed in this life and in the eternal one! Poor me, always in the midst of the world! O my Love! in three days I shall leave this cell of mine, and be once more in the midst of the business of your Work, my Love.

    I must do justice to the truth: even amid so much tumult and an abyss of business, I am never deprived of union with my God" (M. 1.1, p. 86).

    To ensure this habitual union with God, she directed the intention of the whole day from the morning, asking God that she might not have a single thought that was not in accordance with his will (cf. M 1.1, p. 113). But the longing for hermit-like retreat insinuates itself again:

    "Oh! the thought of a desert, especially when I had come back from ecstasy...! O my Love! why do you still leave me on this earth? And often a voice said to me:

    - You must work!

    But when I felt so busy I sought my Love:

    - Oh! let me, my Good, go into a desert! There I will see only the sky as your dwelling. What pain to be always in the midst of the world!" (M 1.1, p. 116).

    She often complains of having to leave the intimacy of union to attend to the duties of her office; and then the voice she had heard in Piacenza echoes in her mind: "You must work" (cf. M 4.1, p. 63, 108f). There is also another consideration that helps her overcome the lure of the desert; she writes on May 21, 1876:

    "The desire keeps coming to me to go and shut myself away on a mountain and never see a creature again. But then the thought that I could no longer have my Beloved in holy Communion in the morning stops me" (M 4.4, p. 63).

    When her excessive occupations pressed hardest, she was assailed by the temptation to leave everything and run to the church to resume union with her dear Good; but she resisted. "I was sure," she explains, "that if I stopped dealing with the affairs of the Work to go physically to his feet, he would first of all take away his union from me." Indeed, every time she gave in to such a temptation, she had to pay for it afterwards with aridity and abandonment (M 4.3, pp. 68-70).

    But envy of the cloistered nuns insidiously returned. Thus again on November 28, 1891, once more on the occasion of her spiritual exercises:

    "As soon as I had a taste of my retreat, oh! how sweet it is! What I feel in the solitude of my room I cannot describe. What bliss those souls who are enclosed must enjoy!

    No! my Good has made me feel several times that he does not like this thought. Yes, my Love! I am most happy to be as you have wished me to be, and I bless your hand that has led me" (M 11.3, p. 122f).

    Here is the best answer to the idle question of which vocation is more perfect, the specifically contemplative life or the active life: the more perfect one is the one to which each person has been called.

    But true apostolic action is not possible without the contemplative dimension. As foundress, Mother Rosa teaches the sisters how to achieve this difficult union and instills in them solitude and silence, the indispensable climate for intimacy with God (cf. Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 12-4-1869, 18-9-1869; and to a sister: 8-1-1871).

    In the book Trials and Consolations she left us a delightful dialogue with a "worker" (a daughter of Saint Anne). The sister admits that she does not know "the Master for whom she works"; she thought she loved him, and in fact never served him without loving him:

    "Oh no! He wants to be loved, and more than work he seeks love. Martha, Martha! - said our Master - you are too anxious! While he took delight in Magdalene, who felt great love for him and gave herself wholly to love. We must do the same, for work must never overwhelm prayer" (TC, p. 370f).

    4. Mother Rosa, teacher of prayer.

    From the first day of the foundation she organized the novitiate in Piacenza with an intense schedule of prayer and thus in an atmosphere of retreat. She herself led the morning meditation, generally on the Passion of Christ, in tones full of unction, in order to train the young religious in the practice of mental prayer. In her instructions to the novices she gave primary importance to contemplative prayer. But the most effective lesson was herself: her example, her hours of contemplation, her habitual absorption in God, as well as her words full of fervor and higher light, that gentle and penetrating gaze of hers that questioned silently, and the whole bearing of one who breathes the atmosphere of the divine. For all of them she was the best incentive to commit themselves seriously to the ways of seeking God.

    From the brief recommendations we find in her letters to the sisters we can infer what her spoken exhortations were like, in personal conversations and in conferences, especially during visitations:

    "Prayer is our only shield of defense" - "It is the key to graces" - "Do not forget to stay always in the presence of God the Father; remember the instructions this wretch gave you" - "Ah! what joy to be united with the good God! But you, my dear, if you stay far from this most loving Bridegroom, what can you ever have? Nothing. Go, go and suck the honey of sweetness; he is its very essence, so run to his spring and drink, get drunk!..." (to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 5-12-1868, 18-9-1869, 16-1-1870, 14-11-1873; to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: 3-12-1872).

    In particular she recommended attention and fidelity to God's inspirations, which requires the spirit of prayer that disposes one to listen to the divine calls.

    "Woe to that creature who has become deaf to the inspirations God in his mercy gives her" (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 21-12-1868).

    5. Alone and without a guide on the hard road.

    One of the most persistent inner sufferings in Rosa Gattorno's life was the problem of spiritual direction.

    As a young woman her confessor was the priest Don Antonio Accinelli, assistant pastor of the cathedral, whom she consulted when she was about to marry. Later she placed herself under the direction of Don Giuseppe Firpo, custodian of the metropolitan church; he was a great help to her in the first months of her widowhood, at the time of her decision to consecrate herself to the Lord and during her stay at S. Francesco d'Albaro. Rosa opened her soul to him with complete trust and submitted all her initiatives to his obedience, especially regarding bodily penances; and he took the task of guiding her seriously, having realized that this was a generous soul, extraordinarily favored by God, as appears from the letters of deep ascetical content he wrote to his spiritual daughter in those years.

    But suddenly Rosa broke off his direction on her own initiative, limiting herself to confession alone; until in May 1865 she left him altogether, to the great regret of the good priest, who humbly accepted the decision, fearing that he had given cause for it. In her Memoirs Rosa seems to allude to certain disagreements or difficulties that made her suffer and paved the way for the change of director. In 1861 she complained to the Lord: "I have no one to ask for an opinion and advice: you have taken everything from me, I have only you, my Bridegroom!" (M 1.1, p. 10).

    At one point Don Firpo, seeing her suffer from diabolical harassment and not knowing what to do, wanted to resort to exorcism and obtained the archbishop's permission, which Rosa flatly refused to accept (M 1.1, pp. 31, 55f).

    "Several times I would have liked to turn to some learned priest," she adds, "but Jesus did not want it; and so I stayed with the one he had assigned me" (M 1.1, p. 57).

    In 1864 she had begun going to confession to Don Luigi Cogrossi, with the archbishop's consent; this priest had a reputation for holiness, and Rosa had gone to see him in his home town, Castelleone, in the diocese of Cremona. Don Cogrossi then accompanied her to Rome when she was received in audience by Pius IX, and introduced her to various prominent people in church circles.

    The Servant of God relates how, on her return from Rome, determined to begin the foundation of the Institute in Piacenza, her confessor - probably Don Firpo - disapproved of what she had done (M 2, p. 45). The matter had a happy ending at the beginning of 1867, when Rosa, now foundress, renewed her filial relationship with her former director (cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 22f, 31, 38, 52-56, 66, 174f, 300f).

    Mother Rosa continued under the guidance of the priest from Cremona in Piacenza as well; he was chaplain of the first community, indeed its first ecclesiastical superior, until she removed him in August 1867.

    Before that date, however, the foundress had discovered in Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a priest of the Mission known in Piacenza for his learning and ascetical life, the man Providence had sent her to advise her in those first steps of the Institute and also in the perplexities of her spirit. The role he played in shaping the foundation has earned him from the Daughters of Saint Anne the recognition of the title of cofounder (20).

    From the first moment the difficulty appeared of reconciling the external relationship, concerning the work, with the internal one of spiritual direction. The foundress became aware of a certain incompatibility with the pious and austere religious because of their different spiritual experience. She herself mentions it:

    "Not knowing where to go to confession, I felt the desire to go to Mr. Tornatore, and the first few times I liked it; but then he made me feel a certain fear: his direction was so different from my former one! Well, I did not let it trouble me much, because my guide was my Jesus in everything and through everything" (M 2, p. 55f).

    In fact, throughout 1869 she felt "alone, without comfort" (M 1.2, p. 29). A hard blow to her sensitivity of faith was the unjust harshness shown her on March 31, 1869, by Fr. Tornatore, misled by the deceptions of the community's superior, who even deprived her of communion (cf. M 1.2, p. 21-29). She nevertheless remained under his direction.

    This heroic faith in God's representative was put to the test again in January 1870, when she learned by divine light that her director was going about telling things about her spirit. She had decided to leave him, but the soul of Fr. Bernardo appeared to her and ordered her to return to the cofounder's guidance (M 1.1, p. 89, 92) (21).

    At the end of 1870 Mother Rosa lamented: "Oh! blessed are those souls who have direction that comforts them, reassures them, lifts them up! But I?.." (M 1.1, p. 94). Similar laments, often very bitter, would recur from time to time in the following years, especially at times of aridity and of her Good's withdrawal, when she felt alone, abandoned in the cruelest darkness. One of the reasons she felt the lack of a director was not knowing whether her penances, so carefully sought out, were according to God's will or merely satisfied her craving for suffering. Usually everything ended with the certainty that Jesus communicated to her directly: I am your guide. At other times her Good's voice reached her through mysterious intermediaries: one was the Fr. Bernardo already mentioned, the other a luminous cloud that came to her aid, clearing up her uncertainties or revealing hidden things to her. This is how she puts it at the beginning of 1871:

    "Now I need to know certain hidden things: and he, my Love, comes, teaches me like a master, furnishes me with most sublime knowledge, sustains me in certain struggles. I find myself alone, but I desire no one, because my Good helps me, directs me, comforts me, gives me life... My cloud is always near me and is very red; and because it prompts and teaches me, I hear a voice coming from it. Oh! sweetness beyond compare!..." (M 1.1, p. 107) (22).

    In that same year 1871 Fr. Tornatore, worried about Mother Rosa's health, tried to forbid her privations in food; this gave her a new reason to close herself more and more to his direction (M 1.2, p. 42f). But the decisive break in communication, not only in the internal forum but also in what concerned the direction of the Institute, came with the order sent from Rome in February 1872 to the cofounder himself, drastically forbidding him to approach the Daughters of Saint Anne in future or to hear their confessions, all because of the part he had played in drafting the text of the Rules. On the following March 13, when she asked for the Father's speedy return, she wished to resume his direction once more (M 3, p. 3, 7). In that situation she turned to the Holy Spirit and found in him light and strength, as appears in some of her notes from the same year: (23)

    "I feel it is affirmed to me by my governing Spirit. What a consolation it is for me, so abandoned by all human help, to have my dear Spirit, who guides me in everything and sustains me so well!..."

    - "Since my director is God, the Being who lives for me made me feel how he wanted me to offer him three penances..."

    - "A voice said to me: I am your Master, be at peace! The peace of conscience I enjoy is such that I see there is a most powerful Spirit who rules and governs me."

    - "How many beautiful things he told me and taught me, especially for the Work!... How many caresses when he says to me: My Rosa, courage, for I am with you! do not doubt!"

    - "Alone as I am..., yet it does not confuse me, because my Jesus resolves every point for me one by one. I feel, and see more clearly, that I am guided by my Spirit. My cloud has been far away for some time..." (M 3, p. 11f, 26; 4.1, p. 4, 6).

    But then came the terrible trial of God's abandonment, and she filled her diary with heart-rending cries:

    "Ah! how painful my present state is! My poor soul, alone, an anchoress in the midst of the great world, an orphan...; and when it finds itself desolate and plunged in the bitterest tribulations..., it has lost its Being and cannot find him anywhere..."

    - "Alone! Not a word of comfort from anyone. Alone! alone! in the midst of so great a Work... And then so many souls that I must direct, the responsibility for them...: alone! with no one to tell what my soul is suffering!..." (M 3, p. 27f, 55f).

    To the loneliness caused by aridity was added the fear of making mistakes, indeed of taking the enemy's suggestions for God's voice, of being the cause of some disaster for God's Work (M 4.1, p. 44f, 44-79, 66f; March-April 1873).

    In June 1873 she felt a strong and repeated urge to confide fully in a certain priest, whose name she would not give, telling him everything, even what passed in secret between God and herself, because that situation had become unbearable for her; she feared that this too might be suggested by the enemy or invented by her own mind. She turned to her Good, asking him for light on what to do; the resistance was strong:

    "My Beloved, you alone, you alone! Ah! go on being my guide; do not let me have to tell anyone what you deign to communicate to me! For a good 20 years now the world has known nothing of my affairs: now that I am so worn down, must I suffer such grief? At the mere thought I feel faint. You, my Good, know how much it cost me to hand over certain writings and tell my affairs to one single person: how could I manage it with others too?... Let me stay as I am! You tell me how I am to conduct myself in everything, and do not let me have to turn to others" (M 4.1, pp. 71-75).

    The inner voice insisted: "Turn to the one I told you to go to!" (M 4.1, p. 76f). In fact, in June she seems to have tried to begin a relationship of direction with that very person (M 4.1, pp. 96-99). It was perhaps Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Order of Minims († 1907), with whom Mother Rosa had kept up from 1870 a spiritual correspondence of some intimacy; this relationship, maintained until her death, does not seem to have reached the level of true direction. The fact is that she went on feeling alone. In that same month of June she wrote: "I have no one to say a word to. There are moments when I feel I am dying; what I feel only God sees; alone I stifle everything..." (M 4.1, p. 103). Then scruples were added, indeed the fear of "going mad" (M 1.2, pp. 55, 58, 68). A voice that often seemed an insidious temptation kept whispering to her: "Do you think you do well to guide yourself? And are you sure that everything is from God?" But the Lord did not fail her in difficult moments (M 4.2, p. 6f), and reassured her: "I am your guide, your comfort" (M 4.2, pp. 44, 76).

    At the beginning of 1875, and again in 1877, she consulted a priest, perhaps the confessor of the Piacenza community, whom she greatly esteemed, but only regarding her penances (M 4.3, p. 14; 4.4, pp. 96-98, 101f). Throughout these years she continues to lament:

    "Alone in this land of exile!" - "Alone, without human comfort!" - "Alone, alone! There is not one creature I can say a word to" - "My God, how painful my state is, full of anguish over certain extraordinary things the Lord works in me, with no one to turn to!" - "Alone, with no one to say a word to! Jesus, you know well that this is how you placed me and kept me: you do not want me to turn to anyone... It is your affair, my God!" - "I am alone with my beloved Master" (M 1.2, pp. 27, 90, 101, 109f; 4,4, pp. 110, 116f, 121).

    In June 1880, during her visitation of the houses, she had the good fortune to make her confession to "a holy religious," greatly favored by God. She went out of her senses before receiving absolution, without the confessor noticing. Afterwards she wrote in her notes:

    "How much a good and learned director is worth at certain moments! Yes, my God, to be guided by one who is learned and holy, as I had the good fortune to find for confession: O my Jesus! you truly granted me the grace of finding a saint; oh! how well he read my soul!" (M 4.5, pp. 183-185, 212).

    In March 1884 she was at last convinced she had found the "learned and holy" director in Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro, minister general of the Friars Minor since 1869, a truly extraordinary man under whose government his Order undertook its restoration after a century of suppressions and ruin (24). But God allowed the confessions she made to him to become a new source of disturbance. Shortly afterwards she wrote:

    "I am alone, Jesus has abandoned me!... I go to confession, and what does he say to me? When I tell him: I am full of sins, I cannot tell them apart, - Calm down, where are they?... So will it be because my Good does not want me to put myself in the hands of anyone's obedience but his?" (M 5.2, pp. 35f, 47-49).

    When she heard the lives of the saints read, saints who had the help of a guide, she felt envious. On August 29 of that year Jesus assured her that it was his will that she put herself under the direction of the Father General; and she promised to tell him everything without reserve, even if it cost her a thousand agonies. But on the 31st of the same month she discovered within herself the real cause of that resistance: having to give up the comfort of Jesus' direct guidance:

    "While I see that my Good's will is clear that I should give my direction to the one I mentioned above, yet I think that if my Love wants this, then he will leave me, he will no longer come to tell me what I am to do; in short, he will no longer be my teacher, but will leave me to receive everything from the one who guides me. Oh! piercing thought!... Oh! what will become of me? how shall I get used to it?" (M 5.2, pp. 73, 80f, 84, 91-93).

    The resistance continued, despite her readiness to place herself under the Father's obedience; every page of the diary faithfully reflects the strong tension of her spirit:

    "Oh! when I lived under the direction of my Good alone...! but now, oh! how hard this state is! I certainly deserved it, because too often I complained of being alone. But now, how do I find myself?... Alone and worse than alone!... O my Love, where are you? Why have you left me so cruelly? If you do not want me to be under direction, oh! a single sign, and I am alone again!... Oh! how I suffer for having given, in some way, the direction of my soul!..."

    - "But tell me, my Love, was it not you who worked in me when you commanded me so forcefully to give my direction to that religious?..."

    - "O my Love, why do you now want me directed by one of your ministers? It pains me, because I have been too badly spoiled: no direction satisfies me, however learned... I cannot adapt..." (M 5.3, pp. 6f, 17, 24-28, 32f).

    The months of 1884 and early 1885 were months of terrible suffering. She feared she had gone too far, especially in giving her intimate writings to her confessor to read. She repeats bitterly: "What have I done?" In a moment of supreme grief she exclaims: "O Jesus, my Good! if I manage to get out of this, I will certainly never do such a thing again! I suffer too much!" (M 5.3, pp. 32-36, 51).

    In March 1885 she says she broke off the direction "because of a strong repugnance," perhaps on the occasion of her third journey to Sicily. It was indeed on this journey that, passing through Naples, she met again Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, a priest since 1879, and formed a deep spiritual friendship with him. Shortly afterwards their correspondence began, and it became more and more frequent. She must have told him of her sufferings regarding direction. Perhaps it was he who suggested the formula she expresses on her return to Rome:

    "Subject, but not bound or tied" to Fr. Portogruaro (M 5.3, p. 57), that is, attentive to the light received from the Lord. Nevertheless the situation remained difficult throughout 1885 (M 4.3, pp. 60, 63, 68, 70-72, 82, 90-92, 99; 5.4, pp. 19f, 26f, 39, 59f).

    She offered the Lord that arid obedience, to which she had bound herself by vow (M 5.4, p. 69). Indeed, she blessed God, because in this way she felt free of attachment to her spiritual Father, which often robs sisters of freedom of spirit, as she had been able to observe in her visits to the communities (M 5.4, pp. 100f; 5.5, pp. 15-19, 53, 71f).

    During Fr. Bernardino's long absences it was even worse, because the ordinary confessor merely heard her accusation and gave her absolution. There was no lack of days of light and peace in loving union with the supreme Good; often comfort also came to her from the soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, first superior of the Palermo house, who died on June 7, 1885, a true example of holiness.

    In 1887 her contacts with Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte became more frequent and had by now become true spiritual direction, to the point that she gave him a good part of her writings to read, though without Fr. Bernardino's knowledge, which caused her fresh worries (M 5.5, pp. 86-89; Letter to Don Gennaro: 24-9-1887).

    For two years now she had received nothing but curt answers from this good Father, and he never asked her anything about her inner life; from his reasoning she had the impression that he did not understand her. She thought of changing director, entrusting herself to one with whom she could communicate without effort; but the Lord made her understand that this would not be good for her, "because the Work would have suffered harm." And, as at other times, she heard: "Be at peace: I am your director and teacher... They will never manage to understand you, since I am the craftsman of the work taking place in you" (M 9.2, pp. 3-5, 10-12).

    She wrote again in February 1888, not without a critical recollection of the ties of the past:

    "Confusion: have I always done wrong?... What it means not to have a guide to act and put a little order! I would never advise a human being to remain without a guide, never! And the guide must be learned, so as never to allow promises and vows for an indefinite time; no! everything for a set time, because illnesses come, age, sorrows, that is, infirmity...: and what happens then? What is happening to me!"

    - "I am an exile in the midst of the great world..., I have no one to say a word to..."

    - "Alone! everything is darkness and pain to me... I thought I was understood by my guide - not at all! quite the opposite! Oh! unhappy the soul that never has the good fortune to be understood! I see my state clearly, but when I explain it I see they take one thing for another... Oh! only those souls will be able to understand me who have loved much and then find themselves down in the most wretched abyss" (M 9.2, p. 23; 9.3, pp. 2, 6, 21; 9.4, p. 7, 38).

    She therefore decided to place herself fully under Don Gennaro's guidance, while continuing to make her confession to Fr. Bernardino; this seems to follow from an undated letter to Don Gennaro himself. But she had to be convinced once again that it was not part of God's plans that she should have any comfort in spiritual direction: on the one hand the distance and having to open her soul by letter, on the other the realization that her dear Don Gennaro too, so clear-sighted in other matters and in the problems of the Institute, seemed instead, by God's permission, to understand nothing of his spiritual daughter's inner life.

    In the following years the same laments recur in the Memoirs because she feels alone, the same envy of souls who have the good fortune to have a director, the same inner voice assuring her: "I am your guide" (M 9.5, pp. 92-113; 9.6, pp. 1-8; 11.2, pp. 71f, 75-77, 89; 12.1, pp. 36, 45f, 152f).

    Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro finished his term as general in 1889; he died in 1895. Mons. Granito di Belmonte was sent to Paris in 1893 to serve at the nunciature there and in 1899 was appointed apostolic nuncio in Brussels; Mother Rosa, who always kept up a spiritual correspondence of great trust with him, had the joy of attending his episcopal consecration in the church of the Generalate on November 26 of that year.

    The Servant of God's last confessor was the Capuchin Fr. Vincenzo d'Alatri, who assisted her at the moment she flew to her blessed homeland. Did what she had foreseen and written down almost three decades earlier come true in that supreme hour?

    "He showed me what will happen at my death...; and the one who has influence over him (Jesus in the Sacrament) will be the one who has my final direction, for I shall live by obedience, but he will take care not to command me things he has not first felt deeply within himself" (M 1.1, p. 164).

We come to the subject that most attracts attention in the lives of the great mystics and that at the same time raises the greatest difficulties from a scientific point of view; indeed, in our case it is precisely what called Rosa Gattorno's psychological normality into question.

In general, prejudice against bodily mystical phenomena comes from their spectacular character, that is, from the suspicion that at bottom there is nothing but an unconscious desire for exhibitionism. So unbelieving or simply positivist scientists list all these phenomena - visions, raptures, stigmatizations, diabolical harassments - under certain common headings in the field of psychiatry: hysteria, hallucinations, erotic sublimations... It must be said, however, that in Rosa Gattorno's case any motive of exhibitionism must be absolutely excluded. Her great concern throughout her life was that no one should notice anything extraordinary there might be in God's gifts, or in her bodily mortifications. Had she not written her Memoirs and her confidential letters to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, everything would have remained hidden.

She wrote on May 21, 1876:

"I overcame myself and revealed a certain thing which, out of shame, I had resolved not to tell. Oh! how it costs me to tell what my Good does in me! Oh! a thousand times I would tell in public the horrible sins I committed, but the graces he gives me, oh! for me that is the most painful suffering I can have" (M 4.4, p. 62f).

Let us try to shed light on this aspect of her spiritual profile, bearing in mind, however, that it is not extraordinary gifts, even the most authentic, that prove a person's holiness, especially since, as was said at the outset, there always remains the problem of distinguishing the field of God's action from that of the subject's own elaboration.

First of all we must recall the teaching of the great master of mysticism, Saint John of the Cross, on the criteria of discernment to be applied to every extraordinary phenomenon. He warns in particular about "locutions," since there are spiritual persons who "very easily form words and arguments, so much so that it seems to the subject that it is not he who does all this, but that another person is suggesting the arguments, answers and teachings to him interiorly. And indeed he reasons with himself and answers himself as if he were one person with another; and in a way it can be said to be so, for although the human spirit is what is at work, it is nevertheless helped by the Holy Spirit to produce and form those true concepts, words and arguments...." The holy doctor does not claim these are hallucinations, but a true divine action that the subject perceives in his own way, according to his facility for giving form to what he experiences. The mystic, finding himself in that still very peripheral zone of the unitive process between infused recollection and rapture - that is, in full command of his sensory and intellectual faculties - translates his unusual experience into visual, auditory, tactile and imaginative forms, without realizing that everything is the product of his own creativity, though under supernatural operation. This takes nothing away from the mystic's sincerity. Such creativity will be more or less fruitful according to temperament, sensitivity, imagination and personal circumstances.

Now, among the human qualities of Rosa Gattorno's rich feminine personality is her creative and figurative fertility, that is, the art of transposing ordinary realities into symbol and allegory. Her book Trials and Consolations is the most splendid demonstration of it.

I think, therefore, that the question of whether the various phenomena reviewed below are supernatural or not is out of place: it is enough to rely on the absolutely unimpeachable sincerity with which the Servant of God commits to paper the moment she lived, just as she perceived it.

Another premise to bear in mind: Mother Rosa lists endlessly interior lights, insights into hearts, foreknowledge of future events, visions..., yet she never speaks of revelations, never of messages to be delivered to anyone, and we never see her base her conduct or decisions on what she has seen or understood, though at times she feels bound to warn, in the strictest secrecy, those who confide in her. She feels guided by God, taught and upheld by her Good, which gives her such confidence and assurance in matters concerning the Work of the Lord that she faces every distressing situation calmly, precisely because she is convinced she is a pure and useless instrument of the divine plan. But we shall deal with this awareness of her mission as foundress later.

1. Interior charismatic gifts.

Besides the ineffable lights and communications that form part of infused contemplative experience, as we saw in the previous chapter, there are also certain free gifts, perceived inwardly under various forms or symbols, about which Mother Rosa herself gives us very precise information.

The light of discernment - Insight into people's inner lives

At the beginning of the foundation, one day Rosa heard these words from Jesus in answer to her desire to be useful to the souls entrusted to her:

"Every time you need to see and penetrate certain hearts, you will see them thus. Whatever you ask me for the good of the souls who are with you and in your care, I will give you all of it, and likewise for what you desire for priests: exactly what you want me to give them through your prayer, I will give them. You will clearly distinguish the good from the wicked; I will make you feel revulsion when they have indecent thoughts against chastity: you will feel it at once and be warned, do not doubt... Likewise for false devotees you will have special lights to distinguish them well..." (M 1.1, p. 63).

Whether a gift of God or a special natural intuition, or both together, the fact is that she constantly experienced an extraordinary faculty of seeing into people's intentions and situations, especially those of her spiritual daughters; the sisters themselves and others who knew her observed this with amazement: they were convinced that Mother Rosa read consciences. She says so repeatedly in her Memoirs:

"I was filled with knowledge, furnished with clear light. I read hearts: there were moments when I saw everything that was passing in people's hearts" (M 1.2, p. 7).

- "How many things I see in certain hearts!... This very day - but I can only remain in great peace - I saw a prelate..., what sorrow!" (M 4.1, p. 70).

- "Seeing in the sisters the smallest things passing within them; so many that I say nothing, otherwise they would notice too much" (M 4.1, p. 110).

She suffers when she sees that someone thinks inwardly differently from what they say with their lips, and she has to pretend not to know.

"I cannot bear duplicity," she often adds (cf. M 1.1, pp. 81, 139-141; 4.1, pp. 82-85; 4.2, pp. 25f, 32f, 73-75; 4.3, p. 57; 4.5, p. 192).

The inner voice - The cloud - Friendly souls.

In moments of perplexity, or of darkness and abandonment, when she feels alone, without the guidance of a director - as has been said - she suddenly hears within her a voice that gives her assurance, peace and light on the problem she faces. Sometimes it is the answer to her prayer:

"Tell me, my Beloved, what must I do?" Often it is a reproach for some infidelity or some resistance to what God wants. At other times the voice of the supreme Good becomes a sensible perception of divine help in the form of a true dictation of what she is to write or say to people.

She writes in November 1873:

"I have letters to write. Since I am an ignorant beast, he dictates to me what I must say. I am with people discussing important matters of the Work: something happens in me, as though there were a person within me speaking for me, because the words come out without my knowing what I am saying. I feel and understand that they are not mine, because I would not be capable of saying them: my God, he makes the most ignorant of creatures speak and act, as I am" (M 4.2, p. 15f).

On December 31 of that year she was visiting one of the houses, where she found a certain disorder about which she did not know how to admonish the sisters. She turned to the Lord, praying: "You speak for me!" She writes: "My Good, I was astonished to hear how well you spoke: I listened to you and repeated it" (M 4.2, p. 26f). She experienced divine assistance in this way especially when she gave conferences to the sisters or led meditations. What she wrote in April 1874, in humble confusion, deserves to be transcribed in full:

"I cannot fail to record what the Lord works in me when I must speak in conference to the daughters of Saint Anne. As soon as I recollect myself and go to the Crucified, my Good - Your ignorant slave must speak and must treat of perfection; you, my beloved Master, prompt me, and I will repeat it - something happens in me which, if the creatures listening to me saw it, would certainly amaze them; but my All does not allow it...

He seems to come close to me; often he dictates to me things from Sacred Scripture, suggests things I never knew, puts other most beautiful things into my mind to say. Often I too enjoy what I am saying. At other times not: I speak as if in the third person, and understand nothing of what I am saying or of what I have said at the end.

What mercy! He sees the need of these creatures, he speaks through the mouth of a she-ass, he does not withdraw, that is, he does not turn away on seeing my wickedness, but for the good of his dear souls he makes use of a most wretched creature to tell and make his will felt to these brides of his" (M 4.2, pp. 78-80).

In the Memoirs she also speaks very often of certain intermediary voices, like the one that seemed to come from within a cloud to guide her in the absence of any other guide. She speaks of this cloud as early as 1869:

"Whenever I need it, it advises me, tells me what to do, how to conduct myself, and I feel comforted in my adversities"

- "I always see it beside me..., and a voice comes out of it that fills me with paradise and I am absorbed... I look at it and ask it: Prompt me, for I do not know what to say, my Being, my dear Love! For I am convinced that it is he who is within it, and I hear the voice..." (M 1.1, pp. 85-87).

Mother Rosa perceives the closeness of the supreme Good, who assists and guides her, in the company of certain friendly souls, that is, of deceased persons to whom she has felt and still feels spiritually bound. One of these souls is that of the holy Capuchin lay brother Fra Francesco da Camporosso, who died in 1866 and was canonized in 1962; another is that of Fr. Bernardo Clausi, whom we already know; she very often speaks of the help she received from him in the doubts and uncertainties that afflicted her (25); there are the souls of some daughters of Saint Anne: in 1874 she felt comforted several times by her "dear friend" Rosa (M 4.2, pp. 53f, 56, 67, 80); later by Sister Anna Serafina, whom she calls "my third angel" (M 4.1, pp. 25-27, 45); but with none would she remain more intimately united than with her most faithful Sister Anna del Salvatore, who died, as has been said, on June 7, 1885, with a reputation for holiness: from that date we find her constantly present in the Memoirs; she also speaks of her in her letters to Mons. Granito di Belmonte and to Princess di Fitalia as a powerful intercessor with God.

Signs and foreknowledge of future events.

It is characteristic of people of faith, who live in the certainty of God's loving providence over human affairs, to watch for the signs through which that love manifests itself. Rosa Gattorno is convinced that she is the object of special assistance from her Good, even as regards the immediate future. And very often she is able to verify that her forecasts prove true. She does not always manage to interpret the meaning of the signs, however, and then she waits to see what will happen.

These signs take various forms. Sometimes she sees a veil of sadness on the Lord's face or his Heart painfully pierced; at other times the veil of sadness covers the face of Mother Saint Anne. One of the most frequent signs is that of one or more stars, which she interprets as announcing the death of some daughter of Saint Anne; if the star is large, the deceased is a superior. The sight of a skull or skeleton likewise foretells someone's approaching death; the first of these warnings came to her in the form of a vision in 1857, when she saw the image of Jesus of Nazareth with the features of a skeleton, a presage of her husband's death (FIOCCHI, I, p. 35). There is also another sign: an "ugly beast" that announces ill-omened things to her; she calls it "the messenger of bad weather" (M 3, p. 68). She foresees wars, epidemics, famines and other public calamities, as well as the success or failure of certain undertakings. Very often she knows of things happening at a distance; she writes, for example, in a letter to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte:

"It is happening in a house in America: painful things! I see everything... But must I tell everything?" (Undated letter no. 345).

Some of her knowledge of distant events and some of her forecasts seem to have been accurate, since they are confirmed by the testimonies in the Process; in five of the letters to Princess di Fitalia, the princess noted her surprise on finding that everything had happened as Mother Rosa had written to her (cf. L 8-3-1891, 14-3-1891, 16-3-1897, 29-6-1897). On the other hand, certain forecasts of political events are doubtful as true prophecies, since they are probably recollections written after the events and thus a retrospective reading of them (26).

It would be idle to raise the question of the prophetic value of the many, many forecasts the Servant of God considered inspired. Certainly the one she wrote in April 1885 about the imminent death of Leo XIII was not of divine origin; it was to be followed by the disastrous election of his immediate successor and then by the election of "a saint" who would do great things for the Church. The saintly pope was in fact Pius X, Leo XIII's immediate successor (cf. M 5.3, p. 85; letter to Mons. Granito, undated, no. 352).

The fact that the Servant of God interpreted as supernatural light what was only the imaginative expression of a hope or fear of hers takes nothing away from her sincerity.

2. Visions and representations.

It is not easy to distinguish visions from signs and apparitions under various forms, just as it is impossible to classify them according to the classical scheme: intellectual, imaginary, corporeal.

Indeed, since Rosa Gattorno almost always experiences them at night, more precisely in a half-waking state, it is often impossible even to determine whether they are dreams or true representations. Sometimes she speaks of real dreams, like the one she tells Princess di Fitalia about in a letter: she saw her own mother dressed as a daughter of Saint Anne in paradise (L 8-1-1896), or the other about something that had really happened to that same correspondent, as the latter noted in the margin (L 23-1-1896).

Since "she was a young girl" - she would recall it in 1870 - she had been favored by God with "beautiful visions" (M 1.1, p. 88). In 1859 in Genoa, during the novena of Our Lady of the Vines, so rich in deep experiences and consolations, she had important visions (M 1.1, p. 3). In the following years they became more and more frequent and very varied: of the person of Christ, of Our Lady, of Saint Anne, of Saint Michael, of Saint Francis of Assisi, of groups of angels, of the glory of heaven, of purgatory, of hell. There is no lack of symbolic and enigmatic visions whose meaning she herself cannot explain, like the one she described in 1887 in a letter to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte:

"I want to tell you a little incident: you will tell me what it means. Listen: last night, it must have been half past eleven, I went to bed because of my head (my headache); I saw the window shutters as if they were all fire, but without flame. When this was over, having lasted a good 10 minutes, there appeared a magnificent rose, beautiful and of immense size: slowly it flew up to heaven. Then another, smaller one, and it did the same; another, much smaller than the second, yet it made the same journey and flew away. What can it be? I could not understand anything: oh! blessed ignorance! I really am a goose. Tell me something" (L 14-5-1887).

The most beautiful visions, usually accompanied by rapture and an intense unitive experience, are those she has from time to time in the chapel before the Blessed Sacrament, in connection with the Eucharist. Indeed, I would say that these are the true mystical visions, while all the others could be counted among those representations which psychologists call "sensory illusions" or "hypnagogic visions," frequent even in normal people (27). In fact the Servant of God herself describes them as something different, as an objectively experienced reality: "I saw with my bodily eyes" - "He showed himself to me so clearly" (cf. M 1.1, pp. 9, 14f, 16, 24, 35).

The first vision, during the novena mentioned in 1859, was indeed an indelible experience of Eucharistic union:

"While the Blessed Sacrament was exposed for Benediction, I saw in the most holy Host the living Blood, which seemed to be pouring out. What this sight produced in me I cannot express: a union, a fire that devoured me! But, foolish as I was, I paid no attention, thinking it was something ordinary. Oh! how great is the goodness of my Jesus!" (M 1.1, p. 2) (28).

Far from being an exhibitionist visionary, Rosa Gattorno always kept this gift of divine goodness secret as well; she confided her many representations only to paper. In her responsibility as foundress she showed concern about spiritual directors who gave too much credence to sisters who claimed to have visions, with the risk of fostering a false spirituality and of making such souls fall into Satan's snares (cf. M 5.3, p. 100f).

3. Bodily mystical phenomena.

Raptures and ecstasies.

The stage of infused prayer called ecstatic seems to have begun at the same time as the first visions in 1859. The first description of an ecstasy properly so called is found in Rosa Gattorno's recollections among the graces received in 1861. Before the Blessed Sacrament exposed she had a vision of the Redeemer's blood; then she adds:

"I remained in ecstasy and did not know, could not say anything more; and all one can say to a God so merciful to a poor ignorant creature is little and nothing. After a good while I turned to my Father Saint Francis, to all the seraphim and cherubim: that they might sing hymns of thanks and gratitude to my God for me" (M 1.1, p. 12).

It seems to have been a gentle rapture, with strong absorption in God and suspension of the faculties, but without loss of the senses.

In 1862 complete raptures were frequent, sometimes even with levitation, during which her spirit was enlightened with ineffable knowledge and unitive embraces. When this happened during community acts, she remained still and insensible, so that no one noticed - she had asked Jesus for this and he had promised it to her - but when she was alone in her little room, her body was at the mercy of the intensity of the ecstasy:

"I abandoned myself with complete freedom, united to my Good, whereas outside, on the contrary, I always distracted myself, kept myself always busy with material things and even fled from sermons, because, out of the immense greed I had for the word of God, I would go to them, (but) I had to leave, because I was always afraid...; but in my room, especially at night, which I spent entirely alone with him..." (M 1.1, pp. 21, 23f, 34f).

Interesting is the description of the ecstatic process, with rapture and vision, that she managed to give in one of her pages:

"Oh! if only I could describe what I saw and felt on the eve of All Saints, in the year 1866! O my Love! I am too ignorant to find words adequate for a fitting account! But what! what human pen can ever describe paradise? With your help, my Love, I will put something on this paper.

At half past three I felt such a strong breathlessness come over me, and something that carried me away. The breathlessness grew, and the rapture increased more and more. I seemed to be dying. I felt that something was about to happen in me. Oh! Love!

When I was completely absorbed in God, I rejoiced, oh! sweetness beyond compare! I saw the feast being prepared in heaven... And the sight of my Good remained always before me...; in short, I kept feeling something as though I were not yet entirely released from the vision, rapture, I do not know. And lo, carried away once more, I find myself beside the side of my Beloved! oh! what I felt!..." (M 1.1, p. 40f).

Similar descriptions abound in Mother Rosa's intimate diary; there is no doubt that these are true unitive raptures, with all the features common to such phenomena. They are often prolonged: "I spend periods when I do not remember being alive; and having come back from ecstasy, I remain absorbed for hours" (M 1.1, p. 98).

"A drowsiness came over me slowly, slowly. It seemed as if they lifted me into the air, always with my God, and so I remained until morning" (M 3, p. 80).

In her memorable conference on the love of God of March 14, 1872, she described to the sisters, speaking in the third person, one of her raptures at the moment of Communion:

"All at once an arrow strikes her in the heart; it burns her left arm. She does not know what to do in that state; she cannot go out. All at once she falls asleep, enjoys, rejoices, feels her God within her, sees his love; she feels the flames of her God's fire burning her. In that state she feels nothing human any more; they prick her, they shake her: she is insensible; and it is such that, if God did not withdraw little by little, she would die. In short, she... sees her God, feels him, tastes him, and at that moment her body is dead to the earth" (29).

It is characteristic of ecstatic experience to lose the sense of time and space, since infused communications are not subject to perceptual or discursive succession or to localized projection. She herself says so precisely:

"Whoever is in that state has no awareness either of the hours or of anything earthly" (M 4.3, p. 4f).

Once the intense moment of rapture has passed, its effects continue for a long time; the senses remain as if asleep, consciousness of external realities returns slowly, while the spirit struggles to free itself from the intoxication of union.

"I remained so united," she writes at Pentecost 1878, after describing an ecstasy she had at night, "that all day long I seemed to be still in the midst of what I had seen and felt" (M 1.2, p. 116f).

Her concern to prevent others from noticing appears constantly; she trusts in the Lord's repeated promise, and prays to him: "My Good, when I am alone, do with me what you will, burn me, consume me, annihilate me, but let no one notice!" (M 1.1, p. 51).

She often has to do constant violence to herself to keep her attention on what she is doing or what is being said to her (M 1.2, p. 113f). But however hard she tries to attend outwardly and however secure she is in Jesus' promise, she does not always manage to escape the eyes of those present.

One day in 1890, while she was speaking to the novices about the love of God, she became so inflamed that they saw her raised about a hand's breadth above the floor for almost half an hour (30).

Before that date, however, these phenomena accompanying mystical absorption had almost disappeared, owing to the harmony achieved between the spirit, invaded by the divine, and the lower part, as usually happens in the higher stage of transforming union. She herself noted this in June 1885:

"I feel little or nothing of rapture, and union with God is different" (M 5.4, p. 22) (31).

Crown of thorns - Stigmata.

Christ Crucified was the center of Rosa Gattorno's spirituality, and so configuration to him, in spirit and in body, could not but be her supreme longing. Her favorite daily contemplation was that of the Passion. As in other genuine stigmatics, this contemplation and that conforming love disposed her to receive the gift of the bodily projection of the Redeemer's wounds, which were already imprinted on her spirit (32). Only, in keeping with her desire not to attract admiration through extraordinary graces, she obtained from the Lord that everything should remain hidden: she had the pain of the wounds, but not the external signs.

Her painful participation in the Redeemer's Passion began shortly after her husband's death. From the sisters' testimonies and from the Memoirs we know that Mother Rosa spent the sacred triduum - Holy Thursday, Good Friday and Holy Saturday - completely withdrawn in her room and in absolute fasting. But no one witnessed what the Lord made her experience in those days, until on Good Friday 1886 Sister A. Camilla Valentini managed by a stratagem to enter her room in Rome: she found the Mother stretched out as if on a cross, in an excruciating agony caused by the pains of the crown of thorns, of the wounds in her hands and feet, of her whole body. She was able to observe at close quarters the marks of the thorns on her forehead and, in the palms of her hands, what looked like a hard nail of flesh. When asked how long these things had been happening to her, the Mother replied: "Twenty-eight years" (the witness says she did not understand clearly whether she meant at the age of 28 or for 28 years). And she confided to her that such sufferings were renewed every Friday, though not with that intensity. She imposed absolute secrecy on her, however, about what she had learned on that occasion. And the sister kept the secret until after the Foundress's death (FIOCCHI, II, pp. 202-204).

Among the fruits of that 1859 novena of Our Lady of the Vines was the desire to share in the pains of the Savior's crown of thorns. One day she felt two angels place the longed-for crown on her head and experienced the pricking of the thorns: "the desire to suffer was great, the pleasure was immense," she writes; "how happy I would have been if they had left it on me forever!"

She obtained her confessor's permission to make one and wear it on her head on the night from Friday to Saturday; but she had to stop, because one night it left a wound on her forehead which swelled, and she had to hide it with her hair so that her family would not notice (M 1.1, p. 6f). We do not know whether the severe and very localized headache she often mentions was due to natural causes or had a mystical origin; a remark of hers on December 28, 1876, might suggest such a gift (M 4.4, p. 88f).

The pain of the wounds in her feet, hands and side, on the other hand, was permanent, renewed more intensely every Friday. In 1862, during the novena of the Savior, she had "very severe pains in her hands, feet and heart." Before that date she had tied a small crucifix to her breast, over her heart, and kept it pressed there day and night for five years, until gangrene set in because it had penetrated the flesh; she was ordered to remove it (M 1.1, p. 32; FIOCCHI, I, p. 45 note 5).

In the brief affective and unitive meditations of Lent 1864 her longing to share in all Jesus' sufferings is evident; in that of the 44th day she writes:

"Tell me, my Love: I think I have been able to do everything to try to follow you in your sufferings, but I do not know how to obtain that nails be driven into my hands and feet..." (M 2, p. 167).

When she made her meditation on the Passion - and later too, when she meditated supported on a cross she kept in her little room - she would have liked to feel herself hanging from real nails and to experience an actual crucifixion (M 2, p. 169f).

The eve of January 1, 1867, when the Servant of God was in Rome, could be given as the date of the invisible stigmatization. The day before, she had meditated in an extraordinary way on Jesus' sufferings in the Passion; at night, her heart on fire with love, she wanted to climb the Holy Stairs, her favorite devotion on every visit to the eternal city. She writes:

"I was carried away and remained in my God, so united with my Beloved that I no longer lived. I felt great consolations. I was seized by the pain in my hands, feet and heart, and when I came to, all my veins seemed filled with boiling blood; the area of my heart seemed open too. What I felt was beyond expression.

Having recovered, I forced myself and went back home... The fire grew so much that I seemed to be consumed. My Love came near me and caressed me; the pains in my hands, feet and heart increased and I seemed to be breathing my last... and I remained in ecstasy a long time..." (M 1.1, p. 49f).

From that date on she would very often mention the permanent pain of the internal wounds. At times she observed, not without concern, that external signs were appearing as well. Thus at the beginning of January 1870:

"I had very severe pains in my hands, feet and side: the spasms were terrible, so that I often resorted to water for relief. Oh! what torments! And they never stop, because they ease a little during the day so that I can work, and then, my Love!

One day they were so strong that, having shut myself in my room, I looked at my feet, where the pains were cruelest, and found in the middle a swelling almost two fingers high, and I had to lie down because the pain was stronger than I was. As soon as I lay down, I was carried away..." (M 1.1, p. 88).

A year later, on a day of great pain, she noticed that "not a little blood" was coming from the wound in her side (M 1.1, p. 101). The shock was greater when, probably on the feast of the Stigmata of Saint Francis (September 17) in 1876, she found the wounds in her feet open:

"My dear Father Saint Francis appeared to me and left me fully strengthened, and with a desire to suffer, and resignation... The following evening, having suffered horrible pains all day, before going to bed I felt such sharp wounds in my feet and hands and in my side that I did not know where to hold myself. Then, looking at my feet, because they were burning so..., oh, I saw them open! My God! Ah, let no one notice!

I have always begged him to arrange things so that no one could notice anything. So now too he made only my feet open, and I still have them in a bad state, but I hope he will close them before I set out on my journey" (M 4.4, p. 75).

Scholars of mystical phenomena in general, and of stigmatization in particular, today attach no importance to whether or not the bodily manifestations are miraculous, but to the cause that produces them. True stigmata are those somatic localizations or projections that originate in infused contemplation of Christ's sufferings in the Passion, even if, as is known of some canonized saints, they were preceded by a deliberate desire to reach that loving identification with the Crucified. What counts is the sincerity of the subject who experiences it.

Burnings in the heart - Exchange of hearts.

Here is the bodily phenomenon Mother Rosa speaks of several times in the Memoirs and in her letters to Don Gennaro. It is not new in Christian hagiography.

The first beautiful mention of these fires of love appears in the notes of the meditations she made day by day during Lent 1864 in Genoa:

"A devouring fire came upon me and consumed me, and there were moments when I seemed to be destroyed in that fire. I rejoiced immensely, yet it was a terrible agony, and most delightful. I felt a great and consoling pleasure in feeling myself destroyed, and I would never have wanted it to stop. Oh! how sweet it is to die of love!" (M 2, p. 144f).

In 1866 we find a similar outpouring about the devouring fire that "makes her faint" from pain and sweetness at the same time (M 1.1, p. 45f). In 1867 the burning becomes ever more intense: she feels herself burned, consumed; it gives her no rest (M 1.1, p. 49f, 58-61). And as early as 1870 she feels a swelling in the region of the heart which often even presses against her ribs. The pain is strong and continuous. She fears others will notice, because it comes upon her even during community acts and while she is speaking with people. The phenomenon recurs whenever she experiences strong surges of love for God. She is often forced to withdraw and shut herself in her room so as not to attract admiration. At other times she needs to take cold baths to ease the burning. It is an agonizing suffering and at the same time a most gentle loving delight, which keeps her united to her Good and makes her exclaim: "Alas! my Good, you are making me die!"

This is how she expresses it in October 1873:

"The swelling of my heart these days was beyond compare; the fire devoured me, destroyed me. The suffering I feel from such a great swelling is beyond description; but far greater is the joy I feel; because it keeps me so united to my Good, no pain troubles me" (M 4.2, p. 12).

In her descriptions she speaks both of the swelling on the left side, the effect of the burnings of love, and of the pain on the right side, coinciding with the renewal of the pain of the wounds in her hands and feet; this is therefore the wound in the side. In 1870 she mentions a scar, different from the one left by the small crucifix she had worn embedded in her flesh; it comes from a wound from the crucified Lord, which seems to want to open (M 1.2, p. 31).

On the feast of Corpus Christi in 1872, while in church, she felt a sharp blow in her breast as of a stiletto piercing her (M 3, p. 43f); the pain of this wound became unbearable at certain moments. She writes in February 1873:

"Today, more than usual, my right side tormented me and was much more swollen; and that burning I feel inside, which burns me in one spot only, as if I had a wound: it is not heat, no, a burning like a wound which, when it comes on strongly, makes me even feel faint. And I see clearly that they notice, because they tell me I change color..." (M 4.1, p. 33f).

On January 16, 1875, she speaks again of the small scar; the pain she feels is "like a thin knife being thrust into her" (M 4.3, p. 12).

When she placed herself under the direction of Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, at first she was ashamed to tell him what was happening in her heart. In one of her letters she tells him that by now "the swelling is fairly stationary...; it grows at night; I no longer have those strepale (batterings)...." Instead, she feels short of breath, and is seized by "the fear that it is a heart disease," the effect of the violent burnings of past years (L undated, no. 347).

Among the various mystical experiences connected with the heart is the exchange of hearts, of which there are several cases in hagiography. It consists in the conviction that one's own heart has been replaced by the Lord's, so that the mystic feels she loves him with his own divine-human heart. Rosa Gattorno seems to allude to this gift too on various dates, though she has not left us an explicit account of the event, which apparently took place at the beginning of her self-giving to the Lord. This is how she recalls it on the feast of the Name of Mary in 1870:

"Abandoned, I threw myself upon the Side of my Good, where many years ago he took my heart, which was inside this miserable breast, and so I remained in him, so that when I came to I was full of peace and comfort" (M 1.1, p. 82).

In 1876 and 1877, and again in 1890, she says several times when speaking with the Lord: "This heart of yours, which is swollen"; or she notes: "the part where his heart is" (M 4.4, pp. 14, 19, 26, 44, 103; 4.5, p. 21f; 11.2, p. 269).

Both in this experience and in the others concerning the heart, Rosa Gattorno seems to have had no model to imitate in the life or writings of any saint. She lived it all in her chosen isolation, carefully protected from others' eyes: an ardent bridal love, suffered and enjoyed in the most jealously guarded intimacy.

4. The devil's part.

The masters of the ways of the spirit have always warned souls against Satan's snares, bearing in mind that this counterfeiter of God's works often "disguises himself as an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14). They distinguish diabolical temptation, that is, the enemy's inner insinuations, from diabolical obsession, which can act either on the inner faculties, through fixed ideas, scruples, fears and images, or on the external senses, through apparitions, representations, voices, noises, blows... There is hardly a mystic who has not had to deal with diabolical harassment; among the best-known saints we may recall Anthony the Abbot, Francis of Assisi, Catherine of Siena, Margaret of Cortona, Teresa of Avila, Francis Xavier, Veronica Giuliani, John Mary Vianney and Gemma Galgani.

It should come as no surprise that Satan directs his attacks especially against God's great friends and, even more fiercely, against those who, like the apostles of the Gospel and the founders of religious institutes, are effective instruments for the growth of the Kingdom. But we must not grant him more ground than God allows him to take. If it is difficult, as was said above, to draw a dividing line between the sphere of God's action and that of human elaboration in the supernatural process, it is more difficult still to detect the devil's presence and to distinguish between his evil arts and the subject's imaginative and sensory creativity.

There are people, even psychologically healthy ones, who are particularly prone to inner anxieties and figurative fantasies. Those, moreover, who are accustomed to seeing their own and others' affairs in the perspective of faith tend to divide the human race into good and bad, those on God's side and those on the devil's. Convinced that they are doing God's work and are his instruments, they easily feel thwarted and persecuted by the forces of evil and see in every opponent an agent or collaborator of Satan; they discover plots and schemes of the powers of darkness everywhere.

Rosa Gattorno recognized that she was prone to anxieties, that is, temperamentally inclined to harbor within herself fears and disturbances that could nest and take shape in her imagination. Saint John of the Cross warns insistently against the danger of assisting the action of the enemy, who uses the subject's suggestions and imagination to disquiet his spirit.

I must confess that the only thing I would have preferred not to find in Rosa Gattorno's Memoirs is this tedious succession of diabolical incursions, almost every night, in grotesque forms; and then her always seeing the shadow of Cepinello, as she humorously calls him, in every difficulty and every vexation arising from the normal course of the foundation.

At the beginning of her new life, in the years 1858-1862, she had to endure violent temptations and anxieties of conscience, especially regarding the Eucharist, the penances she had undertaken and the confessions she had made. The struggle reached such a point that her director, Don Giuseppe Firpo, wanted to resort to exorcism, as if it were a true obsession, which Rosa refused to accept, as was said above. In reality it was nothing but one of those trials of passive purification that accompany every radical renunciation in order to give oneself to God; moreover, it belonged to her special vocation to follow the suffering Christ.

In the following years temptations against faith and to despair appeared, true diabolical suggestions accompanied by frightening apparitions. So it was during the novena of the Immaculate Conception in 1866 (M 1.1, p. 45). The temptations were of every kind except those against purity, "from which, by the mercy of God, I have always been free," she repeats several times.

In November 1874 the tempter tormented her for several days with the obsession that she was going mad, making her see signs of madness in her own behavior. To this was added the temptation to despair, with impulses to throw herself out of the window (M 1.1, p. 75; 1.2, p. 51-55, 58f, 77-79, 84, 86).

The inner temptations were accompanied by external annoyances, noises, blows and commotions which at first, when Rosa was still in Genoa, could be heard from outside (M 1.1, p. 55f). Then came apparitions of monstrous figures which recurred every night in her little room in Piacenza. Misshapen beasts, black shadows in the form of large spiders "with long legs and little body," climbing up the wall or clinging to the ceiling; then they disappeared. Violent shakings that woke her; invisible hands that stirred the straw of her bed and scratched the blanket over her feet...

Her descriptions of these phantoms and the fact that she always saw them after lying down on her back suggest those hypnagogic sensory images, frequent in people of sound mind, which have nothing preternatural about them except the effect they may produce. In Mother Rosa's spirit they left greater courage to overcome difficulties and a renewed desire to work in God's service.

Certainly a shrewd director could have helped her overcome that persecution simply by reducing the phenomenon to its reality; but she was alone; no one knew of that continuous battle until she confided in her two spiritual friends of her last years: Princess di Fitalia, whom she told jokingly about the ridiculous apparitions that bothered her, and Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, her director. He gave her as a remedy to command those monsters to leave her in peace, since "obedience does not want them to disturb her rest"; the method had some effect, at least as regards inner peace, though the disturbances continued. Six months later she wrote to him humorously:

"As for my spirit, I am perfectly calm. The traffic continues: good ones and bad ones came; I had plenty of visits. Evidently they enjoy traveling, especially at night, and although it is poor and almost uninhabited, my poor room evidently pleases them, doesn't it?" (L 2-1-1889, 8-6-1889).

Rosa Gattorno's heart, a woman's heart endowed with rich sensitivity and an exceptional capacity for welcome and affectionate self-giving, was made for loving. And it was also a heart made for suffering. Suffering is part of the Christian logic of self-offering and redemptive love, since God's love for us was revealed in his sending his Son as an expiation for our sins (1 Jn 4:9f); and the Son of God showed his love for the Father and for mankind by submitting to the passion and death on the cross.

This is not only a matter of Mother Rosa's personal spirituality: loving and suffering would also be her destiny as foundress and would form her central message to the Daughters of Saint Anne. In the allegorical poem Trials and Consolations she presents the growth of the Institute as a little boat laboriously rowing through the storms of the sea, until, after a great struggle, it is seen emerging victorious, unfurling an elegant banner bearing the words: suffering-love. With a favorable sea the ship, now very large and well equipped, makes great progress and defends itself successfully against its enemies, now heavily armored and girded with iron; it gains ground and conquers many cities and towns. "Always victorious, she sails into great harbors and flies her banners: suffering and love" (TC, pp. 219-221).

1. "Love, and do what you will" (Saint Augustine).

Whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me (Mt 10:37).

Rosa experienced in all its force the need to renounce the most sacred human affections for the sake of God's preferential love. First of all her own parents, whom she loved deeply and by whom she was deeply loved. After choosing consecrated life, at the moment of leaving for Piacenza to begin the Work of God, she did not hesitate to accept the painful separation for herself and for them; on March 13, 1866, mastering the anguish of her heart, she had the courage to step over the body of her mother, who was sitting on the threshold of the house (FIOCCHI, I, p. 120f). Sixteen years later she also found the strength to leave that same mother on her deathbed, because her presence was urgently required by the sisters of the community in Pisa (Memoirs of Mother Celsa, 1882). In a dream in 1896 she would see her in heaven dressed as a daughter of Saint Anne.

She loved her brothers and sisters. We know of her good relations with Francesco, who would later testify in the informative process of Genoa, as well as with her sister Elisa. Her affection for her brother Federico was no less: despite their ideological distance, she showed great understanding towards him, and he responded with the same love, almost veneration.

But the great sacrifice was separation from her children. The grief she felt when she lost the third of them, Francesco, aged ten months, she would feel renewed many years later. On August 24, 1874, she seemed to hear his voice still calling her: "Mamma, Mamma!" (M 1.2, p. 47). As for Carlotta, her deaf and mute daughter, she took care to place her in the Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan, so that by learning to speak she might later find a suitable place in society; while young Alessandro, who showed signs of a priestly vocation, she entrusted to a private school to prepare him for ecclesiastical studies. But the moment of the terrible choice arrived: having to choose between her maternal duties and God's plan. She described that painful juncture dramatically:

"My children! the mere thought of having to leave them was torture, and I kept telling myself: No! it will never be, no! And the good Shepherd (the archbishop) allowed me to go to Rome... I felt I had already won the victory: never - I kept telling myself - will Pope Pius IX allow a mother to leave her children, a mother who had such immense affection for them..."

But Pius IX's answer, in the private audience of January 3, 1866, was categorical: "God will take care of your children: you take care of God in his work!" (M 2, pp. 11, 16-18, 24-26).

Those words of the Vicar of Christ, which she always believed were inspired by God, calmed her and gave her the courage to go forward. Very often, amid the not always pleasant events in the lives of her two children, a kind of remorse would assail her, but she would always hear Pius IX's answer echoing in her conscience.

Her concerns for the Work did not prevent her from caring for her children with attentive love. She kept in constant touch with them, especially with Alessandro, who caused her so much suffering, until she had the consolation of seeing him converted and of assisting him in his last illness. Her grief at his death was immense; but she had promised the Lord not to weep if she saw him die as a Christian, and she kept her promise (33).

She had learned to raise her natural maternal affection to the level of evangelical charity, which is universal. She expressed it thus in 1872:

"I received a most beautiful lesson on how I must love my neighbor, and this with regard to my children too. How I must conduct myself, and the perfect equality with which I must treat all creatures and love them all in him and for him. To give creatures what was given to me, to save them and lead them to love and serve him. Oh! my incomprehensible Love, what I felt!" (M 1.1, p. 108f).

With the sisters she was demanding about renouncing their own families, but she taught them not to stifle their legitimate affection for their relatives; she disliked coldness in their relations with them. In 1873 she wrote to Sister A. Carlotta Biagini:

"Listen, my dear: I would like you to write to your mother and also a couple of lines to Signora Maria, but I would like them to be all honey, and to tell her many beautiful, consoling words about the state you have embraced, the consolation you feel... Give her your address, telling her you want to be blessed often by your mother" (L 29-10-1873).

O Love, how strong you are!

Of the bodily phenomena listed above, the most frequent, indeed habitual, was the fire in her heart, the sensible reflection of what Mother Rosa was experiencing in her spirit. The most beautiful expressions in her diary are those in which she pours out her love before her dear Good. Here is one of the most fervent pages, written in 1866 after the rapture already described on the feast of All Saints; love and suffering alternate like two impulses of one never-sated longing:

"I found myself beside the Side of my Beloved. Oh! what I felt as I sensed myself drawing near that volcano of love! Oh! how painful life seems to me! O my dear Beloved, ah! let me stay with you and never have to return to this miserable earth! O painful exile! when will you end?

But at once I pulled myself together and said: No! to live in order to suffer! O my dear Beloved! forgive me for being so thirsty to be taken from this valley. But no! - I repeat - to suffer! Exquisite is the honey of your sweetness: how could I not remain hungry? I suffer, and feel this wretched body writhe and struggle...; but no, dear Jesus! with your help it will stay firm on the cross, suffering and languishing for you...

O my Beloved, your love consumes me; I feel a devouring flame burning in me which scorches and consumes me, a continual spasm I can no longer bear; but I do not suffer, because the joy I feel, most delightful, is beyond compare... For pity's sake, fill me with your love!" (M 1.1, pp. 42-44).

She repeatedly declares herself a slave out of love for her beloved Good. There is no lack of painful absences, in which she feels as if forgotten, unworthy even of a glance from the God of Love; but suddenly she feels him near, sweetly drawn by him, and hears within her his voice assuring her of his love and saying to her: "You are my favorite" (M 4.4, p. 76f).

When she experiences such assurance, everything becomes easy for her, every pain desirable:

"Your love, my Good, surpasses everything and is the support, the relief, the security of action. It is the anchor cast to the bottom of the painful sea of our tribulations. Most lovable God, when amid such sad suffering you leave us anchored to your love, it is enough to say to our pains: You are sweet, my beloved ones! And the fear of having displeased you is followed by trust in your forgiveness, the assurance of soon having light on the rest of our actions and, finally, the bliss of perfect union with you, which through love is always tasted, though with greater or lesser intimacy" (M 4.2, p. 89).
