She often finds herself unable to express the ineffable experiences of infused love. At other times she feels invaded, dominated, overpowered by the sweet violence of Love. And then her cry is: Love, how strong you are! which echoes that of the Song of Songs (Song 8:6). So on April 9, 1877:

"I felt great union with my God, to such a degree that my ribs were raised so high that I thought I would die under such fierce torment. Love, how strong you are! When I feel this, I keep saying: it is nothing! It is so strong that if my Lover did not sustain me, I would die...; I already feel myself expiring when I feel like this. Oh! death of love, how sweet and delightful you are!" (M 4.4, p. 131f).

The love of God was her favorite subject when she spoke to the sisters, and it was also the one they most gladly heard from her lips; in her the Gospel saying came true: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Mt 12:34). Her words, the sisters themselves testify, came forth on fire and penetrated hearts, kindling them with the love of God (Summ., p. 63, 872). The text of the conference she gave on March 14, 1872, to the community of Sampierdarena has been preserved, faithfully transcribed by her secretary, Sister A. Vincenza Rapallino. She begins by declaring: "Human tongue is unable to explain what the love of God is." Philosophers, moralists and ascetics "will be able to define nothing." One must turn to the saints who have experienced it: Catherine of Genoa, Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Jesus, Francis of Assisi, Philip Neri. "Neither learning nor human intellect is needed to understand what this love is, which can be had from God alone, and which one cannot describe unless one has tasted it."

Then, leaving aside the examples of the saints, those great lovers, she opens her heart sincerely, though speaking in the third person, to describe how she experiences the love of God and the fires of love. To the objection she senses in her listeners, that this is a free gift of God, she replies that three dispositions are needed to receive it: prayer, the stripping away of one's own will, and the longing to suffer. Even today one feels the emotion of that unprepared outpouring vibrating in every word; it must have made a strong impression on the sisters (34).

We have already mentioned the ecstasy the novices observed in 1890 during another conference on the love of God. The subject often recurs in her letters to the sisters, always in fiery words. Here are some taken from her letters to Sister A. Adelaide Pezzoni, by way of example:

"My dear, what good news you give me! Yes, the Lord will love his Carolina (still a laywoman) more and more, he will pour arrows of love into her heart. Dear Jesus, burn her entirely with your divine fire!..." - "May God bless you and consume you with the fire of his divine love; and may he intoxicate you in the outpouring of the blood he shed from his Side"

- "Daughter, the Heart of this God is so beautiful and so loving that no words can express it. You know that charity burns in this vast Heart: it is the queen; so whoever lacks it cannot say they share in his blazing Love"

- "I want one thing from you, and it is that you strive to love God with a love wholly pure and ardent, on fire. If you reach this, I will tell you: Do what you will, for you will do everything well. Love, and do what you will, said Saint Augustine. Yes, my dear, love this dear God the Father, and you will do everything gladly!"

- "Whoever has not tasted the love of God can be called poor and is unfortunate, dead to all that is greatest, most sublime and holy on earth and in heaven" (L 1869, 22-11-1870, 4-2-1871, 5-4-1871, 5-2-1872).

To Sister A. Celsa Speranza, future superior general of the Institute, she wrote:

"Courage, for Jesus loves you: and what are you doing? Love, my daughter, and then be full of joy in his love" (Undated letter).

The tones are even more fervent in her correspondence with Princess di Fitalia, her confidante in spiritual matters; and the pairing of love and suffering always appears.

A mother's heart towards the daughters the Lord gave her.

The evangelical pedagogy of Saint Francis and Saint Clare of Assisi emphasizes welcoming each brother and sister as a gift from the Lord who called them. Mother Rosa has the same gratitude towards God the Father, who cares for his Work by sending it such numerous ranks of daughters of Saint Anne; she has a mother's heart for each one individually. She follows them in thought and affection in the houses to which they are sent, rejoices at good news of their successes and of their progress in holiness, just as, on the contrary, she is saddened and suffers real torment when one is unfaithful to her vocation, when another falls ill, when God calls them to himself through death. As we have seen, she has the gift - whether charismatic or telepathic - of being attuned to the situations of her daughters far away, as well as of sensing their dispositions when they are present.

Her day is divided between the time given to prayer and that set aside for correspondence with the sisters, especially with the superiors, from whom she wants to be informed of the needs of each sister in their care. In the thousands of letters, written either alone or with the help of her secretaries, one seems to feel the beating of a close and tender heart, both when she consoles and encourages and when she rebukes and admonishes. We also know how she welcomed and helped individual sisters on her frequent visits to the houses.

Amid the setbacks she had to endure as foundress, she found comfort in this motherly care. She wrote in 1878:

"Once recovered from sorrow, one desires nothing; nothing on earth seems to have any sweetness, nothing! The soul feels it can savor one thing only: charity. Oh! what joy it feels in being able to do good and try to set right, to reconcile with God, whoever has gone astray! Yes, in charity the soul rejoices wholly, takes part, and in seeing the well-being of creatures feels great pleasure. Sacrifice, whatever pain it may cost, is always a consolation when one sees a soul relieved" (M 1.2, p. 110).

Conversely, she feels keen remorse whenever she realizes she has been uncharitable towards a sister by speaking about her in front of others:

"I received a gentle inner reproach from my Good, because in these days I let slip that a certain sister was very coarse, and in front of several sisters. When I said it, it seemed to me that my purpose was upright, to rouse them and make them quicker, so that they could do well; but unfortunately my Good reproached me, and I made a firm resolution and wept over my fault with the most intense sorrow. Oh! how good it did me to see the fault I had committed! - Charity! - he kept saying to me - While you were saying that: Charity! My Jesus, what sorrow! Ah! for pity's sake, forgive me! He made me see the ugliness of this imperfection" (M 4.4, p. 93f).

If the love of God was the subject that most fired her when she spoke to the sisters, fraternal charity was the most frequent; indeed, one may say it was the pivot of her pedagogy. And these were not fine reflections on the queen of virtues: Mother Rosa wanted mutual love to show itself in the concrete attitudes of daily life, in mutual attentiveness, in eager cooperation, in overcoming selfishness, misunderstandings, gossip and the other enemies of life together. The superiors in particular were to be models and builders of such unity.

See the three conferences on fraternal charity given in April 1890, those addressed to the voting members of the general chapter on the theme Will and Love in 1895, and those addressed to the superiors in Sicily in April 1898 (M 10.2, pp. 1-6; 10.5; 10.6).

In those conferences and in her letters she insistently urges the superiors: equal treatment of all the sisters, without discrimination or favoritism, without humiliating those from humbler families; understanding of personal conditions and situations; gentleness and sweetness in correcting. Above all, it is the superior's task to create in her community a healthy and joyful atmosphere of true fraternal charity. A few of her many fine recommendations will suffice:

"Ah, dear superior! I assure you that merely writing these two lines about charity I feel a strong desire within me - and to do what? My God, calm, calm this in me, for it makes me suffer too much... When this thought takes hold of my mind, I cannot contain it"

- "Pray and love one another all with the same love, and strive to reach that beautiful unity of thought and action; tend towards one center, which is God"

- "True charity and love among you must be so sincere that one's own good must be the sister's good as well. If you become like this, the Spirit of God will reign in you for an eternity" - "Love one another, and let charity accompany you in all your actions"

- "When I speak of charity, it seems I would never stop; I find everything in it, every consolation: everything in a word!" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 1867, 9-3-1870, 25-3-1872; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, 4-2-1871).

It often happens that when a superior has a difficult sister in her charge, she thinks of getting rid of her by appealing to the major superior to have her transferred elsewhere. In such cases Mother Rosa would reply by asking the superior rather to examine herself and ask whether she had used every means to win her over; indeed, she measured the capacity to govern by this motherly zeal. She had someone write to one such superior: "I understand: when a superior cannot bear with the faults of her daughters, it means she is not fit to be superior: I will call you back."

She wanted the sisters to find in their superior a love so motherly that they would not miss the natural mother they had left to follow their vocation, nor need to unburden themselves to others (cf. FIOCCHI, I, p. 267).

2. The mysticism of suffering.

Rosa Gattorno belongs to the company of so many great lovers who, like Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross, Saint Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi and Saint Veronica Giuliani, made suffering, so to speak, the reason for their existence: a mission, namely that of completing the sufferings of Christ (cf. Col 1:24) by cooperating in his redemptive self-offering.

In such a mission suffering is inseparable from love: love is the cause of suffering, suffering is the expression of love. In Mother Rosa's Memoirs one passes constantly from heart-rending pages, where she lays bare her sufferings of spirit - darkness, abandonment by God, temptations to despair - to others in which we see her enjoying intimate loving union with the Beloved, or experiencing the impetuous fires that make her cry out: "Love, you are making me die!" Her heart utters the same cry of pain and love when she feels the shudders caused by the internal wounds in her hands, feet and side, or by the chain embedded in her flesh.

It was in the process of mystical purification, at the beginning of her widowhood, that she discovered the treasure of suffering. She recalls it beautifully, in her allegorical language, at the opening of the book Trials and Consolations:

"... My Crucified taught me to suffer and, like the bees' honey sealed in those precious combs, he kept suffering for me, and it turned into sweetness. From time to time he gave me a taste of this liquid and, with sublime lessons, made me understand how such exquisiteness could be drawn from suffering, while nature rebelled against it...

My Crucified left me alone and, like the bride in the Song, I wandered through that forest seeking him, taking one step forward on the path and another back. All the little branches were dry and all interlaced in the shape of crosses.

- Are you too joining in my sadness? - I kept saying to them.

When I stopped, my Crucified placed his heavy cross on my shoulders and, taking away my terror of suffering, left me with an ardent love for it. I have loved it much, and I love it greatly" (TC, p. 3-5).

In her first transports of love she would have liked to sacrifice herself radically, all at once, through martyrdom. On March 31, 1862, after a vision of the Host dripping with blood, she had "a most lively, most ardent desire to suffer martyrdom for the faith; and to manage to give vent to this thought of mine," she writes, "what schemes I thought up to succeed! My Good! I will not be satisfied unless I have the good fortune to see myself cut to pieces for you, my dear Beloved!" (M 1.1, p. 24f).

A year later the same longing returned: to die at the stake as a sign of love and to make satisfaction for sinners; and again in 1866 and 1867 (M 1.1, pp. 38, 68, 119; cf. testimony of Sr. A. Fabiana Orsi and Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, Summ., p. 56, 346f).

At last she understood that slow martyrdom, sustained and renewed day after day amid bitterness and darkness, was what the divine Crucified asked of her.

On September 17 of that decisive year, 1862, her spiritual Father, Don Firpo, wrote to her:

"The time of consolations, that is, of spiritual delicacies, seems to be over for you, and from now on you will have only to drink from the bitter chalice of tribulation: it is in tribulation that your lover Jesus wants to unite himself more closely to you; by this sign God's favorites are recognized, the predestined, those chosen for glory" (quoted in FIOCCHI, I, p. 56).

To live in order to suffer! would be her answer whenever the desire for death presented itself to her spirit as the means of escaping the prison of the body and flying to the supreme Good.

Carrying the cross with Jesus.

The Christian's suffering, according to Jesus' invitation (Mt 10:38; Lk 9:23; 14:27) and Saint Paul's theology (Gal 2:19; 6:14), has a name: the Cross. And it is Mother Rosa's favorite name. She confesses that as late as 1859, greedy for the great consolations of those early days, she was not used to "fighting under the banner of the holy Cross, so delightful and dear." She was a "beginner" (M 1.1, p. 4). But she soon entered fully into the school of the Cross: it would always be her "companion," her "bed of rest" (M 3, p. 25). One day when she was full of bitterness, holding the cross very tightly, she spoke to it thus: "Is it true, my treasure, that you are always my companion?" And she heard a voice that comforted her: "Only from the Cross does one learn to love!" (TC, p. 329).

Not content with having the image of the Crucified constantly before the eyes of body and spirit, she wanted to make her love tangible by tying a small cross tightly to her breast, taking her brief rest lying on a cross, and often remaining suspended from a large wooden cross she kept in her little room in Piacenza. But it was the very mystery of the Cross, more than its material form, that had shaped her life.

And she would have liked each of the daughters of Saint Anne to become a true lover of the Cross. Encouragements of this kind are very frequent in her letters; here are some:

"Courage on the way of Calvary, if you want to be crucified with your Beloved and die with him on the delightful bed of the Cross"

- "Every new day, a new cross! Blessed is the one whose dawn breaks amid thorns and sorrows!"

- "In paradise there is no more cross, there are no more sufferings there: only Love, Love... Be cheerful, be cheerful, for Jesus loves those who suffer: whoever does not want to suffer does not want to love!"

- "Whoever wants to follow me - says the Master, showing us a cross - let him take up his cross and follow me. What language is this, then, heavenly Bridegroom? O blessed souls! He gives me that treasure which the world does not know and which he offers to his beloved brides, and he even wants it to be heavy, so that one day we may come to taste his delights"

- "This holy Wood, the bridal bed of his most beloved brides!" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 27-5-1869, 1-1-1870; to Sr. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1869, 16-1-1870; to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: 23-12-1868, 6-2-1870).

On July 27, 1890, she received special light on the three degrees of the cross, or three ways of carrying the cross, and she gave many other conferences to the sisters on this subject. The first degree is that of religious who carry it on their shoulders for the love of God, but always complaining and seeking comfort from the superior, from the confessor... The second degree: those who carry it pressed to their breast, never lay it down, find happiness in it and are generous in suffering. The third degree: the true lovers of the Lord, who know no comfort but suffering; they carry the cross pressed to their breast and try to suck from it the wormwood, the essence of suffering, without seeking the slightest comfort: "suffering alone is their refreshment; only at the Lord's feet do they weep and secretly shed their tears, and they hold the holy cross pressed to their heart, the love of the seraphim, the joy of those who love! These are the holy souls."

And she concluded:

"O my Love, how much I too desire to love and to be able to learn and possess this third cross!... Ah! sweet Love! whoever does not love you is too unfortunate. How happy I would be if I could make everyone know you and love you! Poor creatures" (M 10.4, p. 3f; 11.2, pp. 318-325).

The value and benefits of suffering.

It is impossible to transcribe the whole variety of beautiful thoughts on suffering scattered through both the Memoirs and the letters. We shall be content with a selection of the most notable expressions, beginning with the spiritual diary, where they pile up, each more beautiful than the last:

"It is sweet to suffer for the Beloved!"

- "Why do I not possess all the sufferings there are in the world?"

- "To live without suffering is to die"

- "In suffering one finds a sweetness beyond expression"

- "Suffering, suffering! you are too sweet for me not to burn with desire to possess you!"

- "My Good, you know that suffering is my sweetness, my life is suffering, because in suffering I feel your life and your strength ever more"

- "My God, to suffer with you, to die for you!" - "O my Jesus, Savior, my dear and lovable Bridegroom! you alone, then, to suffer and love for you alone!"

- "Suffering, you are always sweet to me, because you come to me from my Jesus... Whoever does not love suffering cannot know what it contains... Oh! if everyone knew you, surely all would desire this in order to have from you the true Good" (M 1.1, pp. 59, 118, 120; 1.2, pp. 15, 17, 20, 87, 100, 121; 2, p. 93; 3, p. 16; 4.5, pp. 36, 71, 216).

No less ardent and profound are the sentiments we find in her letters, especially those in a warmer and more spontaneous tone. She acknowledges that for her, speaking of suffering is almost a vital necessity:

"You will say to me: this blessed Mother can talk of nothing but suffering, always the same story! My dear, where else am I to find occupation if I do not linger where I know I can have sweetness, love and peace?" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 20-10-1871).

"My dear, I fear I am boring you by always talking to you of nothing but suffering; but what can I do? when I start talking about it, I stop to think about it, I taste its sweetness, I lose myself in it and cannot find my way out, because I never find I can have my fill. Ah! blessed are those souls who can have their fill of it! they already taste that divine nectar which is found only in the essence of suffering" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 5-4-1871).

Suffering, as Mother Rosa sees it, is the normal condition for following Christ in this earthly exile; if God now and then opens a flash of light and consolation to us, it is only to help our weakness. Her own life was almost a pilgrimage in the dark across the desert, gladdened only by an occasional refreshing oasis. Only those who follow Jesus to Golgotha and to the agony of the cross share in the triumph of his glory.

"One can stay on Tabor only to take a little rest, and Jesus usually takes weak souls there, for if he did not refresh them they would die on the way; but the strong ones (go) always forward, spurred on, until they have reached Golgotha and are crucified there with him, to rise again all beautiful and radiant and enter triumphantly into the glory of heaven" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 12-8-1870).

It is precisely this hope of eternal glory that must sustain loving souls in the sufferings of this life; here is the time for suffering, there will be the time for rejoicing.

"A brief suffering for an eternal joy," she often repeats. And she likes to quote the well-known couplet of Saint Francis of Assisi: So great is the good I hope for - that every pain is a delight to me (cf. L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 3-10-1867; to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 5-1-1886).

But already in this exile suffering itself becomes ineffable joy for those who know how to discover the treasures hidden in it:

"One feels the suffering and does not suffer, because every pain is bound to an abyss of joy beyond compare"

- "Whoever has never tasted the delights of suffering does not know what it means to rejoice"

- "Who can describe the delight of suffering? No one. At least so I think, because not even I can explain it: the more I study it, the less I can. What a mystery: to rejoice so much in such dreadful pains!"

- "My Good, my only treasure, what are my pains compared with such consolation?... Press your arm down harder, make me suffer more, if for so little you give me so much!" (M 1.1, pp. 119, 179; 1.2, p. 69; 4.1, p. 107).

Here appears the now classic alternative that Saint Teresa of Avila formulated thus: Either to suffer or to die! and that Saint Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi changed to: To suffer and not to die! The dilemma revives each time the welcome thought of death surfaces in Mother Rosa's mind as the end of suffering (cf. M 1.1, pp. 137-139). She writes in March 1878:

"Today I had further news about my death. Oh! what a sweet life dying is! But to suffer and not to die would be my choice. I regret it only because I will no longer be able to suffer, but you are too beautiful!" (M 4.5, p. 44; cf. L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 5-1-1886).

She wrote on July 23, 1890:

"Oh! how sweet suffering is! I would like to live a hundred years just to suffer. What have you put into this suffering? what delights have you hidden in it, my Love? 24 years of vocation: by God's mercy I can assure you that I have never had a single hour's respite from suffering, and always new ones, each like the other, yet always different" (M 11.2, p. 303).

Mother Rosa does not merely pile up praises and exaltations of suffering; she likes to specify its many benefits and advantages, especially in her letters.

a) Suffering is the proof of love.

- In 1868 she encouraged Sister A. Vincenza Rapallino to regard suffering as "the most precious moment for giving the Lord proofs of love" (L 4-12-1868).

"Whoever does not learn to suffer will never know how to love," she wrote to Fr. Agostino Donadio (21-9-1871). And to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte: "Whoever loves must follow the Beloved in pains and sorrows" (12-3-1897).

b) It unites us to the Redeemer's sacrificial offering.

- She wrote in her spiritual diary:

"Ah! my Good! in no way do I intend to avoid pains, sorrows or sacrifices, whatever the martyrdom, but let every sword that pierces me always be turned towards me, as you please, towards me who am your victim. A voice said to me:

- Yes, you are!

So every time they make me suffer greatly, I say:

- My Good, are you suffering? Alas! Let all the pains be mine alone, but not yours, O my Beloved!" (M 1.1, p. 171).

c) It helps us expiate sins.

- First of all one's own sins. Every suffering is for her an opportunity to pay off the debt of offenses against God: a debt of love and gratitude for the pardon received:

"Let us bless the hand of the Almighty, who strikes us gently and charitably makes us pay our debts in this foreign and brief passage. My exile already numbers 38 years, and I can say with joy that, having had the good fortune to spend them always under the lash of suffering, my only joy, my treasure, in suffering alone have I been able to find my delight, all my consolation" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1869).

d) It helps us share in the sufferings of others.

- In May, finding herself at Lourdes and having found no remedy for her ills, she made this prayer to the Virgin: "My Mother, accept this pain and let it be reparation for what others would have to suffer" (L to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte: May 1888).

e) It purifies and prepares for love.

- In God's plan, sufferings serve to purify and beautify the souls God loves most (M 1.1, p. 79).

"Oh! land of tribulations! I embrace you, because I know that you will purify me in the pains you contain" (M 4.2, p. 50).

"Before entering this Vesuvius of love, which is the Side of my Jesus, we must have been scrubbed clean by the lash of the foaming soap of suffering" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 20-10-1871).

f) It makes us advance in perfection.

- "What a dear Bridegroom!" she writes to Sister A. Francesca Camisa. "How well he knows how to treat his beloved ones, by what means he graciously and gradually trains them in perfection!" (L 15-10-1869).

g) It is a sign that our actions accord with God's will.

- This was a deeply rooted personal conviction of hers: her continuous and renewed suffering was like the seal of authenticity on her service to the Work of God. She proposes the same criterion of discernment to her daughters:

"Courage, my daughter! Why get so upset? Listen: along with consolations we also need bitterness; otherwise I would fear it was not God's work" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 2-12-1871).

How to accept sufferings and make them fruitful?

Here, as in other aspects of her evangelical pedagogy, Mother Rosa proves an outstanding spiritual guide to the souls entrusted to her. It is impossible to transcribe the full variety of her recommendations on how to sanctify suffering, almost every one of which begins with that Courage! of hers, so motherly in tone. A useful anthology of the spirituality of suffering could be compiled from them.

Experienced in what she teaches, she often alludes to her own sufferings - physical ills, struggles, setbacks - as though she wanted to give courage by sharing in such a gift of God. She often says to a sister she sees suffering: "I wish I could relieve you by taking all your suffering upon myself." She teaches them, first of all, to give a reason for accepting sufferings: "Jesus gave all his blood for us, and we must do the same: yes, blood for blood!" (L to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini: 19-10-1873). Then she teaches them to discover God's loving hand in their pains and to feel also the caress of the same hand that sends or permits the affliction. God, in fact, soothes our wounds and sweetens our pain (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 5-4-1871, 5-2-1872).

"My dear, when that blessed hand of the eternal Father strikes us, ah! how sweet its blows are! Yes, my dear: I would do nothing but kiss it and clasp it!" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 14-4-1869; cf. L to Sr. Francesca Camisa: 16-12-1868, 17-8-1870).

The important and difficult point is to keep inner peace and joy of heart unchanged under the weight of the cross (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 1867, 26-5-1873). To achieve this disposition one needs a good dose of patience and much faith:

"Come now, courage! You will soon see that the Lord will console you; but an ounce of patience and two of faith in God, and you will have everything, I assure you. But peace, and little fussing; day by day embrace the cross the Lord sends us; remember: new days, new crosses" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 12-8-1870).

It will not always be easy to be cheerful amid the anxieties that oppress us; then at least resignation is needed - not the passive kind that makes a virtue of necessity, but the kind that consists in courageous conformity to God's will (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 4-11-1869, 20-10-1871; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 23-3-1871).

"Courage! resignation! Let these be our two shields to sustain us in all the immense adversities found in the Work of the Lord" (L to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 8-6-1872). But the secret of suffering well lies in loving well. Love changes the harshness of pain into sweetness and gentleness.

"How sweet it is to love God in suffering!" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 5-2-1872).

Everything must be accepted from God out of love, everything offered to him with love; one must expect reward from him alone, never from people, and seek comfort in him alone. With one's eyes on the Savior in agony on the cross and on the Sorrowful Mother, every torment is accepted and borne with love (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 2-12-1868, 1-7-1869, 27-9-1870; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 26-3-1871; to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 29-10-1873).

Suffering acquires its greatest value when it becomes pure suffering, without comfort from either people or God, as was Jesus' suffering on the cross. It is then that pure love, guided and sustained by pure faith, reaches its perfect degree. Every personal aim, every satisfaction, even spiritual, disappears: there remains only the sole and naked will of God. This is how she expresses it in a letter to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte in January 1888:

"I am writing to you from bed, where I have suffered and still suffer much. May the most holy will of God, our All, be done in everything. Oh yes! how I would have wished it!... Pure suffering is my food!"

Among the many descriptions found in the Memoirs, we choose this one from 1873:

"For very many days, indeed some months, my life has been a continual martyrdom. I feel no satisfaction in suffering, since it has turned into a state of indifference; I can meditate little, because during the day, even when unwell and with a headache, I must attend to the Work of God... So only at night, purely, can I give vent to prayer..., and then I stay with my God; but alas! during this time, in the morning a thousand doubts arise in me, and often I am seized by a melancholy in which I do not know where to find peace... I find an anguished tribulation" (M 4.2, p. 2f).

3. Sufferings of every kind.

Reading Rosa Gattorno's notes, we are almost tempted to count her among those people, especially women, who see life as a true "vale of tears" and find their identity, so to speak, in suffering sought and cultivated. A gentle pessimism envelops their inner feelings and their dealings with others. But Rosa Gattorno is anything but a pessimistic woman; deeply joyful, she spreads courage and zest for life around her. She does, indeed, find in every circumstance the side that wounds her sensitivity; but she accepts it with faith, because she knows that pain is an essential part of her destiny. In 1872 she wrote to Fr. Agostino Donadio:

"I am suffering immensely, I do not know where to draw breath, the weight of afflictions suffocates me and saps my strength, my poor brain is a crater of Vesuvius, because all kinds of great upheavals pour into it. One thing alone sustains me: the will of God."

Bodily ills.

She never had robust health. She herself speaks of fainting spells caused by weakness, bouts of fever, severe headaches, stomach troubles, swelling, irregular pulse... The sisters who accompanied her on her journeys witnessed the fatigue these cost her and the sufferings she could not always hide. The doctors, however, were never able to determine what her ailments actually were, because she would not submit to any visit or examination, not wishing to show her instruments of penance and their marks.

Moreover, both her diet and her terrible bodily mortifications contributed to a permanent weakness and endangered her health, often seriously, causing her intolerable spasms. Add to this the pain of the hidden stigmata and above all that of the inflammation of her heart, which left her exhausted. And then the grueling work of every day. Such a life cannot be understood without special divine assistance. How did Mother Rosa bear her ills? First of all by not letting them rule her life: they did not make her slow the pace of her activity or give up her journeys in the service of the Work of God, still less exempt her from the common observances. In her letters she often alludes to her illnesses, rather in a humorous tone. From those written to Mons. Granito di Belmonte, her spiritual Father, one can glimpse her spiritual attitude towards her bodily ailments:

"This donkey is so worn out that it cannot stand up: I feel a slow little fever consuming my bones, I am swollen like a balloon. What a pity! But everything is little for Jesus... Here I am, with bowed head I adore his designs. I suffer a lot, you know! but, like the hedgehog, I stay curled up at the feet of my dear Crucified" (17-8-1885) - "It is very sweet to be accompanied by such continuous pain. Every so often I am obliged to apply a linseed poultice to relieve the spasm, for I had never felt neuralgic pains before... My God! there are moments when it is stronger than my strength and I feel faint. But resigned to God's will, how calmly I relish it all!" (17-5-1888).

A few days after the date of this letter she set out on a long journey to France. Certainly her dear Good very often came to her aid, even miraculously. Just as she obtained healing for her sick daughters - many cases are attested in the processes - she would confidently ask for a remedy for herself too, when she knew that otherwise she could not be useful to the Institute. At the beginning of 1889 she had a serious swelling in one leg; informing Don Gennaro, she told him:

"Let it always be as pleases my God. He sent it to me: in everything fully resigned and calm, cheerful, as if this donkey were carrying nothing, though this morning it would not stand upright at all, I kept feeling faint; but now I am a little better. Let my Jesus do what he pleases: always happy to be able to suffer!"

And thinking of so many in the world who must bear even more painful sufferings, she ends with one of her fine surges of love: "I would like to be able to absorb all the pains of the world, if it so pleased my sovereign Lord!" (24-1-1889).

A few weeks later she was almost sure she had obtained the grace of improvement:

"I threw myself at the feet of my dear Crucified: My Love, you sent it to me, and you will see to it" (Feb. 1889). But at the end of that year she felt very ill: "I had a bad time of it!" she writes. "It is little for my sins!" This did not prevent her from setting out for southern Italy. She found relief in repeating: "It is sweet to suffer for Jesus!" (25-1-1890). To Princess di Fitalia she complained that she now felt obliged to take care of her body: "It won't obey any more: once I gave it orders, now it has found a way to make me obey it: what do you think of that?" (26-9-1889).

Sufferings of the spirit

Endowed with great sensitivity, she could not remain indifferent to others' situations, especially when they involved people to whom she felt most attached. We recall her sufferings over her children and her brother Federico. Nothing afflicted her so much as the sense of offense against God. In 1890 she wrote to her friend Princess di Fitalia:

"Dear Emilia, I feel my breast breaking with sorrow, thinking how dear Jesus is offended and by whom. I don't know what I would do; I feel such a courage that, were it not for God, our sweet Love, I don't know where I would go. Let it be, and let us pray hard" (28-5-1890).

For one who loves God, indeed, the evil of evils is sin. All her life Rosa Gattorno wept over what in her humility she called "my great sins," "my wickedness," not because she doubted God's forgiveness, but precisely because she felt so lovingly embraced by the mercy of supreme Love. The mere thought that she could still offend him tortured her terribly.

It is well known among students of spirituality that one of the most effective means of purification is the struggle against temptations, the most terrible of which concern the foundation of faith and trust in God. Sometimes these are genuine diabolical obsessions, at other times simple clouding of the mind that fixes itself tenaciously in the inner faculties in the form of scruples, fears, anxieties and despair. The torment of the spirit reaches its height when the soul feels it has lost its God forever, seeing itself irremediably damned.

God did not spare Rosa Gattorno this price of Love's victory, common to almost all the great mystics. She often speaks of the very subtle temptations with which the enemy pursued her; only against impure suggestions did she feel specially protected by a special grace of God.

Now she feels rejected by God, convinced that her communions are sacrilegious (M 4.2, p. 4f); now the tempter persuades her that everything she experiences is "false and diabolical art, the effect of human sensitivity" (M 4.3, p. 10f); now he makes her see that her life is nothing but "an abyss of wickedness," which has led her to certain damnation (M 4.2, pp. 61-63; letter to Fr. Donadio: 9-10-1872). She is often seized by the obsessive fear of going mad, indeed she thinks she already is, because she does everything "without judgment, like someone out of her mind" (M 4.3, pp. 55f, 65; 4.4, p. 108f; 5.4, p. 27f).

In the years 1875-1877 she was the victim of very fierce temptations to despair that drove her nearly mad. On May 29, 1875, while at Torricella, she wrote:

"Violent agitation. It seemed to me my nature was changing and that I would go mad from one minute to the next... What I feel being suggested to me is horrible, as if it were already happening: Look, you will do this and that. Do you see that you are no longer in your right mind, do you see that you will be forced to throw yourself out of the window? Ah! you resist, but in a moment you will no longer be able to resist..." (M 4.3, p. 63f).

This almost obsessive impulse to throw herself out of the window returns constantly in those years, always at night. Sometimes she feels physically pushed by the tempter, dragged to the windowsill, and always threatened: "I will throw you out of the window!" (cf. M 4.3, pp. 21-26, 70-75; 4.4, pp. 1-13, 46, 49f, 52f, 125). On February 23 she summed up the merciless struggle thus:

"For some time the fierce one has taken up diabolical suggestions, always the same: that he will throw me out of the window, that he will kill me, that he will make me lose my mind and I will be left an idiot, that my end will be despair, because I live in sin and constantly renew my sacrileges: yet he never points out a single one to me. In short, the turmoil he stirs up in my poor mind is beyond belief" (M 4.4, p. 36).

The battle culminated in April 1877 with very strong temptations to suicide (M 4.4, p. 139).

It may seem inconceivable that such a situation, continuing for months and years, could form part of God's plan, even as something he permits, and that it could coexist with the heroic exercise of hope, indeed with the trusting intimacy of unitive love. But it is a more than frequent fact in the history of Christian hagiography. At the end of the most pitiful descriptions Mother Rosa now and then adds remarks such as these: "Though I am in the midst of an abyss of pains, yet something keeps me in an indescribable peace."

"When I offer him such miserable pains, he makes me feel an inexpressible inner peace" (M 4.4, pp. 89, 105).

The soul emerges from these battles purified and strengthened in faith and hope, disillusioned with itself, humbled and stronger in fidelity to Love. Mother Rosa does not doubt that God will triumph in her, but she suffers at the thought of possible third-party victims. In 1889 she confided to Mons. Granito di Belmonte:

"It is always an ugly thing to fight an enemy who hates me, and I hate him more: I feel something - we are always at blows! Those who suffer are the poor creatures caught in the middle... - I am always in the midst of battles. It is true that victory is certain for me, but the cannon shots always wound and strike open wounds, because there is no time for them to heal" (3-5-1889, 29-8-1889).

Together with temptations come those other inner sufferings that belong to the great and supreme purification known as the night of the spirit, a true purgatory in this life: aridity, abandonment, God's absence. They are torments that only one can understand who, having experienced the ineffable sweetness of loving union with God, sees herself deprived of so great a good, with no possibility now of placing her love in anything but him. This pain of love, which surpasses every other, has inspired the most sublime pages of the mystics of all ages; we find them very frequently in Mother Rosa's spiritual diary.

The first experience of aridity, the effect of passing into infused contemplation, occurs when, as Saint John of the Cross teaches, the soul feels invaded by God and the lower faculties - senses, imagination, intellect - remain suspended, without an object, while the will, an eminently arid [affective?] faculty, is strongly drawn by God. In one of the first, beautifully autobiographical pages of the book Trials and Consolations, Mother Rosa recalls such an experience precisely at the beginning of her mystical ascent:

"My Crucified left me in the dark, off the path, without intellect, unable to reason. Everything was closed, the night was horrible and dark, and I could not understand where I was. I would have liked to reason, but, as I have said, this faculty had been taken from me, and not even the comfort of tears was granted me" (TC, p. 6).

This probably happened in 1859, on the eve of the feast of the Most Holy Redeemer, as she relates at the beginning of her Memoirs:

"While I was expecting great consolations, being used to them, especially on feast days, I found myself instead arid. Alas! how can this be? Perhaps it is I who have done something, and so my Good has gone away from me. What have I done? And I was very distressed; I did not know where to find peace..."

It was her spiritual Father who made her understand that this pain was of greater value before God than sensible consolations (M 1.1, p. 4). But it is one thing to know this in theory, another to experience it at the moment of trial. Indeed, what makes souls suffer in such a situation is not aridity itself but the fear that it is the result of God's displeasure at some infidelity. Here is a truly expressive page written on September 4, 1867:

"Plunged into a stormy sea of tribulations, my laments were not heard. A thought said to me:

- Did you not have the desire to suffer?

- Oh! yes - I answered.

And I abandoned myself entirely to that suffering. I tried to absorb it all with resignation, surrendering myself to the will of my eternal Father. But it became so strong that I could not help turning to my God and Father for help. But no! I saw him unmoved. I turned to my Beloved: he too seemed almost displeased. Meanwhile the sufferings grew ever stronger, and I cried out:

- Help, have pity!

I prayed to Mary, but she did not let herself be seen.

- Oh! what have I done?

I prayed to Saint Joseph and to Saint Francis my Father: they too were not moved to pity.

But the heaviest pain added to all this was seeing the eternal Father and Jesus so unmoved, one with a look of indifference, the other almost of displeasure.

- Oh! what have I done to you, Being of my life? Have pity on me! increase my suffering as much as you will, but do not show yourself displeased. Oh! the pain is too strong, it overwhelms me!

Thus the suggestions (of the enemy) grew stronger.

- See! - he kept saying to me - Everyone has abandoned you! Turn to me!...

What a battle, my God! Weeping, I began to say:

- My Father, allow me to shed these tears... (M 1.1, p. 45f).

More terrible than mere aridity is the state of abandonment, in which the soul feels as though God has left it for good, finds every road closed and sees itself as if in a dark prison without a chink of light. The Servant of God described this torment, equivalent to the pain of loss in purgatory and hell, a hundred times in heart-rending terms. This page from 1874 will serve as an example:

"The pain I feel is too great... Alas, I fell into a terrible temptation to despair: the grief of having been able to displease the Being of my life, and that for this my Love had unhappily abandoned me! Grief beyond compare! I was in agony. Oh! with what a sword my breast was pierced! I called him, I begged his pardon, but nothing!... My soul writhed. The pains that came upon me were of every kind, so that I fainted. When I came to, my words were:

- I have lost my God!

Three days I remained in that painful state: I shall never be able to forget them. On the fourth, as soon as I had received holy Communion, a gentle voice said to me:

- Rosa, how much you have made me suffer! - I heard the voice of my Beloved.

Alas! sadly it is true. Forgive me! what have I done?...

I was in a state I cannot describe, because one has to experience it to know what it is like. What pain it was! But I remained in ecstasy... Meanwhile my soul was clearing itself of that dense cloud and returning to its former state: peace and resignation in adversity... When I came to, I realized I was a different person..." (M 1.1, p. 166f).

This is usually the outcome of every period of God's absence, which often lasts several days: the encounter with her beloved Good, who makes her feel the tenderness of his love, fully makes up for the pains she has suffered. Through the Memoirs one can follow the victories of pure faith in those secret tortures which for many years had no other witness or confidant than the pages of her notebook.

That plunge into the night of the spirit bears fruit in total purification, which opens the way to pure love. Often she has the sensation of being damned; she seems to feel the very pains of hell; and it is precisely at that moment that her heart utters its most moving outpourings of love:

"The poor soul, amid the despair of the damned, finds that it has lost its Being. It cannot find him anywhere. Yes, my God! I go to the tabernacle, and find myself as if mute...; wherever I turn I see nothing but a precipice; I look at my actions to see whether I can find anything in them to comfort me..., I see myself ever more destitute, I can see nothing that I have: everything vanishes before my nothingness. What pains these are! I do not speak of the fear this state causes: I can only say that these are the pains of hell. I have lost my Beloved, the only object of my life!" (M 3, p. 27f).

The further the soul advances in knowledge of the divine perfections, the poorer and more unworthy it feels, and it comes to the conviction that it is impossible to close the distance. The more irresistibly it feels drawn towards its center, which is God, the more unreachable it finds him. She expresses it thus in an unsurpassable page from May 1874:

"The anguish is most cruel when you, my Good, flee and leave me in the pit into which I have fallen, with nothing to hold onto to climb out. And worse still - this is the greatest of sorrows - you no longer listen to me, and however hard I try to find you, I can never find you. Only my wickedness stands before me, forming that inner wall which seems to have divided everything between me and my God. I will never again be allowed to see him: the height is such that I see it is insurmountable" (M 4.2, pp. 90-92).

Eleven years later, in 1885, the path of pure faith had become less turbulent and her descriptions are calmer. The night is darker than before, "the sky is bronze," but there is more security, more peace. One might say that walking in faith had become a habit; moreover her experience of God is now peaceful, the raptures and other bodily repercussions are left behind; although the pains seem new each time, the spirit is not afraid:

"What new pains! I do not understand myself: I feel an inner peace, nothing reproaches me, I no longer see anything of that horrible abyss. But my prayer is arid, dry. I feel little or nothing of rapture, and union with God is different... I find myself, if I had to put it into words, like a soul between light and darkness that does not understand where it is: it walks, but does not know where; it lets itself be led as if by an unknown guide.

I do not feel any anguish that should distress me; I do not even feel terrible pains, because my sweet Love says nothing to me. Well then, I wait in peace and resignation for the hour of his coming. Yes! my Love will come and take me out of this poverty and teach me how to rise; I do not doubt it: he will give me strength to get up again" (M 5.4, pp. 22f, 40f, 74f).

But this was not the end of the Bridegroom's painful absences. On February 13, 1888, she confided her sorrow to paper:

"As I write I weep. I do not know how I do not die of such cruel pain. He who was always my Father, Bridegroom, Master, in short my All, the Being of my life, I am no longer allowed to see, nor to have a single thought that assures me I will return to his grace" (M 9.3, p. 6).

And the fears returned of being damned, of having lost her God forever, as appears in the letters written at that time to Don Gennaro (4 letters in Feb. 1888).

In this aspect of spiritual growth, too, Mother Rosa, taught by her own experience, became a sure guide for her spiritual daughters. In the book Trials and Consolations she includes a dialogue with a "worker," that is, a daughter of Saint Anne, in which we read this wise advice:

"Prayer is necessary, especially when we are in aridity... The effort we make renders our prayer more acceptable to God than when we find relief, recollection and union with God in it. God allows beginners the satisfaction of feeling consoled in prayer, so that they may cling to that pleasure and thereby go forward, though without progressing; but those who pray without pleasure, without consolation, guided only by faith, walk the way of perfection and take giant strides along it" (TC, p. 371).

In much the same terms she replies in her letters to sisters who complain of their difficulties in the life of prayer, relying on the authority of Saint Teresa (cf. L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 3-10-1867, 26-8-1872; to Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio: 20-2-1867). She also wrote to Princess di Fitalia:

"You tell me that you are cold. No, my dear, it is Jesus who is at work, and knowing he has good soil, he works it with aridity of spirit, hidden from your eyes... Courage! for in time of trial much is gained... Yes, the pain of love! To love and not to feel and not to see the Beloved is a most painful thing, but this hard trial is rewarded by our dear, most sweet Jesus with certain caresses of his" (15-1-1886).

External tribulations: obstacles and opposition.

Setbacks, misunderstandings and persecutions are the normal lot of all who commit themselves to following Christ. Rosa Gattorno's life could be no exception. From the time she accepted her mission as foundress by God's will, she understood that it is the hallmark of every evangelical undertaking to have to face, first, the demands of human prudence and then opposition, not only from enemies of the interests of the Kingdom but also from good and well-intentioned people who do not share or understand the views of one who acts under divine impulse.

She was conscious of being an instrument of God, albeit an unskilled one: her foundation was the Work of God. It is no wonder that she saw in every opponent an adversary of God's plan, indeed an unwitting collaborator of the evil one. Hence her deep suffering, especially when she discovered hypocrisy, ulterior motives and hidden personal interests in her opponents. Nor should we forget her tendency to turn every unforeseen event into a motive and opportunity for suffering. In fact she had to endure real slander, all the more painful because it came from people to whom she had given trust, affection and sacrifice (cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 181f, 186-189, 199-220), or from those she deeply venerated as ministers of the Church.

There is no need to list the many occasions that embittered and purified her spirit, already so tried by inner pains. We shall merely touch on her feelings in such situations.

At the beginning of her Memoirs she wrote, recalling the year 1858:

"The family troubles were beyond compare; but, always clinging to my Good, I kept repeating: Oh! my sins deserve worse, even hell itself..." (M 1.1, p. 2f).

Her own account of what happened in Piacenza on March 31, 1869, because of the slanderous accusations raised by the superior of the house herself, is the best testimony to her conduct in such cases and above all to her prompt and generous forgiveness (M 1.2, pp. 21-28).

After summarizing the five persecutions she suffered in 1868 and 1869, "fireworks on every side," she adds:

"One thing alone comforts me, and it is that no rancor has ever remained in me towards whoever caused me so much pain, whoever it might be; on the contrary, I feel very great affection towards them and have increased my prayers for them, and I always tried to do them whatever good I could" (M 1.2, pp. 28-31).

And here too one of her very candid introspections surprises us. One day she began to suspect that the tendency mentioned above was leading her to discover malice where there was none and to magnify the causes of suffering out of a certain secret pleasure in suffering; Jesus gave her the answer:

"My beloved, whatever they do to you, I receive the same pain: your sorrows are mine. Do you want to know why you suffer so much at seeing your daughters and those close to you act so maliciously? Be at peace, for there is nothing human in it; but since you must feel painfully everything that offends me, you feel more than appears" (M 1.1, p. 169f).

The thought that Jesus suffers with her - indeed, that behind the misunderstandings and obstacles she meets he is always there to sustain her and help her fight - gives her courage and confidence. In May 1872, amid terrible sufferings caused by the difficulties she met in getting the Rules approved, she wrote:

"How sweet it is to live in Jesus, resigned to God's will! Today the pains are of one kind, tomorrow of another; today a cross with spikes, tomorrow with nails. All of them are planted there by Jesus! Certainly, if this dear Love plants sharp blades in them, he will also (give) the strength to receive the wounds and will not let us be crushed beneath them. And if that happened, we will always be happy to have been victims for our Beloved" (M 3, p. 44).

As in her other sufferings, in external tribulations too she continually experiences the Lord's consolations and the joy of finding a way to unite herself with him in suffering. She often exclaims: "O sweet suffering, you give life to those who love!" (M 4.5, p. 130).

"Tribulations are treasures that bring great victories" (L to Don Gennaro: 18-3-1890).

"Let us rejoice amid tribulations, our only pledge and comfort!" (L to a superior: 8-12-1868).

"Courage, daughter! only in tribulations do the Lord's works grow" (L to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza: 27-8-1880).

In her letters to Mons. Granito di Belmonte we see the degree of evangelical maturity she had reached in bearing the external setbacks affecting the Institute:

"I see you are distressed; but I am perfectly calm and, in my continual suffering, I find peace and consolation in suffering itself. For my sins everything is little; I have only one thing that comforts me: the will of God. Holy indifference governs my soul; I do what my poor strength allows in the Work of the Lord, so as to manage to spend it all for my God. It is very sweet"

- "Man is a slave: he acts and builds as long as God pleases; but woe if he stretches out his most holy hand: the oppressed become victorious. So it will be" (L 14-3-1890, 5-5-1899).

4. Completing in one's own flesh the sufferings of Christ (cf. Col 1:24).

The reason for Rosa Gattorno's penances.

Bodily mortification, in one form or another, is a constant throughout the history of Christian asceticism; indeed it is inherent in any spiritual striving, even in other religions. The motives can be various, as are the interpretations this phenomenon gives rise to from an anthropological point of view. Certainly there can be aberrations that have nothing to do with a religious relationship with God, such as Manichaean hatred of one's own body, masochistic satisfaction, fanaticism, a delirium of self-destruction, pharisaical exhibitionism... But the traditional practice of works of penance is rooted in evangelical metanoia, which is a permanent striving for conversion and therefore for asceticism and renunciation, as a condition for following Christ (cf. Mt 16:24), as reparation for one's own sins, a renewed struggle against one's disordered tendencies until mastery over them is gained (cf. 1 Cor 9:27), and as a way of keeping the spirit free and ready for the Lord's call...

From a theological point of view, however, there is a deeper justification: to share in the mystery of the suffering Christ, of redemptive pain, offering the Savior a kind of supplement of voluntary suffering so that he may continue his sacrificial self-offering to the glory of the Father. Many great penitents have made Saint Paul's motive their own: I rejoice in the sufferings I bear for your sake, and in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, which is the Church (Col 1:24).

All this together constitutes the reason for Rosa Gattorno's atrocious and, let us say, excessive penances, though she lived in an age in which the asceticism of relentless violence against one's own body seemed to have been left behind. She herself was aware that she had committed herself to a way of life that was out of place; this was the main reason why for many years she did not confide in a spiritual Father, convinced as she was that she would find no one to approve that daily "butchery" of her limbs. To this must be added her almost humble modesty, which led her always to keep her instruments of penance and the place where she used them hidden from human eyes.

I would not rule out, as the starting point of her craving for mortification, a certain reaction against her own body or, better, against a past of indulgence towards natural attractions. Let us not forget that she always called herself a convert, with a debt to pay to the Lord. Only in such a context can sense be made of the frequent insults with which she vents her aversion to her body, calling it "beast of burden," "donkey," "pig," "miserable beast," and that kind of pleasure in keeping it subdued and tortured. She sees in it as it were the instrument of her offenses and infidelities against her beloved Good. Naturally there is also the felt need to make reparation for herself and others. From time to time we find invectives like this:

"I always hated you, O wretched donkey of mine! and now I do not know what I would do to you. You, yes, you will be and were my enemy, the one who drew me away from Jesus!" (M 3, p. 47).

But the real reason is nothing other than the debt of love towards the crucified Savior, from whom every redemptive sacrifice receives its origin and value. She recalls how her craving for bodily penances began in 1858:

"I took the cord of Saint Francis of Assisi and (there came to me) a great desire to afflict this miserable beast of a body. Had I been allowed, I would have made a slaughter of it: so much did I hate it for having been so wicked" (M 1.1, p. 15).

In time her feeling of hatred for her body diminished: she rejoiced in the sufferings she inflicted on it, but regarded it as a good instrument of gain for the soul:

"O suffering, I feel you killing my flesh, but you make my soul just as beautiful! If once I hated this rotten body, now, because of what I feel the soul gains through it, I wish it less ill, and I would say that at times I feel moved to pity" (M 4.2, p. 86).

At certain times she resorted to penances to give vent to her love and also to counterbalance the sufferings of her spirit (cf. M 4.5, p. 59); or simply to satisfy her insatiable thirst for suffering. Often her penances aimed at making effective her prayer of petition for her own needs, for the needs of others, for sinners, for the souls in purgatory, for the Church (M 1.2, p. 118).

But the link with the Redeemer's life and passion always returns; from each of his sufferings she takes occasion to mortify her taste and every satisfaction, as well as to invent new forms of penance. She would have liked to make her body a true image of that of her beloved Crucified.

From time to time she felt the need to give her penances a purpose, precisely in order to avoid the danger of regarding them as ends in themselves. One day in 1872 it was the Lord, her "director," who showed her with what intention she was to practice some of them: "fasting for the conversion of sinners, eating herbs for the provision of the Institute, the chains so that, chained, bound tightly to his Heart and to his love, I may consummate the wounds they cause me, and that they may help me soon to reach most perfect union with you, O my eternal All" (M 3, p. 26).

During Carnival in 1876 she redoubled her scourgings to the point of drawing blood, and poured out her heart to Jesus:

"Ah! if my blood in these days, when your Heart receives so many wounds from such ugly amusements - how many sins, alas, my Good! - oh! if only I had enough blood to shed for all!..." (M 4.4, p. 37f).

Mother Rosa's penitential regime.

Among the Servant of God's manuscripts there is one in which, under obedience, she describes retrospectively the whole unheard-of variety of penances she imposed on herself as a program from the beginning of her self-giving to God (35).

As early as 1856, at the age of 25, she had bound herself by vow to perpetual fasting: one meal a day, always meatless. She observed it strictly until her death. She had also vowed to Our Lady not to eat fruit (M 1.2, p. 42).

In 1858, after her husband's death, she arranged her bodily mortifications as she pleased. Her rest was no more than two hours, spent leaning on a table or on the floor. She denied herself heating in winter until 1876, when after a serious pleurisy she had to accept the relief of a little warmth. She put chickpeas in her shoes to feel discomfort when walking.

In 1859, with her confessor's permission, she put on a leather bodice bristling with iron points; she also bound her legs and arms with similar devices. On her breast she wore a small crucifix, which remained embedded in her flesh for five years, as mentioned above.

But her own particular invention was a chain of thick iron wire with double crossed links, fastened around her waist and tightened so that it could no longer be removed. She wore it like this for more than forty years; it had sunk into her flesh, causing her unbearable spasms; she had it removed three days before she died. Over this chain she wore another, thicker one, pressed tight against her flesh.

From the time she joined the Franciscan Third Order she wore under her clothes, day and night, a coarse habit with the cord.

It is not surprising that her parents, seeing her weakened, attributed it to that regime of abstinence and penance; hence their complaints against her confessor, Don Giuseppe Firpo, who allowed it. She, on the contrary, was convinced that her strength increased the more she mortified her body (M 1.1, pp. 4, 16-18).

During her stay at S. Francesco d'Albaro to recover her health, good Don Firpo tried to make her stop her penances, but the effect was the very opposite: her health got worse; then he felt inspired to authorize them again, and she regained her strength. The confessor understood that there was a mystery of divine design that had to be respected (cf. M 1.1, p. 25; FIOCCHI, I, pp. 45-49, 56f). And so it would be for the rest of her life: humanly speaking, an existence like Mother Rosa's cannot be explained, with a tortured, undernourished body, in permanent vigil, subjected to exhausting work and journeys...

In 1863-64 she felt inspired to make a whole year of rigorous fasting, taking no food or drink other than four ounces of bread and a sip of water every twenty-four hours. It was like a trial of the regime she had begun: not only did her health not suffer, it grew stronger, to the point of allowing her to resume her apostolic activity intensely. She writes in her diary:

"I was like one who lives only on the love of the Beloved. Every pain my poor mind suggested I loaded onto this poor donkey, with every kind of penance, and every day I increased them. Many my Love suggested to me and many I devised myself to oppress this ugly pig even more. I devised every kind, and always tried to ask the eternal Father whether what I was doing pleased him" (M 2, p. 140).

Here is the doubt that very often assails her at moments of greatest longing for penance: but is it God's will? For many years, as we have seen, she confided this secret of her spiritual life to no one. Almost always she felt within that the Lord was pleased; but sometimes the devil suggested to her that all this was an attack on her own health. So on March 30, 1871:

"For three months I have had two irons clamped tight on my arms, and they have sunk so deep into the flesh that they cause me atrocious spasms. Oh! what pain! Every movement is a new torment; keeping my arm resting to write, what I feel, my Love!... I did not have the courage to take them off. What could I do? Ask someone? Oh! rather die! But the evil serpent told me I would have to pay for it if I died like that...

While I was struggling like this, the pain stopped..., and so it seems to me that it is God's will that I should no longer think of removing them..." (M 1.2, p. 39f) (36).

On December 8, 1887, authorized by her confessor, she took heart for a more rigorous program of penances:

"I will take the discipline to the point of blood every evening, I will tighten the chain I wear so that it sinks well into the flesh, the usual fasting and abstinence, which I cannot increase further except by eating only bread - that would be noticed and arouse suspicion, no! - I will cover my arms well with hair shirts, I will sleep badly and little, I will work hard... But I am exhausted: age and continual pain..." (M 9.2, p. 3-5).

In her last years, at the command of her director Don Gennaro, she had to reduce her forms of penance, keeping only the chain, and to moderate her strict diet somewhat.

On her journeys, and after the generalate was moved to Rome, she missed her little room in Piacenza, her hermitage, where she could freely abandon herself, without human witnesses, to her mortifications, sleeping on the wooden cross with a thick chain for a pillow, and remaining suspended from the other cross with the nails. She was glad to be able to return there and find a kind of spiritual refreshment.

Hard on herself and insatiable in abstinence and bodily torture, she was on the other hand careful to prevent excesses among the sisters in the practice of penance, especially when it was at the expense of proper nourishment. In her letters to superiors she urges them not to allow any imprudence in this regard.

The virginal heart, while it succeeds in freeing its affective potential to focus it on uncreated Love, increases its capacity to love all that God loves. Such focusing becomes all the more fruitful and effective the more vital the union with the supreme Good.

One of the first manifestations of true love guided by faith is piety - true piety, not the devotional or sentimental kind that comes between the soul and God and robs love of that dynamic restlessness of one who lives not for herself but for God and others. At the crucial moment of her life Rosa Gattorno was able to direct the richness of her affectivity so as to develop an authentic piety centreed on the fundamental contents of faith: the triune God, Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary, certain saints as models and protectors, the Church, the Institute, her spiritual daughters, the poor.

1. God, true Love. The supreme Good.

She wrote on the first page of her Memoirs, regarding the decision she made in 1858 to give herself fully to God:

"By the Lord's grace I noticed that all earthly affections were fading away; nothing gave me pleasure any more: my God alone was the pasture of all my delights" (M 1.1 p. 1).

In her fervent and very frequent conversations with God she likes to address him with titles of deep meaning: the Being of my life, my All, my Good, the supreme Good, Love... She also likes to set her own littleness against the "infinite ocean of God's greatness," that ineffable divine essence in comparison with which "whoever comes to taste it finds everything earthly nauseating" (M 1.2, p. 2). She who has experiential light of such greatness cannot understand "how man can live without knowing God, the supreme Good" (M 11.2, p. 78f).

God alone suffices.

She often expresses her aspiration, common to all souls accustomed to infused contemplation, to withdraw from everything that is not God and to remain with him alone. She wrote on January 17, 1875:

"A voice spoke to me thus:

- Live in God alone and seek nothing else. Converse with him and seek no other relief but in him. Let him be enough for you in everything...

- Yes, my Good, in you alone!" (M 4.3, p. 15).

There are moments, she says, when "the world and all creatures are secondary objects, as if separated, worthy of attention only to gather the fruits to offer to my Good, my Love" (M 4.3, p. 56).

In the book Trials and Consolations, replying to a "shepherd" who was trying to unsettle her about her walking without a guide, she includes a beautiful outpouring expressing all that God represents in her journey of faith:

"I beg you to speak only of the greatness of God and of his omnipotence and mercy. These three subjects alone give me great satisfaction, both in hearing them spoken of and in pausing to reflect on them by myself...

Oh! the mind reasons, and in such immensity it has room to run without ever meeting an obstacle to halt its reasoning. The intellect unfolds to the greatest insights of the soul in its relationship with its God, that endless ocean of greatness, power and mercy.

The further the mind advances into it, the vaster it sees the space, ever new themes unfold, and the majesty of God appears in ever larger proportions. And since the soul is always subject to him, how painfully it groans when, through the darkness in which it finds itself wrapped because of sin, it feels itself separated from him!" (TC, p. 313).

What in her was a maturing of faith, strengthened by unitive experience, she instilled in the daughters of Saint Anne as the goal of the necessary purification of the affections. On October 17, 1898, she gave the novices a warm exhortation on the true love of God and said to them:

"A religious must always think of Jesus, of loving him and of being all his... What a beautiful thing to be completely detached from relatives, from superiors, from that sick person, from the confessor!..." (FIOCCHI, II, p. 281).

Whoever loves God cannot remain indifferent to an offense against so great a Good. We have already seen how deeply Mother Rosa's heart suffered at seeing God offended.

"Only one thing intimidates and frightens me: offense against God," she repeats in her letters to superiors.

The triune God.

Recalling her contemplations of 1864, she describes, not without some imprecision in theological terminology, the light she received on the mystery of the Trinity, the great mystery of love that makes of three Persons one God, of creating and sanctifying love that communicates itself to mankind (M 1.2, p. 1f). On Easter day 1866 she had another infused communication, with a vision, on the same mystery (M 1.1, p. 39).

Here we must note her particular devotion to the first Person, whom she calls by titles of filial tenderness: my dear eternal Father, dear, lovable, most tender Father, Joy of my soul. The eternal Father defends her in temptations, comforts and sustains her in difficulties, gives her victory in her struggles (M 1.1, p. 75, 78).

She warmly recommends to the sisters love for the eternal Father and trust in him (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 22-8-1869, 12-2-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 15-10-1869, 1-12-1869, 11-6-1871). At the end of her letters she often uses the formula introduced by Fr. Tornatore: "May the blessing of our eternal Father be with us." She writes to a superior:

"Love this eternal Father and make your daughters love him, for if they love this God and Father, our one and only Good, they will become perfect and be able to do whatever they wish, and everything will be well done" (L to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 22-5-1871).

In another letter she addresses a fervent plea to the Savior on behalf of the daughters of Saint Anne:

"My Jesus, more than this work, what should matter to you but that your Father be glorified? These poor creatures, the daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, have him continually on their lips and call upon him in all their actions; they hold him in their hearts because they love him as Father... In short, you may well say: These are the true daughters of my eternal Father, because they expect everything from him and rest in him alone..." (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 1-6-1871).

At the initiative of Fr. Tornatore, deeply devoted to the first Person of the Trinity, the Institute adopted the practice of dedicating the month of January as the month of the eternal Father (cf. L to D.G. Granito di Belmonte: 8-1-1887, 16-1-1889) (37).

No less tender and trusting was her devotion to the Holy Spirit, "joy of hearts," whose mission in them is to rekindle divine love and consume every earthly affection (M 1.1, p. 39). In 1872, when she found herself so alone without the guidance of a director, she felt secure under that of her "governing Spirit":

"What a consolation it is for me, so abandoned by all human help, to have my dear Spirit, who guides me in everything, directs me and sustains me so well, even in days of such a painful state. He acts and leads everything excellently. I find nothing but misery, shame and confusion" (M 3, pp. 9, 11f).

Trust in God's providence.

The trust in divine fatherhood that Jesus asks of his disciples was in Mother Rosa's life not only an effect of faith but also something experienced almost daily, even in the form of real miracles, in matters concerning the Institute's progress, especially in financial straits. She often observed the immediate effect of prayer in such situations: an unknown person bringing what was needed to pay a debt, unexpected supplies arriving from far away at just the right moment, the resolution of a difficulty when things seemed most tangled... (cf. M 1.1, pp. 71f, 103, 145; 3, pp. 61f, 65f; 4.1, pp. 7, 85-87; 4.4, p. 99f; L to Princess di Fitalia: 12-11-1889).

As a rule she does not turn to intermediate intercessors but entrusts herself directly to the most holy Trinity, to the eternal Father. She is reassured by the Lord's promise to her: "You will have everything you need" (M 1.1, p. 103, 118). It seems quite natural to her that, since this is God's Work, he should be the one to deal with whatever difficulties arise. Indeed, the promise is renewed to her from time to time:

"I was weeping: I told my eternal Father to send me his providence: he appeared to me so beautiful that I remained in ecstasy, and he told me very clearly that he would see to everything needed for his Work" (M 1.1, p. 172).

One day, amid external difficulties, she complained to the Lord: "Tell me, my Love, why do you not hear me?" And she received the immediate reply: "I have refused you nothing of what you have asked me" (M 1.1, p. 143).

She would have liked her spiritual daughters, especially the superiors of the houses, to be animated by the same trust, to the point of wresting a miracle from God the Father if need be. She often says so in her letters. She writes to one of them:

"I feel God's providence so strongly in me, and I would like to be able to pass it on to all the daughters of Saint Anne" (to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 22-7-1892).

She was fully convinced that when we leave the care of ourselves and our affairs to God, thinking only of him, he will take care of our problems, as Saint Peter recommends (1 Pet 5:7):

"Providence will come, do not worry... God will think of us if we think only of him. Have the novena for providence to Saint Joseph repeated, and ask him to give you humility, and through this virtue to give you providence" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 3-8-1872).

God's will in everything and through everything.

In the book Trials and Consolations Mother Rosa imagines a lively dialogue with a "shepherd" who would like to dissuade her from going on, since she is walking off the road. She answers every insinuation:

"I will do nothing but the will of God!"

At last the "shepherd" says to her irritably:

"Oh! what a head! the way you talk is that of an ignorant creature." To which she replies: "You are right, I have no other knowledge than the will of my Lord!" (TC, pp. 365-367).

Here is the pivot of her spirituality, and also the cause of her inner anguish, since for so many years she had to face alone the uncertainties of her inner life and the decisions concerning her responsibility as foundress: is it God's will? This torment, as we have seen, is present on many pages of her spiritual diary. God's will, God's pleasure, God's good pleasure, what is pleasing to God - these synonyms are also at the center of her teaching of the sisters:

"If you knew what consolation I feel merely in pronouncing these words - God's pleasure - and still more when the sweet thought awakens vividly in me of being, or being able to become, pleasing to him! I feel completely beside myself, so that if I had to face the cruelest martyrdom I would feel nothing..." (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 4-2-1871).

- "A 'thy will be done,' said with resignation in a time of battles and afflictions, is worth more than having the gift of raising the dead to life" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 20-10-1871).

In the bitter months of 1872, when she had to suffer so much over the matter of the Rules, her letters reflect the serenity of her spirit abandoned to God's will.

"Let the whole world talk: we do the will of God!" she writes to Sister A. Francesca Camisa (11-6-1873).

So too at other times of trial and suffering. And when it becomes hard to discover God's will, or one has to wait for uncertain future events, there is the disposition of abandonment into God's hands, without ever losing peace:

"Let us put everything into God's most holy hands; let him do with us as he pleases" - "Be cheerful, without worries, and trust in the Lord" - "Now I have done my part, God will do the rest" - "Let us leave it to the Lord, who works everything for the good of our soul" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1-7-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 25-1-1869, 6-8-1870, 9-3-1870).

"Let us leave everything in God's hands...; may the divine will be fully accomplished in us: in it everything is satisfied, since it is for us the sole object of our life" (L to Fr. Donadio: 22-4-1870).

  • Jesus Christ, the Beloved.

    • From what has been said so far, one might almost speak of a certain theocentrism in Rosa Gattorno's spirituality.
