In reality, however, her piety, which is faith and love, opens with all its impetus to the incarnate God, her beloved Bridegroom, her Beloved, as she likes to call him. The affectionate meditations of Lent 1864 bear witness to the intensity of her love for Jesus, specifically for the suffering Jesus (M 2, pp. 77-187). But on every page of her Memoirs, in every letter, Jesus appears as the object of her love, the center of her life.

    "When one has Jesus, one has the whole world."

    - "To grow in the spirit and love of Jesus": this is the ideal of every daughter of Saint Anne (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 16-12-1868, 1-10-1869; Circ. 1886). She would have liked them all to be in love with, mad about, sweet Jesus.

    "If you knew how much Jesus loves you," she wrote to a postulant, "you would certainly be mad about him and would do nothing but clasp him to your heart and say to him: Speak to me, command me!" (L to Caterina Rapallino: 1868).

    "Live for Jesus," "see Jesus in everything" are frequent recommendations in her letters.

    Dear crucified Love.

    Following Christ demands readiness and courage; one must answer the Master's call as Peter and the other apostles did; he is not satisfied with mediocrity but wants generous hearts: so Mother Rosa spurs on her daughters (L to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: 12-2-1867; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 23-4-1867).

    Jesus is the model, the mirror in which a daughter of Saint Anne must look at herself, learning from him to find true joy in adversity and to practice the Gospel virtues. One must "make good use of the lessons of such a teacher and be studious in order to please him and fully satisfy his will" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 4-2-1871).

    She invites them to go to the school of Bethlehem, where the "God made small" gives us splendid lessons in detachment, self-emptying and poverty. She likewise recommends attending the school of Nazareth, which speaks of hiddenness and obedience.

    But no chair is richer in profound lessons than that of the school of Calvary.

    It was at the beginning of her new life that Rosa Gattorno received from God a sign that was to stamp her spirituality with its most distinctive feature. In her father's house there was a large crucifix before which she spent long hours of the night in prayer. One night she saw it come down from the cross and fall into her arms; she then put it back on the cross, nailing it there. This happened a second and a third time. She then understood that she must accept to live crucified with the crucified Savior (38).

    The Crucified would henceforth be her lot, the center of her love, her comforter, the guide and master of her life.

    In the expression my Crucified, repeated a thousand times, one feels all the ardor of her heart vibrating. The favorite theme of her contemplation is the Lord's Passion; more than a meditation, it is a sharing in his sufferings, with a longing to reach full configuration to him.

    She likes to meditate with her head resting at the feet of her Crucified. She ends every letter with these or similar words of farewell: "I hold you close in my Crucified," "Always yours in my dear Crucified," "A strong embrace in my sweet Crucified."

    In hard moments of uncertainty or adversity, clasping the cross to her breast, she entrusts herself confidently to him: "Oh! my Crucified will see to everything." "My Crucified will guard his Work." "My Crucified will not abandon his slave."

    Nothing is more beautiful than the introductory pages of her book Trials and Consolations, where every paragraph begins with the exclamation: My Crucified!

    To follow Jesus on the road to Calvary, carrying the cross, and to remain crucified with him: this was the ideal of her life. She wrote in 1862:

    "Now I find myself on a rough sea, a poor battered little boat swamped by the waves: I hold fast only to the anchor of the holy Cross, so as not to sink and to reach the blessed harbor of my Good. Oh! terrible pains!... Press the dear banner of the Cross upon my breast, but add to it the strength to carry it well and climb the mountain of sorrow, Calvary, and, ever victorious, close to you, to die crucified with you" (M 1.1, p. 23).

    Her mystical experiences include sweet embraces from the Crucified, like the one granted her on September 18, 1885, at the moment of Communion: Jesus crucified appeared to her, came down from the cross and embraced her lovingly (M 5.5, p. 1).

    As foundress she wanted identification with the Crucified to be the longing of all the daughters of Saint Anne. She wrote to one of them:

    "Daughter, where are those cruel pains of yours?... I cannot find even enough to relieve the least of Jesus' sorrows. Let us always reason with the Crucified before us, not beside us (39); let us see in all our actions whether they conform to his example, and then everything is reduced to nothing and our sufferings become a fine nothing, less than nothing..." (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 15-1-1870, 28-2-1870).

    The crucified Redeemer is the mediator before the Father. Mother Rosa has boundless trust in the intercessory power of the blood of the Mediator of the new Covenant, which speaks more eloquently than Abel's (Heb 12:24): "Only the blood of my dear Crucified can do everything with the heart of his eternal Father: knock and do not tire, and it will be opened to you" (L to Emilia di Fitalia: 5-3-1885).

    Her Christ-centreed piety is not confined to the cross and the Savior's sufferings. Accustomed to living the paschal mystery in its entirety, every year she rejoiced intensely in contemplating the triumph of the Risen One, after sharing mystically in the whole Passion on Good Friday.

    On Holy Saturday 1862 she lived the joy of Jesus' resurrection to such a degree that she could not contain herself for joy and, to curb its force, she began to sing (M 1.1, p. 21). On Easter Sunday 1866 she had a vision of the feast being held in heaven, after which she gave vent to her joy in an ardent prayer to the risen Lord, to the eternal Father, to the Holy Spirit and to the Virgin Mary (M 1.1, p. 37f).

    The Sacred Heart of Jesus, school of love.

    In the course of the nineteenth century devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus had developed greatly, a development that reached its height under the pontificate of Leo XIII. Rosa Gattorno soon found in her Beloved's open side the treasure of love. But for her it was always the Heart of the sweet Crucified. On May 2, 1867, during a night watch in the hospital at Cento, she wrote for Caterina Rapallino (later Sister A. Vincenza) a reflection in the form of a dialogue between Jesus and his bride, urging her to enter the Heart of Jesus: the way and the door are nothing other than suffering with him; it is not enough to meditate on his sufferings, one must "taste the pain: suck with peace, delight and love" those very sufferings.

    "If you do this," Jesus added, "you will be granted every permission to enter, living always in this loving cavern of my Side." She promptly accepted this condition:

    "From now on your bride will think of nothing but suffering" (40).

    The feast of the Sacred Heart was every year an occasion of extraordinary graces. She very often mentions the Redeemer's Heart in her diary and letters. In 1873 she happened to celebrate this feast during a journey on which she suffered cruelly. She went into a church where there was an image of the Sacred Heart to thank him and offer him that suffering.

    "As soon as I looked at him," she writes, "he smiled at me. My Good, are you pleased with my suffering and my actions? How glad I am!" (M 4.1, p. 107).

    This was not the only time Jesus' smiling face reassured her of his pleasure. At other times, however, she found his face sad, which she interpreted as a sign of some fault committed perhaps inadvertently (cf. M 4.2, p. 54f). On February 10, 1876, feeling drained of strength, she asked the Lord to help her so that no one would notice her weakness; completely absorbed in ecstasy, she saw a stream flowing from the Heart of Jesus into her mouth and nourishing her. When the vision ended, she felt strong and robust (M 4.4, p. 31). One night in March of that year she had a new vision: "a most beautiful Heart, all aflame, with a white circle around it," wrapped in great splendor; it left her flooded with immense sweetness and enlightened with new teachings (M 4.4, p. 39f).

    She received another similar favor in December 1877:

    "My Good gave me such sweetness in opening his Side to me! It seemed that the sweetest honey of his love was pouring into this Heart of his... Ah! Love! why do you pour so many graces into so perverse a creature?... I have no more tastes, no more pleasures: only you! And for you I live, for you and in you I will die" (M 4.5, p. 21f).

    And here is another of her outpourings of love, from September 1880:

    "Oh! most sweet Heart, source of all my relief! Yes, in you alone my soul, oppressed by the toil of sufferings, finds refreshment and life; in you I find my life and all my pains are sweetened in you, Vesuvius of love! for whoever rests upon you sleeps no other sleep than that of love. In you alone, yes, I experience everything; from this Vesuvius every kind of treasure springs. Oh! how blind man is! he does not know where the true good lies" (M 5.1, p. 28f).

    Her mother's heart, when she writes to the daughters of Saint Anne, finds no better way of expressing her affection than to meet each one in the Heart of Jesus. One could go on forever collecting the warm expressions in which she affirms at once her love for the Lord and for the sister she is writing to.

    Every day she made a kind of offering of her Institute to the eternal Father on the mercy seat of the Heart of Jesus, not as an organized and functioning structure but as a living reality made up of individual persons, each with her own vocation, her own striving for holiness, her own responsibilities and problems. This was her prayer as foundress:

    "My God! to you I entrust these creatures you have committed to me. Now I place them for all this time in the Heart of your Son Jesus; cover them with heavenly dew, so that they may be protected from every slightest danger. In this loving retreat of the Heart of Jesus may they learn the true school of your divine Love. My God, bless them and strengthen them in suffering; pour out on them your choicest blessings" (L to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 25-5-1871).

    3. The Eucharist, the mystery of love.

    From her youth Rosa was distinguished by her Eucharistic piety. In the first years of her widowhood she spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament.

    And it was precisely while she was in adoration, in 1859, that she had her first vision of the Lord (M 1.1, p. 2). The Eucharistic mystery would become vital for her, as nourishment of the spirit in the Sacrament, as a bond of self-offering in the Sacrifice, and as an attraction of love in the Tabernacle.

    Communion, the life of the soul.

    From 1855, with her confessor's permission, she enjoyed the benefit of daily communion, uncommon at that time (FIOCCHI, I, p. 53). And already then she was favored with the mystical gift of a sensible taste when holding the sacred Host in her mouth, with an "indescribable consolation" (M 1.1, p. 18, 30).

    Nothing in the world would have made her give up communion. On journeys she made great sacrifices in order to receive it; one must bear in mind the strict discipline of the Eucharistic fast then in force; sometimes she fasted for three days, eating nothing from one communion to the next, faithful to her rule of not eating meat (M 4.5, p. 56; cf. Summ., p. 864). We can understand her grief on that terrible March 31, 1869, when her superior, Fr. Tornatore, deprived her of holy communion after fourteen and a half years in which she had never missed it (M 1.2, p. 23).

    Communion was the privileged moment of her mystical ascents. She remained in thanksgiving for about an hour, kneeling on the floor and leaning with one arm on a chair, motionless and insensible to everything outside. To those who asked her what she said in such long hours, she replied: "Before Jesus, time has no time" (FIOCCHI, II, p. 358).

    Often her inner absorption was so intense that, to avoid rapture, she had to plead: "O Love! ah! for pity's sake, I am in church, I am afraid they will notice; wait until I am in my room. Move away, for pity's sake!" (M 1.1, p. 127f).

    To prolong the effects of sacramental communion through the day and night she made frequent spiritual communions, especially on journeys whenever she caught sight of a church steeple; and very often she experienced the effects of the sacrament as though she were actually receiving it (M 4.4, p. 106; 4.5 p. 118).

    She encouraged the sisters to feed fervently on the Eucharistic bread and then to live the day giving themselves to work in the strength of this nourishment. In a circular of April 23, 1893, she urged them all to give such importance to holy communion that it might "bind together all the actions of the day."

    United to the sacrifice of the altar.

    She had grown used to uniting herself with Jesus, Priest and Victim, in the sacrifice of the Mass; but one day she received special light on the universality of the one Sacrifice, offered continually in every latitude of the world, and she became devoted to this practice:

    "While I was hearing Mass and offering the Sacrifice of the altar to the eternal Father, a very bright light appeared to me, together with a voice that said to me:

    - God is very pleased with this sacrifice of yourself in that chalice, together with his beloved Son; but he would be very pleased if you offered yourself as victim in all the Sacrifices celebrated on the altars of the whole Catholic world.

    And I did not delay in doing so. As soon as I had done it, I was absorbed in God, and my intellect clearly saw all the Sacrifices offered and to be offered in all the Catholic churches. I rejoiced greatly; and so every morning I renew the offering: Here, my God, is your victim, who unites herself with Jesus, your Son, to be immolated on the altar in the bloody chalice offered to you as Victim of expiation for sinners" (M 1.1, p. 123f).

    Some years later she describes a similar offering, "most pleasing to the eternal Father" (M 1.1, p. 179).

    The treasure of the Eucharistic presence.

    The "great mystery of our faith" had become the constant object of her adoration and love. She remained absorbed before this "one immense treasure of our soul" (L to Emilia di Fitalia: 4-9-1889). Very often this faith became experience through vision, especially during adoration before the Blessed Sacrament exposed, but also when she contemplated him enclosed in the tabernacle. One day in 1866 she prayed thus:

    "Fill me, for pity's sake, with your love! Oh! why do I not stay forever before your ciborium where you, my Beloved, are enclosed? What are five or six hours a day? Nothing! Let me stay near you without ever moving again... Light of my eyes, my sweet Love! If people knew you, they would surely leave everything and come to the foot of your altar to enjoy your delights. But how can I make them understand me?..." (M 1.1, p. 43f).

    She was happy when, on her visit to Pius IX in January 1866, she obtained from the Pope an autograph granting her the faculty of reserving the Blessed Sacrament in the house (FIOCCHI, I, p. 109). In Piacenza she wanted her little cell next to the chapel, so that even during the night she could direct her acts of adoration and her affections to Jesus in the Sacrament through the small window opened in the wall.

    She often speaks of the long periods she spent absorbed in close union with him, sometimes the whole night through (M 3, p. 79; 4.1, pp. 12f, 18; 4.4, pp. 26f, 95f, 114f).

    One of the forms of her piety, always original, was to transport herself in spirit to the chapels of the various houses of the Institute to join her spiritual daughters in their homage of love to the Lord present in the tabernacle (M 4.1, p. 87f).

    She taught them to turn to him in difficult moments:

    "If you are upset, run to the church and cry out, weep with Jesus, and then, once you have dried your tears, back to work, all things to all people and full of sweet unction to pass on to others" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 13-5-1872).

    Eucharistic adoration, though not prescribed by the Rule, became customary in the houses of the Daughters of Saint Anne that had enough sisters, especially in the Motherhouse. But because of their mission in the service of the Church they could not devote themselves full time to such an act of worship; so Mother Rosa gladly accepted the offer of the Bishop of Piacenza, Mons. Scalabrini, to direct an institute for deaf and mute girls he had opened in 1880.

    Her interest in those girls, as the mother of a deaf and mute daughter, combined with her desire to see Jesus adored in the Eucharist. On December 8, 1884, with the clothing of the first five deaf and mute girls, the community of the Tertiaries of Saint Anne, Perpetual Adorers of the Blessed Sacrament, came into being (41).

    4. Holy Mother Church.

    Rosa Gattorno's deep sense of the Church would deserve a treatise of its own. It is not only submission to the representatives of the hierarchical Church, but a true ecclesial spirituality inspired by faith and nourished by veneration and love. Having grown up in a family setting where she had to deal with Freemasons and anticlericals, she had to mature her fidelity to Mother Church from an early age, a fidelity that became service and apostolic activity, seeking from the outset to ensure the authenticity of her initiatives through the approval and guidance of diocesan authority.

    It was obedience to the Archbishop of Genoa, Mons. Charvaz, that led her to accept in 1864, at the insistent request of the Servant of God Don Giuseppe Frassinetti, first the presidency of the Children of Mary and then the office of superior of the newly founded Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, the new Ursulines. And it was the same archbishop who verified the genuineness of the divine impulse urging her to found a new institute and encouraged her to go in person to Pope Pius IX to be assured, from the lips of the supreme Pastor, that this was God's will.

    As foundress she was deeply convinced that the institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne was not only God's Work but had been born in the Church and for the Church. Mother Rosa made her own the ideas of Fr. Tornatore, who wrote in a circular letter of 1876:

    "The heavenly Father, who planted our poor Institute in the garden of his Church, looks upon it with special favor. He has increased its houses and multiplied its members... and with the growth in the number of sisters he has been pleased to strengthen it ever more in the spirit of its vocation."

    As a true daughter of the Church she experienced the vicissitudes of the Bride of Christ as her own; indeed, she saw in her Institute's internal sufferings almost a repercussion of the common tribulations of the people of God. She expressed this in a letter during the troubled days of the seizure of the Papal States:

    "It is a time of work and much suffering in this work of the Lord: the Church is in tribulation, and so everything that belongs to her suffers anguish and pain" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 28-12-1870).

    But there was also a mystical repercussion, which she describes in her Memoirs. At times suffering touches the very foundation of her faith in an atrocious passive purification:

    "I am in the deepest desolation: horrible temptations against the Church. And who am I? My God, I am a monster of wickedness! when for the Pope and the Princes of the Church, the Cardinals, and the Bishops, what would I not do? My life is nothing to offer for the prosperity of holy Church. Alas! how painful this state is to me!" (M 5.2, p. 46, 1884).

    On Good Friday 1885 she had an experiential share in the sufferings of the Lord's Passion. Amid upheavals and agonies, the spasms of dislocated bones, in the crucifixion, she felt identified with the sufferings of the Church, the mystical Body of Christ, in which the Passion is constantly renewed:

    "What I suffered, my God! First something came over me that I cannot describe, and I said: O my Love! what is this I feel? - It is the pains the Church is suffering!" (M 5.3, p. 74f).

    The book Trials and Consolations ends with a beautiful allegory of the suffering Church: seven tablets red with blood, held up by bands of fire; Saint Peter weeping, while a legion of angels sings mournfully; the faithful souls dressed in mourning amid a mass of indifferent people. "Every so often a loud groan came forth...: it was heart-rending...: it is the Church suffering!" Rosa offers herself as a victim to make reparation for the cause of such sorrow and to console Mother Church (TC, p. 380f).

    She prayed and had others pray for the Church. She offered her permanent fast, as well as the pain of the invisible stigmata, "for holy Mother Church, for the supreme Pontiff, for the Cardinals and Bishops" (M 1.1, pp. 135, 161).

    She was not, however, one of those prophets of doom who see everything black in the life of the Church and its future. In February 1878 she had a vision of the state of affairs at that historical moment and understood that "the abyss in which the world now lies will change in an instant, and the beautiful triumph of the Church will come" (M 4.5, p. 31).

    This ecclesial faith of hers centreed above all on the Roman Pontiff. For Pius IX she had not only feelings of obedience and veneration but true devotion, since at the feet of this Pope she had felt confirmed, as has been said, in her charism as foundress and encouraged to leave the care of her children to God. In her writings she calls him "this holy Pope," "the great saint" (M 2, pp. 66, 69). After the occupation of Rome she thought of the Pope's situation: "The head of the Church imprisoned, Pius IX, my Father: oh! what anguish!" (M 1.2, p. 29).

    On January 9, 1876, she was again received in audience by Pius IX, and afterwards, full of emotion, she passed on to the sisters the Holy Father's words of affection and encouragement (L Circ 1876). The following year, in another circular signed by her together with Fr. Tornatore, she expressed herself in these terms:

    "He (Pius IX) has a singular affection for our Institute, because our Institute was raised up by the Lord in his Church to honor in a very special way that venerable Matron in whose womb the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of Mary was accomplished, from the definition of which mystery the Holy Father Pius IX derives that great glory by which he shines above all the Popes as the sun shines brighter than the stars. That is why our Institute, in these early days, has founded and is founding most of its houses in the Papal State and, so to speak, around his Throne, because between the Holy Father Pope Pius IX and our Institute there is a secret sympathy..." (L Circ. 1877).

    It is easy to understand the grief Mother Rosa felt on February 7, 1878, when, while at Spello, she received the sign of the death of her beloved Pius IX (M 4.5, p. 23f; Summ., p. 616). From that day on she would commend herself, and have the sisters commend themselves, to the intercession of the holy Pope in the needs of the Institute.

    Her enthusiasm for Pius IX, as popular as he was controversial, did not prevent her from showing the same devotion to his successor Leo XIII, as she expressed in the circular of January 1, 1879.

    It must not be forgotten, however, that while her personal relations with diocesan bishops and with Popes Pius IX and Leo XIII were easy and full of consolation, the same cannot be said of her dealings with the Roman dicasteries concerning the Institute's place in the structures of the Church. The foundress had to endure setbacks, misunderstandings and even harsh humiliations, which more than once sorely tested her unshakable trust in the hierarchical Church. This is how she puts it in her metaphorical language:

    "Having tied up the boat as well as I knew how, I tried to make my way to my Good in his great temple, to his Vicar. Oh! what a surprise! In such a sorry state, ragged as I was, a poor slave of the Lord, I kissed the foot and hand of his Vicar. O most humble sovereign!

    O mercy of God! The Vicar asks me about the little ship, wants it near him and prophesies its future to me. O my Savior! how eagerly I had run to fetch the little boat to bring it where the Vicar wanted! But a stormy sea rises, a contrary wind rages and dashes me against a reef... After a short struggle my little ship came out more beautiful... Brought to the feet of Peter, I could say nothing to him except to ask him to say many things to my God for me: that I was bringing the little boat to the feet of his Vicar, so that it might be incorporated into his Church" (TC, pp. 218-220).

    The first great trial was the order received in February 1872 from the Holy Office, through the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars and Cardinal Vannicelli, Protector of the Institute, to withdraw and burn all copies of the Rules and to remove the cofounder, Fr. Tornatore. Mother Rosa obeyed without delay; she stayed up all night to send the order to all the houses; the next day she wrote to the Cardinal's secretary:

    "May God's will be done upon our heads; and I, a miserable creature, with my head bowed to the ground, adore all his dispositions and submit to the will of the Church" (FIOCCHI, I, p. 232; Summ., p. 320).

    Another delicate moment was the situation created in 1881 when the general chapter rejected the amendments proposed by the Holy See, the most important of which was the establishment of a general council. The foundress bore, with God's help, the harsh rebuke of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. In a humble letter she acknowledged the fault unintentionally committed, and the chapter's action was retracted. It all ended with a letter from the same Cardinal praising the full submission of the superior general and her council to the dispositions of the Holy See (42).

    Mother Rosa felt compensated for so much bitterness in the audience granted her by Leo XIII in April 1885: the Pope questioned her at length about the Institute and was very pleased with what the Daughters of Saint Anne were doing. Comforted by the papal blessing, she came out of that audience "drunk with consolation" (FIOCCHI, II, p. 57f).

    The third and last great trial that further refined her fidelity to the hierarchical Church was the apostolic visitation of the Institute, begun on July 28, 1898, by the Benedictine abbot Dom Domenico Serafini by order of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; it had been prompted by certain unfounded accusations of administrative irregularities and by the printing of the volume Trials and Consolations, which had been reported to the Holy Office. When the visitor presented his credentials and explained the purpose of the measure, Mother Rosa could not control her emotion; she said through her tears: "I already know that I am good for nothing, that I ruin everything: so I resign here and now...." Then, encouraged by Dom Serafini himself, she recovered and cooperated with him in complete sincerity (FIOCCHI, II, pp. 179-188; Summ., p. 345). A month later, on August 30, 1898, thanking the Piacenza community for their tribute on her name day, she gave a very beautiful address to the religious and said, with a clear allusion to the trial she was undergoing:

    "Yes, love your Mother, love her in holy Church... Daughters, I want one promise from you on this day: that you be faithful to the Institute and to holy Mother Church. No, daughters, do not let slander, trouble and anguish make you falter in your holy vocation... I too was slandered, despised, mistreated: and not even the slightest thought against my holy vocation ever came to me..." (FIOCCHI, II, p. 277f).

    Death overtook the foundress while the apostolic visitation was still in progress. The visitor himself, by then a Cardinal, was invited to testify in the informative process of Rome and gave a sincere tribute to the Institute, which he knew well.

    She observed, and wanted others to observe, the same attitude of obedience and veneration towards the prelates of the dioceses where the Institute had houses. When it was necessary for the approval of the Constitutions, she had no difficulty in gathering laudatory letters of recommendation from many bishops who were satisfied with the life and services of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

    She was extremely demanding about respect for priests. In 1880 she sent a strong rebuke by letter to a novice mistress because she was not teaching the young women to show outward reverence towards God's ministers (L to Sr. A. Francesca Savignoni: 23-3-1880). She would not tolerate their being spoken ill of.

    "Jesus is jealous of his ministers"; he has reserved to himself the right to judge them (cf. L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: undated; to Emilia di Fitalia: 21-6-1893). On March 18, 1874, she wrote a page of great affliction, unable to calm her spirit after having spoken unfavorably of a priest, in secret, "to someone who could remedy certain scandals." She made acts of repentance and humiliation, "holding fast to Mother Church" (M 4.2, pp. 57-61).

    She urged the sisters to help parish priests with catechetical instruction and other pastoral needs, but without any payment (Summ., p. 484).

    Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, who directly witnessed Mother Rosa's reactions to the sufferings she had to bear, testified in the informative process:

    "Throughout her life, on the many occasions when churchmen caused her and her Institute displeasure and very serious opposition, the Servant of God made it a rule never to let others know anything that might give occasion to diminish the reputation of those churchmen" (Summ., p. 11).

    5. The Virgin Mary, most sweet Mother.

    Marian piety, tender and filial, occupies in Rosa Gattorno's religious life its theologically proper place, so to speak, indeed almost a secondary place compared with the reality of God and the centrality of the Redeemer.

    Even before becoming foundress she recited the Office of Our Lady (M 1.1, p. 11). She invoked her as Mother, as Advocate, as Teacher...; she turned to her in difficulties and battles (M 1.1, p. 19). Mary entered fully into her unitive experiences when she contemplated the Lord's Passion (M 1.1, p. 36), and also when she rejoiced in the triumph of the Resurrection. On Easter 1863 she addressed this fervent prayer to Mary:

    "Ah! Mary, most beloved Mother, remember this poor creature, who lies here below plunged in darkness, for you keep me with you so little and then I return to this miserable earth... O Mary! by the joy you feel today, free this poor creature from her chains..., and give me Love alone. May my life be forever to suffer and endure for Jesus... Ah! be my Teacher and teach me what I must do to make myself less displeasing to my dear Jesus and to pay the many debts I have incurred through my faults..." (M 1.1, p. 38f).

    On the eves of Marian feasts she used to spend the night "in contemplation, always with Mary" (M 1.1, p. 81), often favored with visions that left her greatly consoled. She writes in 1876:

    "I spent the night with my dear Mother Mary. She stayed beside me all night; she comforted me, and I felt something of peace, resignation and strength descend into me so that I could resume my work the next day. Now she exhorted me and gave me most beautiful lessons, now she assured me that what I was suffering was very dear to Jesus and that he was with me. O most sweet Mary!... The next day, full of vigor, nothing could cast me down... O Mary, my sweetness! you are always my comfort in the atrocious pains in which I find myself" (M 1.1, pp. 92f, 96).

    One day in May, having experienced Mary's presence as "a soothing dew" after throwing herself at her feet in a moment of "despair," she poured out her heart in expressions like these:

    "O Mary! through you I am saved, through you I am a religious! The fire of your Son's love, Mary! with your own hands you lit it many times in this heart of your Son. Oh! well then, Love, why do you not make me die of it?..." (M 4.4, p. 56f).

    From time to time similar outpourings of love for Our Lady burst forth from her burning heart:

    "Mary, most sweet and dearest Mother: I was and am yours! Ah! press me to Jesus so that I may die of him!" (M 4.4, p. 108)

    - "Mary, Mary! you are my life! Ask your servant, and she will always, always obey you" (M 4.5, p. 19f)

    - "My life, after my God" (M 5.3, p. 29)

    - "Mary, most holy Mary, Mother of my Love" (TC, p. 30).

    In her letters to the religious she urges them to place everything in Mary's hands, as she herself does, or to remember that the Sorrowful Mother suffered in her heart pains more atrocious than any a religious can meet.

    She ended almost all her journeys with a visit to some shrine of Our Lady. In her last years she made four visits to the Holy House of Loreto, where she would remain for hours, motionless in prayer, as if in ecstasy (Summ., p. 351).

    The first name given to the planned Institute, in Genoa, was Daughters of the Immaculate. When the name "Daughters of Saint Anne" was adopted in Piacenza, the foundress wanted the link with the Immaculate to remain in the name as well, as Fr. Tornatore also wished.

    At the foundress's own wish, the church of the Generalate in Rome was dedicated to Maria Mater gratiae et misericordiae. This was the title of the "Madonnina," a small image that the Venerable Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi had always carried with him and which later passed into the hands of Fr. Tornatore. Mother Rosa made it the object of her special devotion, placed it in the chapel of the motherhouse in Piacenza and, in gratitude for the healing she obtained on April 29, 1883, and for the help received in building the house in Rome, had it crowned by Bishop Scalabrini. When the church on Via Merulana was consecrated, the image was transferred there (43).

    6. Saint Anne, Mother of the Institute.

    Entrusting the direction of the new Institute to Fr. Tornatore meant a costly sacrifice for the foundress: having to change its name and adopt that of Daughters of Saint Anne.

    "I could in no way bring myself to love her and take her as my mother," she candidly admits, despite the vision she had had of the Immaculate and of Saint Anne (M 2, p. 57). But she soon let herself be won over by the cofounder's fervor for the Mother of the Mother of God.

    In fact it was the beginning of a form of spirituality with which she fully identified in her task as foundress. She chose to receive the habit on the feast of Saint Anne, July 26, 1867, and to take the name Anne, placing it before her baptismal name, an example followed by all the Daughters of Saint Anne.

    One may say that rather than a devotion centreed on the Saint as such, it is an aspect of Marian piety: for Mother Rosa, Saint Anne is worthy of veneration and enjoys a special power of intercession because in her womb the immaculate conception of the Mother of God took place; hence she and Fr. Tornatore wrote the Institute's full title in this form: Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate. Mary's Mother thus becomes the model for each of her daughters through her docility to God's plan and her care in nourishing and tending the child Mary even amid a mother's sufferings and worries. This was expressed in one of the leaflets intended to make the Institute known:

    "The proper aim that distinguishes the Daughters of Saint Anne... is to profess a very special devotion to glorious Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate... The Institute (professes) moreover, among other virtues, the compassion of Saint Anne's heart, by assisting the sick in their homes... Likewise they take in poor girls at risk, to keep them from losing their innocence and virtue: and here too they honor the care (Saint Anne) had for the Immaculate Child and the zeal that this care must have given the Saint to see all the young girls of the world innocent" (44).

    In her Memoirs she not only attributes a supernatural origin to the Institute's name but also recognizes as an infused gift the love she began to have for the Saint after her apparitions in Piacenza:

    "The holy Mother was beautiful as she caressed me. She came very close and communicated to me a love for her so strong that, I must confess, I could in no way bring myself to love her and take her as my Mother... Love for Saint Anne had penetrated me so strongly that all my reluctance vanished, and it grew so strong that I invoked her in all my needs and always found myself satisfied: in providence, on journeys, in everything..." (M 2, p. 57f).

    She feels supported, guided and enlightened by the holy Mother in every concern; she is convinced that the progress of God's Work is due to the help of such a teacher. But she also finds in her habitual closeness a kind of mirror that helps her discern when things are going well and when not:

    "My star, Saint Anne, marks the day for me every morning, because if I am to go through tribulations, she appears to me pale and sad; if there is to be a death, or things the sisters do that are not right and are against the holy Rule, she is covered with a black veil..." (M 4.5, p. 143f).

    She regarded Saint Anne as the first superior of the Institute; as a sign of this she tied the key of the Piacenza house to a small statue of the holy Mother (Summ., p. 606). In her annual circulars she ardently urges the sisters to devotion and love for the Saint, proposes her as the model of a true religious, and insists on the effectiveness of her protection over the Institute's path: "She rules it, defends it, governs it" (L Circ: 1876, 17-7-1899). She wants her invoked in every community, her image to preside not only over every chapel of the Institute but over every activity of the sisters, and the sisters to strive to spread devotion to her among the faithful.

    The communal expression the Daughters of Saint Anne repeat very often is the aspiration Blessed be, etc. We read in the circular of 1877:

    "This aspiration contains a profession of faith by which we believe that Mary, in the womb of our holy Mother, was conceived Immaculate in the first instant of her conception... And since this aspiration is almost continuous from morning to night, through it the Institute makes, as it were, a continual act of faith in the immaculate conception of Mary."

    Mother Rosa did not fail, however, to warn the sisters against the danger of a shallow devotionalism. Saint Anne is not the goal of true piety: the same maternal role she had in her life, that of giving Mary to the world and, through Mary, giving Jesus to the world, she exercises now as well; if she draws the affection of her daughters, it is to make the love of Mary and Jesus grow in them (cf. L Circ 1887).

    "How many incidents I could point out to show you how the holy Mother, Mother of the great Mother of God, wants to be invoked by her daughters in their needs and loved as a Mother who leads us to the great most holy Virgin and to the blessed God! She loves us, so that in these two hearts of Jesus and Mary you may all be purified, consumed in this most sweet love" (L Circ. 27-5-1892).

    Indeed, I would venture to say that with the passing years one notices in the foundress's writings almost a need to ground genuinely her ideas on Saint Anne's role in the Institute's spirituality, to find a more theological setting.

    Some might consider strange and without biblical support a spirituality inspired by Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate, but devotion to this great Saint is fully grounded in the veneration the Church has paid for centuries to the Mother of the Mother of God, especially in the East, where a liturgy and iconography of great expressive value have developed (45).

    The Special Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne made a deeper study of the biblical basis of the Institute's spirituality: Saint Joachim and Saint Anne are seen in the line of the anawim who awaited the Lord, among whom "Mary, Mother of the Lord, stands out" (cf. Spiritualità di Avvento, p. 15-19).

    7. Saint Francis of Assisi, "our Father."

    Rosa Gattorno knew how to combine her eminently contemplative life with a concrete and creative piety, which she passed on to her religious. She dedicated January to the eternal Father, March to Saint Joseph, May to the Virgin Mary, June to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, July to Saint Anne.

    Her devotion to Saint Joseph was linked to her faith in divine Providence; she called him "my dear protector." She invoked Saint Michael the Archangel as her defender in dangers, especially in the struggle against the demons, and as her guide on journeys.

    But the saint to whom she felt closest, after Saint Anne, was Saint Francis of Assisi. In the church of the Generalate in Rome she had an altar dedicated to each of the Institute's patrons: Saint Anne, Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Francis of Paola and Saint Michael.

    There is a connection between her longing to reach full transformation into Christ crucified through love and suffering and her devotion to the stigmatized saint of La Verna, almost an evangelical and mystical harmony.

    In 1858, as a sign of the new life she had begun, she took the cord of Saint Francis. In 1861 she put on the Franciscan habit, "like that of the friars, of the same cloth, obtained from them." She wore it day and night under her usual clothes, at great sacrifice (M 1.1, pp. 15, 8).

    From then on the seraphic Father became the spur and model of her self-giving to Love by the way of total stripping. She prayed in these terms:

    "My Love, consume me! It is all yours, O my Love! it is true, for if there were anything that did not please you and was not yours, oh! tell me, and I will at once say like my Father Saint Francis: that if he had anything that was not God's, he would get rid of it at once. O my Love! and I would burn it!" (M 1.1, p. 11) (46).

    On September 24, 1861, while staying in the country at S. Francesco d'Albaro, she made her profession in the Third Order of Saint Francis. "And I chose this good Father," she notes, "as my advocate and the protector of my soul" (M 1.1, p. 13).

    At first she would have liked to place her Institute within the great Franciscan family, with the title "Daughters of Mary Immaculate, Minims of Saint Francis of Assisi." And although, as we have seen, she agreed to the cofounder's wish to place it under the protection and guidance of Saint Anne, she did not mean thereby to set aside Saint Francis either from her personal spirituality or from the commitment of God's Work.

    In the vision she had at that juncture her seraphic Father had appeared to her together with Mary Immaculate and Saint Anne (M 2, p. 58). One of her favorite aspirations was the well-known one of the Saint of Assisi: "My Good, my All" (M 4.1, p. 102). Every year she celebrated with fervor his feast (October 4) and that of his Stigmata (September 17), receiving great consolations on them (cf. M 1.2, p. 79; 5.1, p. 21f; 11.1, p. 23). In 1880 she wanted to prepare for the feast of the Stigmata with a scourging to the point of blood; weak as she was, she had to ask for strength through the Saint's intercession. The next day she had such a fire of love that she was obliged to withdraw to her little room:

    "O Love! I took my Crucified in my arms and, as usual, laid my head on his side, and there, what did I feel? You, my dear seraphic Father Saint Francis, could tell it, your tongue could explain it, but I cannot!" (M 5.1, p. 24).

    She dedicated her Wednesday fast to Saint Francis. She invoked his help very often. In her little room in Piacenza she always had an oleograph of the Saint, which was very dear to her. To encourage her religious to accept difficulties and sufferings, she reminded them of the seraphic Father's couplet already quoted:

    "So great is the good I hope for - that every pain is a delight to me." In a letter to Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte she tried to justify her neglect of her body in illness by the example of her model: "Saint Francis, what did he do with his body? I have done nothing but try to imitate him as much as I could" (L 12-1-1889).

    In 1871 she had a strange foretelling of her death, at which moment she wished to have the consolation of seeing herself a daughter of Saint Francis: "My Love came to console me. He showed me what will happen at my death...: the tertiary's habit will be my habit, and the rest that of Saint Anne" (M 1.1, p. 164).

    She always felt bound to the sons of Saint Francis. In her Genoa years she was on familiar terms with the popular Capuchin lay brother Saint Francis of Camporosso († 1866), who is said to have foretold how much she would have to suffer to achieve success as foundress (Summ., p. 315); she had real veneration for him; in the Memoirs she calls him "my Fra Francesco"; she had some apparitions of him (M 4.1, p. 5).

    In Naples she met a Fra Angelo, a Franciscan lay brother deeply in love with the Child Jesus; she often spoke with him. She was also in contact with the Venerable Ludovico da Casoria, a Reformed Franciscan of remarkable social initiatives († 1885); at his death Mother Rosa wrote: "How beautiful is the soul of Father da Casoria! Oh, how great he is in heaven!" (M 5.3, p. 81; 7, p. 4).

    The Institute's expansion to America, with the Bolivian mission, began with an invitation from the superior of the Franciscans, Fr. Simpliciano della Trinità, who turned to the foundress because in his view the Daughters of Saint Anne were also "daughters of Saint Francis" (FIOCCHI, II, p. 15).

    The Capuchin missionaries entered Eritrea as chaplains to the Daughters of Saint Anne, after much urging by Mother Rosa; when the apostolic prefecture was later established, there was close collaboration with them.

    For several years, as mentioned above, Mother Rosa's confessor was the minister general of the Franciscans, Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro. Finally, in her last moments she was assisted by her last confessor, the Capuchin Fr. Vincenzo d'Alatri, from whom she received the Anointing of the Sick (FIOCCHI, II, p. 293f).

    In 1873, when the misfortunes of the suppression of religious Orders in Catholic countries were still being felt and there was an atmosphere of pessimism about their future, Mother Rosa foresaw by higher light the glorious revival of the sons of Saint Francis with the dawning of better days for the Church:

    "I saw in the distance peace for the Church and, moreover, the fine vocations that would come to the Orders of Saint Francis, and likewise among women religious; but it was very far off..." (M 4.1, p. 16).

Rosa Gattorno's life demonstrates the Christian principle that true charity has two inseparable dimensions: one that has God as its object and goal, the other that extends to all people, indeed to all beings.

We already know how her spirit and heart burned with this twofold impulse of love. Let us now turn our attention to apostolic dynamism, an essential demand both of love for the Redeemer and of love for one's neighbor.

1. Zeal for the good of her spiritual daughters.

Freed by God's will from family ties, yet without extinguishing the flame of love for her own, Mother Rosa lived intensely for her new religious family, loving each Daughter of Saint Anne with a mother's heart, a love expressed in attentive concern, care, sharing in their personal situations, and longing for their spiritual progress and their fidelity to the commitments made at profession.

Above all she wanted to see fraternal unity in the communities, enlivened by a generous, understanding and welcoming charity, to the point of "giving one's life" in the service of others (cf. L to Sr. Francesca Camisa: 23-4-1867).

In her letters to superiors she expresses her joy when she hears that such a climate of unity exists:

"You cannot believe how much consolation I felt on hearing how well you all get along together. O blessed Charity! Well done, dear daughter! May God pour his choicest blessings upon your head!" (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 28-8-1880).

She suffers, on the other hand, when she sees divisions, grumbling, an atmosphere of suspicion and distrust. She rebukes one superior for not putting an end to grumbling, which she herself encourages by listening to accusations and impassioned reports (L to Sr. A. Sismondini: 9-4-1880). In the circular letter of August 20, 1893, we find harsh words for superiors who, instead of bearing difficult sisters with love, write to the superior general: "Change her for me, change her for me!" Likewise for those who cannot keep their sisters' problems and faults secret and do not rather help them gently to amend.

Her heart always lives among the sisters. In one letter she tells how, returning from Sicily, she met a holy religious who, after looking at her attentively, said to her traveling companions: "Only half of Mother came back from Sicily; the other half she left in Sicily." And she comments: "He spoke the very truth: I confirmed it to myself. So, dear daughters, I am and will be with you!" (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 26-3-1885).

She sympathizes with troubled sisters and teaches others to do so, sharing their difficulties with expressions of unspeakable tenderness, yet without sentimentality. She writes to one of them:

"I carry your sufferings with me and always make an offering of them to God, so that one day they may shine upon your head and you may occupy with greater glory that beautiful place Jesus has prepared for you. Courage!" (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 10-10-1889).

And to another:

"You cannot believe how sorry I am to see you so distressed. I will not have it! The trials that hurt us most are those we feel, but for that very reason we must not dwell on them. No! a generous offering to God, and that is enough!... Courage, dear daughter, for I share deeply in your sorrow; but God permits it so that we may detach ourselves from everything and belong more and more to him... Do not fear, for I am always with you!" (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 13-7-1887).

Her concern for the health of individual sisters becomes almost a recurring theme in her letters. First of all for their spiritual health: she feels real anxiety at the mere thought that one of them might be unfaithful to the Lord. Writing to a superior in America about a young professed sister in crisis, she orders her to do whatever is necessary for her, transferring her wherever appropriate, sparing no journeys: that vocation must be saved (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 29-10-1898).

Regarding care for bodily health she shows great solicitude. She urges them not to overdo apostolic work and household chores. She wants to know about everyone's health, especially those suffering from some illness; for the seriously ill she wants news every day.

She who all her life tormented her body with penances and fasts is anxious about the "excesses" the sisters may commit in penitential practices. It is worth more before God, she teaches, to have good health so as to be useful to the community and to apostolic works than to render oneself useless through indiscreet privations and excessive work. "Your health comes first, then the rest," she wrote to Sr. A. Pierina Della Valle (20-8-1895). Above all, she urges superiors, never economize at the expense of the sisters' health (cf. L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 9-5-1867; to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi: undated; to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 17-10-1885).

There is, however, no conflict between poverty and charity. In a circular of 1883 she makes this observation:

"In our visits we find that thrifty superiors keep the sisters better fed and clothed than those who are wasteful. So we recommend economy, both for love of poverty and out of devotion to one's own Institute."

In 1885 she wanted to set up a "fine infirmary" in Sicily, where the sisters of the region could be cared for, in order to spare the sick the strain of transfers (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 29-6-1885).

What she recommended to superiors she practiced herself.

"She visited the sick sisters even at night and when no one noticed" (Summ., p. 359). And when human remedies did not relieve the illness, she turned to divine help and obtained miraculous healing, as happened more than once. Yet she knew that illness, too, becomes a true gift of God, a privileged instrument of purification:

"Illnesses are sent by God, and he is pleased to visit us through them. Better illness than wickedness. Illnesses bring us closer to God and draw graces upon the houses..." (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 24-8-1889). (47).

2. Active charity towards those in need.

Purified by suffering and humiliation in her widowhood, Rosa discovered, so to speak, her own identity in her dedication to the sick poor, caring for them both in hospital and at home: in them she found the image of her Crucified, who now filled her heart. Once foundress, she would have liked, through the zeal of the Daughters of Saint Anne, to meet every bodily and spiritual need and every social ill, opening homes for the elderly, kindergartens, nurseries for infants, foundling homes, assistance to prisoners, refuges for penitent women, schools for the poor... (cf. FIOCCHI, II, pp. 145-166, 271).

She called the Daughters of Saint Anne "poor servants of the poor" (L to Emilia di Fitalia: 12-5-1893). Her preference was for the sick poor; in the various foundations the first work of charity was almost always home care for the sick; even in those whose aim was schooling, free care for the sick was not to be lacking. The cholera of 1867 was a kind of trial by fire for the new Institute, and the more widespread epidemic of 1884-1887 was almost its public proving: the Daughters of Saint Anne gave themselves heroically, especially in Naples and Sicily; some died victims of the contagion (FIOCCHI, I, pp. 153-158, 179f; II, 69-89).

The foundress's legitimate pride in her daughters' heroism is reflected in the circular letters of these years.

Those were also times when the work of mercy of feeding the hungry had a very concrete meaning, even in Europe: the soup distributed in so many convents and shelters, especially in industrialized cities, where a defenseless proletariat, the product of capitalist liberalism, struggled every day to survive. We read in the circular of January 31, 1880:

"God's mercy has called us, his ministers, to relieve so many wretched people, giving them food and clothing every day. In the Motherhouse alone 3,000 beggars are fed daily with good, well-seasoned soup. What a grace this is, sisters! What a sign of the Lord's special love for us!"

In all, the Daughters of Saint Anne distributed 4,522 bowls of soup daily at three places in the city of Piacenza (L to Sr. A. Letizia Sordi: 15-1-1880).

She not only encouraged the sisters to spend themselves in initiatives responding to social realities but also spurred on the Institute's benefactors and friends. In her letters to the Princess of Fitalia she insistently urges this spiritual daughter of hers to be generous towards "the wretched in soul and body." On August 18, 1892, she wrote asking her to help a poor mother of four abandoned by her husband. On November 15, 1896, she expressed her concern for so many poor people in the coming winter, which promised to be harsh. Again on September 13, 1897: "If you do not help me, what will become of my poor this winter?"

Yet she knew how to distinguish mere philanthropy from authentic Christian charity, which gives with love and humility, without condescension or bureaucratic structures. She wrote in the circular of January 20, 1892:

"Be humble with the poor; always remember that you are the last and most wretched of all the creatures who serve the Church and have the good fortune to belong to her."

She could not bear any harshness towards the sick. She wrote to a superior about some sisters who were treating them badly: "Tell those wretches that they are a disgrace to the house and to the whole Institute" (48).

Her spirituality of the sick and the poor sprang from faith in Jesus' words: Whatever you did for one of these least brothers of mine, you did for me (Mt 25:40) (cf. L Circ year 1876).

At the beginning of her new life, in 1858, this faith had been a real experience, like that of Saint Francis of Assisi when he kissed the leper, overcoming his revulsion, and then found sweet what had before been bitter to him. Rosa kissed the ulcers of the sick and sometimes even passed her tongue over them (FIOCCHI, I, p. 43).

Having found Jesus in those who suffer, she found it all the sweeter to contemplate the wounded Redeemer himself. One night, tired after a whole day spent serving the sick, she was rapt in ecstasy and felt the consolation of sucking the wound on the Lord's shoulder: coming to herself, she felt completely reinvigorated (M 1.1, p. 59f). Another time, in 1864, after a similar experience while contemplating the Lord's Passion, she wrote:

"My soul was so strengthened that, returning to my work, I felt neither distress nor the smell of my sick. It was sweet to serve them, and I felt I was doing everything in my God" (M 2, p. 107).

In 1867, while in Rome, she went to the hospital. She wanted to satisfy her craving to suck the sores of the sick, but had to desist, both so as not to attract attention and so as not to be rapt in ecstasy by the spiritual sweetness (M 1.1, p. 61).

She taught the same spirituality to the Daughters of Saint Anne, namely, to ground charity in seeing Christ in the needy and the suffering. That same year she wrote to the sisters at the hospital in Cento:

"Take comfort, you who toil for your Jesus. Ah! you are always conversing with Jesus, because in touching those sick people with charity you touch Jesus... Jesus is found in those sick creatures. Ah! what a thought, my daughters! I assure you that I feel I am dying with the desire to come and be with you, to share in your works of charity..."

- "Seeing Jesus in the sick, how easy you will find meditation on the Passion of Jesus!" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 23-4-1867; 7-1867).

It is interesting, however, to note a development with the passing years, almost a purification of the motives of apostolic charity, the effect of a higher identification with the supreme Good. On January 18, 1875, Mother Rosa made the following profound self-examination:

"Little by little, creatures are becoming for me something to cultivate and love, no longer as I know I still felt before, with a sensible compassion for their ills, or wanting them all to be holy, yes, but regarding them as if, in the help and good I did them, or at least thought I did them, I found in them a certain pleasure that it seemed to me the charity shown them ought to bring them.

Now I find nothing, nothing: purely my Good. I cannot look at even the smallest created thing with a simple glance unless I first turn that glance, too, to him..." (M 4.3, p. 18f).

We find a similar reflection ten years later, on July 17, 1885 (M 5.3, p. 109f).

Among the works of mercy there is yet another: instructing the ignorant. The apostolate of education in schools for the poor, serving the sons and daughters of the poor, appeared as a form of apostolic zeal in the very first years of the Institute, a service to society that would in time acquire considerable importance. In this field of charity too, Mother Rosa took care to give the Daughters of Saint Anne fully evangelical guidelines on how to treat the girls, with due respect for the person, always taking Mother Saint Anne as their model. But she soon became aware of the danger threatening the Institute's spirit if the sisters assigned to teaching began to feel they were of a higher rank.

In one of her circulars she expresses her concern at seeing that some of them seek to become "teachers":

"Oh! if this desire of yours came from a sublime sense of evangelization, of nourishing those hearts with the catechism and so making them strong in our holy Religion! But unfortunately there is much to deplore on this point" (L Circ.: 20-1-1892).

3. Missionary universalism.

Rosa Gattorno's heart was a volcano in constant activity, insatiable in love. Here is one of her outpourings in a letter to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

"I would like to draw the whole world, give to everyone, feed everyone. Oh! if only I could make gold flow from my veins for the poor! Do you know what I would do? I would draw it out myself, vein by vein, until they were dry. Oh! would I be satisfied? No! it is too ardent!..." (L undated, no. 76).

One could compile a fine anthology of the outpourings of her longing to make her dear Good known and loved, which leap out from the pages of her spiritual diary. Here are a few:

"My Good, what can I do to make you known to the whole world? Oh! how many there are who do not know you! and those who have known you flee from you because they have never seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry aloud for all to come and love you" (Year 1862: M 1.1, p. 30).

"Oh! why do not all love you? Do you see, O my Good, the burning thirst I have to save souls?" (M 1.1, p. 33).

"O my Love! make use for once of this wretched instrument of yours to revive faith and convert sinners!"

- "All you souls, come! Ah! love Jesus, do not offend him!... I would have run through all the streets crying out for people to love Jesus. I threw myself face down on the ground and begged the eternal Father earnestly to let me die a martyr to save the souls he has redeemed. Am I not your instrument? (Year 1867: M 1.1, pp. 60, 119).

"O my Love! how I burn with the desire to make you known and loved by all! May your name be blessed by every tongue. My God! Oh! if only I could make everyone feel what I feel!" (M 1.2, p. 87).

Many of these outpourings were committed to paper after some of her most intimate experiences of the great mysteries communicated to her by infused light. She then thinks that so many others could share in such a good. On Easter 1863, after a vision that filled her with consolation, she wrote: "O Love! why do you not let unbelievers see it a little?" (M 1.1, p. 186f).

She often expresses her longing to go out into the world to convert sinners, to suffer for them, to die a martyr for the salvation of the world, to see God loved by all.

When she was about to present the text of the Rules to the Pope in June 1871, while a shadow of harsh uncertainty weighed on her spirit, a joyful future of missionary splendor appeared on the horizon of her faith:

"This horizon seems very dark for us, but the right hand of our eternal Father can dispel everything in an instant, and the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, can enjoy the most beautiful light throughout Catholicism and carry it to shine in the most idolatrous lands, and there plant the standard of Saint Anne!" (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 2-6-1871).

She would like to make every Daughter of Saint Anne a spokeswoman for Jesus, to make all people hear the message of the Love that saves; she wished all of them had the gift she experiences when she feels herself a mere instrument of the One who makes her speak.

She wrote to her close friend Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

"Jesus will put words on your tongue that you yourself will not know how you pronounced... Love, and remember that it was Jesus speaking in your heart and you were his echo, another" (L undated, no. 76).

What matters above all is to evangelize by one's life (L Circ 20-8-1895). One of the sisters testifies at the informative process: "She wanted and required us to act as missionaries in the hospitals, first by our bearing, then by charity and, finally, by word" (Summ., p. 650).

Mother Rosa's apostolic heart knew two moments of deep joy: one when she gave her motherly embrace to the sixteen sisters of the first expedition, which left for Latin America on November 23, 1878, a promise of rapid expansion on that continent; the other on the day she presented to Leo XIII the four members of the first mission to East Africa, in November 1886.

In her many letters to the missionary sisters one feels her heart beating with a kind of holy envy of their good fortune in being able to toil and suffer in the vanguard of the Kingdom of God. She would have liked to have enough Daughters of Saint Anne to meet all the requests that reached her. She wrote to the superior in Eritrea, Sr. A. Pierina Della Valle:

"My God, how painful it is to have no sisters!... Come on, courage! I wish I were ten years younger and strong; I would go and work as a cobbler! But I am very old and always good for very little" (L 8-11-1895).

From Saint Francis of Assisi she had learned to see the missionary vocation as a free response to divine inspiration; the superiors of the houses in Italy were to keep her informed of sisters who showed a "vocation to go to the missions," but were to add "an exact and scrupulous report on their conduct," so as to ensure that missionaries were well chosen (L Circ. 25-3-1887, 23-4-1893).
